Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), and results were synthesized without meta-analysis because substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity made a pooled estimate inappropriate. Structured exercise showed the most consistent favorable signal, although effects were generally smaller or less certain in trials using active comparators. Sleep/circadian and bright-light interventions showed possible short-term benefits in selected studies, but findings varied by intervention, comparator, and assessment time, and sustained benefits were inconsistent. Evidence for multicomponent lifestyle programs was sparse, and no eligible randomized trial evaluated a whole-diet intervention alone as an adjunct to antidepressant treatment. Overall certainty of the evidence was low to very low because of risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Lifestyle-based interventions may provide additional benefit as adjuncts to antidepressant treatment, particularly structured exercise and selected sleep/circadian interventions; however, the magnitude and durability of benefit remain uncertain. Substitution of lifestyle interventions for antidepressant medication was not evaluated in this review.

title: Disentangling semaglutide's effects on motivation in major depressive disorder: A mediation analysis.
text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) improve effort-based decision-making in major depressive disorder (MDD), but whether this reflects their metabolic effects is unknown. We examined whether this effect is statistically mediated by metabolic change. Exploratory, post-hoc secondary analysis of a 16-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (NCT04466345) of adjunctive oral semaglutide versus placebo in 72 adults with MDD and overweight/obesity. The Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task yielded an effort-discounting parameter (k) via a subjective-value model. Mediation by change in body mass index, percent body fat, glycated hemoglobin, and insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) was tested using bootstrapped mediation models (n = 46-53) and generalized estimating equations (GEE; n = 33-36), with depressive-symptom and cognition change as competing mediators. No adjustment was made for multiple comparisons. Semaglutide significantly reduced effort discounting (GEE treatment × visit β = -1.78; 95% CI, -3.34 to -0.23; P = .025). Modeling metabolic change did not attenuate this effect; the total indirect effect was opposite in sign to the direct effect (+2.04; direct, -2.93), a suppression pattern that did not survive exclusion of high-influence observations. Depressive-symptom and cognitive change did not account for the effect; reverse models showed no mediation of metabolic improvement by Δk. Semaglutide's effect on effort-based decision-making in MDD was not statistically mediated by the metabolic variables assessed, nor by change in depressive symptoms or cognition. These exploratory findings are consistent with a weight-independent effect but do not establish a central mechanism. Limitations include the post-hoc design, small effective sample, unadjusted comparisons, and functional unblinding.

title: Peripheral Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor Changes and Clinical Response to Electroconvulsive Therapy and Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Major Depressive Disorder: A Systematic Review.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading contributor to the global burden of disease, and a substantial proportion of patients experience inadequate responses to conventional treatments. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a key regulator of neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity, has been investigated as a potential biomarker of antidepressant response. However, its clinical relevance following brain stimulation remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluated changes in peripheral BDNF concentrations and their association with clinical outcomes following electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in adults with MDD. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, and searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE (Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online), PsycINFO, and LILACS (Latin America and the Caribbean Literature on Health Sciences). Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria, including two randomized controlled trials and nine non-randomized investigations. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, a meta-analysis was not performed, and findings were synthesized narratively. Peripheral BDNF responses varied across interventions, biological matrices, and sampling intervals. While many studies reported increased serum or plasma BDNF following ECT, others documented substantial clinical improvement without corresponding biomarker changes. Evidence following rTMS was less consistent, with insufficient data to establish a reliable association between BDNF changes and antidepressant response. Overall, peripheral BDNF changes did not consistently parallel clinical improvement, and current evidence does not support their use as a standalone biomarker of antidepressant response. Further adequately powered studies with standardized biomarker measurements and longitudinal clinical assessments are warranted.

title: Association of neurotransmitter-based polygenic scores with antidepressant treatment outcomes in patients with major depressive disorder.
text: Biologically informed polygenic scores (PGSs) may help interpret genetic associations with treatment outcomes. Here, we computed neurotransmitter-based PGSs (NeuroPGSs) for patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and assessed their association with SSRI treatment outcomes. By targeting genetic variants involved in key neurotransmission pathways, we developed PGSs for serotonergic (5228), gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA, 4103), dopaminergic (7061), and glutamatergic (5690) variants. We leveraged data from two cohorts of patients who received SSRIs for at least 4 weeks: the International SSRI Pharmacogenomics Consortium (ISPC) and the Pharmacogenomics Research Network Antidepressants Medication Pharmacogenomics Study (PGRN-AMPS). Treatment response was defined as ≥50% reduction from baseline depression symptoms, measured using 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD-17) in ISPC and 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS-C16) in PGRN-AMPS. Remission was defined as HRSD-17 ≤7 (ISPC) or QIDS-C16≤5 (PGRN-AMPS). The association between each NeuroPGS and antidepressant response or remission was evaluated using logistic regression models, adjusting for age, sex and five genetic principal components, with statistical significance determined at Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p<0.05. The GABAergic-based PGS was associated with SSRI response (aOR per SD = 1.45, 95%CI: 1.14-1.85). Patients with the highest GABAergic PGS (10th decile) had 2.59-fold higher odds of response (95%CI: 1.46-4.60) compared to those with the lowest decile (1st decile). These exploratory findings support further evaluation of NeuroPGSs; independent replication and assessment of incremental predictive value are needed before clinical application.
source: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences

title: Drug cost structure of psychotropic medications in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder: A multicenter study in Japan.
text: Psychotropic polypharmacy is common in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (MDD), but the category-level contribution of psychotropic medications to drug costs remains unclear. In this study, our primary objective was to describe drug costs by category within schizophrenia and MDD. We estimated daily psychotropic drug costs using 2021 discharge prescription data from the Effectiveness of Guidelines for Dissemination and Education in Psychiatric Treatment project, including 2923 patients with schizophrenia and 1535 with MDD in Japan. For each medication, the daily dose was multiplied by a market-share-weighted average drug price per milligram, calculated using data for brand-name and generic formulations. Costs were aggregated by medication category. In schizophrenia, antipsychotics were the dominant cost category, accounting for 87.6% of total drug costs. In MDD, antidepressants were the largest cost category, accounting for 58.9%, followed by anxiolytics/hypnotics and antipsychotics. Total daily drug cost was significantly higher in schizophrenia than in MDD (685.3 vs. 333.2 JPY/day), whereas anxiolytic/hypnotic costs were significantly higher in MDD than in schizophrenia despite lower total drug costs. These findings indicate distinct disease-specific drug cost structures and quantify the contributions of both main and adjunctive medication categories to total drug costs. These findings may provide useful information for considering medication costs in clinical practice.

title: Characterizing the efficacy of zuranolone across patient subgroups and symptom domains in Japanese patients with major depressive disorder: a pooled analysis of two placebo-controlled trials.
text: Zuranolone has been reported to reduce the 17-item Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HAM-D17) total score as early as Day 3 in Japanese patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), with the reduction in the HAM-D17 total score being maintained after the treatment period. This post hoc pooled analysis aimed to evaluate the treatment effects of zuranolone across baseline characteristics and to characterize how changes in specific symptom domains-core, anxiety, and insomnia-were associated with the early reduction in the HAM-D17 total score and its subsequent trajectory, using pooled data from two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials. Data from the Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials were combined for efficacy and safety analyses. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either oral zuranolone or placebo daily for 14 days and followed up for 6 weeks. The endpoints included the change from baseline in the HAM-D17 total score, response and remission rates, subgroup analyses, and subscale scores (core, anxiety, and insomnia) and their relative contributions to the between-group difference (zuranolone vs. placebo) in the HAM-D17 total score. The pooled full-analysis set included 284 and 278 participants in the zuranolone and placebo groups, respectively. The treatment effects were consistent across subgroups defined by baseline severity, sex, episode recurrence, and other characteristics. The HAM-D17 subscale analyses indicated reductions in scores across the core, anxiety, and insomnia subscales during the treatment period, with reductions in the insomnia subscale score accounting for the largest between-group difference. During the follow-up period, the reduction in the insomnia subscale score tended to decrease, whereas reductions in the core and anxiety subscale scores were relatively maintained. Zuranolone showed consistent treatment effects regardless of baseline characteristics. During the treatment period, early improvement in depressive symptoms was accompanied by improvements across all symptom domains, and improvements in core and anxiety symptom domains appeared to be relatively maintained during the follow-up period. These symptom domain-specific temporal profiles could suggest patterns of antidepressant response and symptom change following treatment with zuranolone. Given the exploratory nature of this analysis, these findings should be interpreted descriptively and require confirmation in future hypothesis-driven studies.

title: Glutamatergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder: From receptor and glial abnormalities to circuit pathology and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies.
text: Major depressive disorder is a heterogeneous psychiatric disorder that cannot be fully explained by classical monoamine-deficiency models. Increasing evidence indicates that glutamatergic dysfunction provides a central framework for linking molecular, glial, synaptic, and circuit-level abnormalities in depression. This narrative review focuses on glutamatergic dysregulation as the organizing mechanism of major depressive disorder. We summarize core abnormalities involving context-dependent N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor dysfunction, impaired α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity, altered metabotropic glutamate receptor signaling, and disrupted astrocytic excitatory amino acid transporter 2-mediated glutamate clearance. These changes converge on excitation-inhibition imbalance, leading to unstable cortical-limbic activity and contributing to emotional dysregulation, anhedonia, cognitive impairment, and impaired stress adaptation. We further discuss upstream mechanisms that regulate glutamatergic dysfunction, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor/mammalian target of rapamycin signaling, neuroinflammation, epigenetic regulation, and microbiota-gut-brain axis-related peripheral crosstalk. At the circuit level, we emphasize abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex-amygdala, amygdala-nucleus accumbens, prefrontal cortex-hippocampus, and lateral habenula pathways. We also consider how monoaminergic and opioid systems modulate glutamate-dependent synaptic and reward-circuit plasticity. Finally, we review therapeutic implications, including ketamine and related N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor modulators, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor facilitation, astrocyte-targeted strategies, anti-inflammatory interventions, circuit-based neuromodulation, and biomarker-guided patient stratification. By centering diverse pathological findings around glutamatergic dysfunction, this review provides a focused mechanistic framework for understanding major depressive disorder and developing precision, mechanism-based treatments.

title: Therapeutic Processes in Virtual Reality-Based Avatar Therapy for Treatment-Resistant Major Depressive Disorder: A Qualitative Analysis of Patients' Experiences.
text: The therapeutic benefits of virtual reality-based avatar therapy (VRT) compared with conventional psychotherapies remain unknown in individuals with treatment-resistant major depressive disorder (TRD). Accordingly, this study aimed to explore patients' lived experience of VRT to identify perceived therapeutic processes and benefits, better understand how virtual reality and dialogue with an avatar contribute to therapeutic change and examine how these experiences differed from those associated with conventional psychotherapeutic approaches. A total of 12 individuals with TRD who had completed 8-12 weekly VRT sessions (mean 10.75 sessions) after previously receiving at least two conventional psychotherapies were selected from a clinical trial. Semi-structured interviews conducted following completion of the VRT were analysed using an inductive qualitative content analysis approach. Six themes describing the therapeutic processes underlying VRT were identified: immersive role-play, putting theory into practice, the structure of therapy, emotional investment, an atypical therapeutic stance and externalization of internal processes. In addition, three perceived benefits emerged from these processes: integration of therapeutic concepts into daily life, development of mentalization capacities and enhanced self-determination. Finally, confrontation emerged as a transversal theme linking both the therapeutic processes and their perceived benefits. These findings suggest that VRT combines therapeutic processes common to conventional psychotherapies with distinctive features that may influence how benefits are experienced by patients. Future research should examine whether these distinctive processes account for VRT's added therapeutic value and contribute to clinical improvement.

title: Efficacy of Lumateperone 42 mg in Major Depressive Disorder: Subgroup Analysis of a Phase 3 Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
text: Objective: Lumateperone is an FDA-approved atypical antipsychotic to treat schizophrenia, bipolar I or II depression, and major depressive disorder (MDD). Post hoc analyses of a randomized, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Study 501) evaluated the efficacy of lumateperone 42 mg adjunctive to antidepressant therapy (ADT) in demographic and clinical subgroups of patients with MDD with inadequate ADT response. Methods: Adults with DSM-5 criteria for MDD with inadequate response to 1-2 courses of ADT, Montgomery- Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) Total score ≥24, Clinical Global Impression Scale-Severity (CGI-S) score ≥4, and Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology-Self-Report 16-item (QIDS-SR-16) score ≥14 were randomized 1:1 to 6-week oral lumateperone 42 mg+ADT or placebo+ADT. Efficacy was evaluated in the overall population and patient subgroups by demographic (age, sex, race, ethnicity, and region) and baseline disease characteristics (MADRS Total score, ADT type, number of ADT failures [in current episode and lifetime], and presence of anxious distress). Results: The modified intent-to-treat population comprised 481 patients (lumateperone+ADT, n = 239; placebo+ADT, n = 242). Lumateperone+ADT significantly improved MADRS Total score (least squares mean difference [LSMD], -4.9; P < .0001), CGI-S score (LSMD, -0.7; P < .0001), and QIDS-SR-16 Total score (LSMD, -2.4; P < .0001) at Day 43 versus placebo+ADT. Lumateperone+ADT significantly improved MADRS Total score (P < .01) across all demographic subgroups and baseline disease severity versus placebo+ADT. Significant improvements (P < .05) in CGI-S, QIDS-SR-16 Total scores, and MADRS response and remission rates were also observed across most subgroups. Conclusion: Lumateperone+ADT demonstrated robust efficacy over placebo+ADT across a broad range of demographic and clinical subgroups of patients with MDD. Clinical Trials Registration. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04985942. Prim Care Companion CNS Disord 2026;28(6):26m04289. Author affiliations are listed at the end of this article.
source: The primary care companion for CNS disorders

title: Intravenous Ketamine or Esketamine in Adolescents With Major Depressive Disorder: A Systematic Review.
text: The therapeutic efficacy and safety of intravenous ketamine or esketamine in adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD) remain insufficiently defined. This systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) aimed to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of intravenous ketamine or esketamine in this population. A comprehensive search of four international databases (PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library) was conducted to identify RCTs comparing intravenous ketamine or esketamine with intravenous midazolam in adolescents with MDD. Three RCTs involving a total of 134 adolescents with MDD were included. Two trials assessed the antidepressant effects of intravenous ketamine compared with intravenous midazolam, with inconsistent findings. No significant advantage of intravenous ketamine over intravenous midazolam was observed in reducing anxiety symptoms (1 RCT). One trial compared intravenous esketamine with intravenous midazolam and evaluated antidepressant, anti-suicidal, and neurocognitive outcomes, demonstrating the superiority of intravenous esketamine. Both intravenous ketamine and intravenous esketamine were associated with significantly higher rates of dissociative symptoms (1 RCT each), and intravenous esketamine was also linked to a higher incidence of psychopathological symptoms (1 RCT). Systematic reporting of adverse events was provided in only one of the three included RCTs. Given the limited number of studies, small sample sizes, and methodological heterogeneity of the available RCTs, the current evidence base remains preliminary and insufficient to support definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of intravenous ketamine/esketamine in adolescents with MDD. These findings highlight the need for further adequately powered RCTs to establish robust and clinically meaningful evidence.

title: Physical Comorbidity, Clinical Correlates, and Inpatient Management Burden in Hospitalized Patients With Major Depressive Disorder.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is frequently accompanied by physical comorbidity, which may complicate inpatient assessment and management. However, large-scale patient-level studies investigating physical comorbidity and its impact on inpatient resource utilization among hospitalized patients with MDD remain limited. This study aimed to characterize the profile of physical comorbidity in MDD and examine its adjusted associations with indicators of inpatient management burden. In this large-scale cross-sectional study, we analyzed data from 8463 patients with MDD admitted to a major psychiatric center. Patients were stratified according to the presence or absence of physical comorbidity. We assessed the prevalence and spectrum of physical comorbidity, compared demographic and clinical characteristics between groups, and used multivariable regression models to identify factors associated with physical comorbidity, as well as to examine its associations with length of stay, internal medicine consultation, and the use of physical therapies. Physical comorbidity was identified in 56.9% of hospitalized patients with MDD. Among those with physical comorbidity, 65.2% had physical multimorbidity (≥2 conditions). Diseases of the circulatory system (80.7%) and endocrine, nutritional, and metabolic diseases (35.4%) were the most common disease categories. Older age, farming occupation, and greater severity of depressive episodes were independently associated with physical comorbidity. Physical comorbidity was also associated with a longer length of stay and substantially higher odds of requiring internal medicine consultation. This large inpatient cohort demonstrates that physical comorbidity is common, multisystemic, and clinically relevant among hospitalized patients with MDD. These findings support the routine assessment of physical health and timely multidisciplinary care during hospitalization, particularly for older patients, farmers, and those with severe depressive episodes.

title: Establishing the Clinical Role of Digital Therapeutics in Major Depressive Disorder Treatment: A Consensus Panel Perspective.
text: Digital therapeutics for major depressive disorder (MDD) are evidence-based clinical interventions that can help address barriers in access to effective specialty/secondary care, patient preference for nonpharmacologic options, and continuity of care between visits. Despite growing evidence of efficacy, clinical adoption lags and current health care systems do not provide guidance for clinicians on their evaluation or implementation. In May 2026, a multidisciplinary expert consensus panel convened virtually to discuss the role of digital therapeutics in the management of MDD across primary care, specialty psychiatry, and community mental health practice in the United States and Europe. The panel developed four consensus statements regarding the evaluation, selection, and implementation of digital therapeutics for MDD. Digital therapeutics were identified as a distinct clinical category that should be evaluated using principles similar to other evidence-based MDD treatments, with efficacy as the primary selection criterion. Digital therapeutics may be incorporated across multiple stages of stepped-care management, including bridge-to-care and augmentation treatment. The panel identified clinician unfamiliarity, implementation challenges, and uncertainty regarding patient engagement as key adoption barriers. The consensus recommendations are intended to help clinicians select evidence-based digital therapeutics, position them appropriately within stepped-care management of MDD, and address the barriers preventing translation of current evidence into routine clinical practice.

title: Diagnostic and predictive value of structural and high-order functional brain topology in major depressive disorder.
text: Conventional neuroimaging analyses for major depressive disorder (MDD) predominantly construct brain networks based solely on pairwise regional functional couplings. Accumulating microscale neuroscientific evidence highlights the essential role of higher-order interactions (HOIs, interactions among three or more brain nodes) in capturing the intricate spatiotemporal dynamics of the human brain. This study aims to integrate machine learning techniques with neuroimaging topological features to systematically investigate the impact of non-pairwise interaction patterns in the brains of MDD patients on system dynamics, and to develop diagnostic and predictive models for MDD clinical manifestations. Firstly, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data were acquired from 154 MDD patients with first-episode, drug-naïve and 153 age and gender matched healthy controls (HCs). Graph-theoretical analysis was applied to DTI-derived tractography data to quantify structural topology metrics, whereas persistent homology was adopted to extract higher-order functional topological signatures from rs-fMRI time series. Second, feature-level fusion was performed, and then a classification model was constructed using support vector machine (SVM) for MDD diagnosis. A repeated nested validation strategy with 50 repeated stratified 70/30 hold-out splits was adopted. Classification performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Subsequently, a prediction model was built based on the selected fused features using ridge regression, and the prediction performance was evaluated based on the correlation between the predicted values and the actual scale scores. Compared with HC, MDD patients exhibited significant alterations in structural and functional topological metrics within key brain networks, including DMN, VN and FPN. The classification performance of the SVM model integrating multimodal neuroimaging features achieved excellent classification performance, with an AUC of 88.2%. Additionally, multimodal imaging features demonstrated robust predictive capacity for suicide risk level in MDD patients (r=0.604). By integrating structural and higher-order functional topological features, we are able to effectively diagnose and predict MDD, highlighting the crucial role of higher-order interactions in the pathological mechanisms of brain networks in depression.

title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

title: Real-World Status of Augmentation Therapy With Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Claims Database Study.
text: This study investigated pharmacotherapy treatment patterns, focusing on atypical antipsychotics (AAP) augmentation therapy, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) who initiated antidepressant monotherapy in Japan. This retrospective cohort study was conducted using a large Japanese claims database. Patients with MDD aged ≥ 18 years who were subsequently prescribed antidepressants between June 2013 and June 2020 were enrolled. We identified patients who initiated antidepressant monotherapy as the first line of treatment (LOT1). Treatment patterns, including the number, duration, and sequence of LOTs, were examined before and after AAP augmentation therapy. In total, 50 355 patients received antidepressant monotherapy in LOT1; the most common therapy was selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The use of AAP augmentation therapy increased with progression of LOTs. Overall, 3811 patients (7.6%) received AAP augmentation therapy after a mean of 1.4 LOTs and 270 days from treatment initiation. Although 37.9% of these patients changed to other treatments in the next LOT within 180 days, 46.4% continued AAP augmentation therapy for ≥ 180 days. Among patients receiving antidepressant monotherapy in LOT1, 14.6% underwent ≥ 3 LOTs and the most common treatment pattern was SSRI-SSRI-SSRI. The proportion of patients receiving AAP augmentation therapy was low. Although few LOTs were required before AAP augmentation therapy, the claims-defined interval before AAP augmentation therapy was relatively long. Approximately half of the patients demonstrated prescription persistence with AAP augmentation therapy for ≥ 180 days. These findings may help clinicians refine treatment strategies regarding the timing of AAP augmentation, providing a basis for future research on how such adjustments might influence therapeutic outcomes in MDD.

title: Association of Self-Reported Clinical Behavior With Guideline Adherence in Schizophrenia and Major Depressive Disorder After Guideline Education.
text: The Effectiveness of Guidelines for Dissemination and Education in Psychiatric Treatment (EGUIDE) project is a nationwide Japanese educational program promoting guideline-concordant pharmacotherapy for schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (MDD). Psychiatrists' self-reported clinical behavior (CB) scores after EGUIDE training are partially associated with objective quality indicators of specific practices. However, their association with comprehensive objective measures of overall guideline adherence remains unclear. This multicenter observational study included 1897 EGUIDE-trained psychiatrists. CB was assessed online immediately after training. The Guideline Adherence Rate (GAR) was calculated for 5328 patients with schizophrenia and 3538 patients with MDD whose discharge records were linked to their psychiatrist's CB score. Associations were evaluated using unadjusted patient-level Spearman correlations, without modeling clustering within psychiatrists or institutions. Sensitivity analyses aggregated the data to the psychiatrist-year level, adjusted for institution type, psychiatrist experience, and patient age, and used generalized estimating equations (GEE) to correct the patient-level inference for clustering. CB scores showed positive but very weak correlations with GAR (schizophrenia, ρ = 0.09-0.14; MDD, ρ = 0.08-0.11; all p < 0.001). Squared coefficients (approximately 0.006-0.020) indicated that CB scores accounted for < 2% of the rank-order variation in GAR. These associations remained statistically significant in psychiatrist-year-level, covariate-adjusted, and clustering-corrected (GEE) sensitivity analyses. Post-training self-reported CB scores were weakly associated with patient-level GAR. Given the cross-sectional, unadjusted analysis and the non-independence of patients treated by the same psychiatrist, these findings do not establish CB as a reliable proxy for actual clinical practice. University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000022645.

title: The molecular and neurochemical basis of altered intrinsic neural timescales in major depressive disorder: a multimodal imaging-transcriptomic investigation of esketamine and sertraline treatment.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by dysfunction in higher-order cortical regions involved in emotional and cognitive processes; however, its neurobiological basis remains unclear. Pharmacological treatments, including esketamine and sertraline, produce rapid antidepressant effects. We investigated the local intrinsic neural dynamics underlying these antidepressant effects using intrinsic neural timescales (INT), which measure the duration and capacity of information integration in localized brain regions. A total of 57 healthy controls and 41 patients with MDD were included. All patients with MDD received six intravenous infusions of esketamine (0.25 mg/kg) and two weeks of sertraline treatment. All participants underwent resting-state fMRI to quantify INT alterations at the voxel and brain network levels, followed by spatial correlation analyses linking autocorrelation metrics of INT signals to transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas and PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor maps. The spatial correlation between PLS2 scores and case-control t-statistic maps did not pass rigorous spin permutation testing (r = 0.484, p = 0.068) and did not meet the conventional significance threshold of 0.05. Accordingly, all subsequent enrichment analyses based on PLS2 results are presented as exploratory preliminary observations for hypothesis generation. Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD exhibited significantly elevated INT levels in the left and right precuneus. Following treatment, patients with MDD showed significantly increased INT in the left occipital midline region and left calcarine cortex. At the brain network level, INT levels were significantly reduced in the default mode network (DMN) in patients with MDD compared with healthy controls. Compared with the pre-treatment state, the cerebellar network (CN) showed significantly elevated INT levels after treatment. Partial least squares regression analysis suggested potential associations between INT alterations and spatial gene expression gradients particularly those associated with immune responses, hormonal regulation, neutrophils, regulatory T cells, and glutamatergic synapses. Cell-type enrichment analysis identified excitatory and inhibitory neurons as key cellular contributors. Alterations in INT also correlated with cortical 5-HT1b and NAT receptor density, suggesting a role for inhibitory neurotransmission in temporal integration deficits. This study advances understanding of treatment-related brain abnormalities in patients with MDD from the perspective of local neural dynamics. These findings support a multiscale pathophysiological framework involving brain connectivity dynamics, molecular architecture, and neurochemical regulation in MDD.

title: Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder.
text: Although antidepressants remain the main pharmacological treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), therapeutic response varies, highlighting the need for molecular markers that predict treatment response, as well as insights into the biological processes underlying antidepressant efficacy. Candidate-gene and cross-sectional epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) have reported DNA methylation signatures associated with antidepressant response; however, findings remain inconsistent. To date, no longitudinal EWAS has examined methylation trajectories across multiple time points during antidepressant treatment in MDD. Within the Early Medication Change trial, DNA methylation data was generated for 162 patients with MDD (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 matched healthy controls. Patients were assessed at four times across eight-weeks of standardized antidepressant treatment, while controls were assessed twice. Differentially methylated positions (DMPs) and regions (DMRs) were identified using longitudinal EWAS models and the comb-p algorithm. Baseline methylation levels were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56 through two and six DMRs, respectively (e.g., TNRC6C, CAT), whereas no single DMP reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP associated with improvement in depressive symptoms (YLMP1) and three DMRs showing methylation changes over time (e.g., GPR126, PM20D1). Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs associated with diagnosis and temporal effects. This study provides first longitudinal evidence of regionally coordinated DNA methylation changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy, revealing alterations in genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammatory processes that are associated with clinical response. Replication and functional validation will be essential to determine their relevance for personalized antidepressant treatment.

title: Medicating inhibitory control? Treatment with serotonergic antidepressants predicts stop-N200 amplitudes in major depressive disorder.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent chronic mental illness often treated by serotonergic pharmacotherapy and complicated by sex differences and comorbid anxiety disorders (COMs). Deficits in inhibitory control are a transdiagnostic feature of MDD and COM, though the presentation of these deficits may be impacted by competing cognitive demands, symptoms severity, sexes, and medication status. This project includes 233 participants from the Tulsa 1000 study who completed concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic functional resonance imaging (MRI) during a stop signal task (SST). We examined how serotonergic antidepressants, biological sex, and comorbidity with an anxiety disorder uniquely relate to neural indices of inhibitory control for healthy controls (HCs), MDD, and COM using linear mixed effect models, type III ANOVAs, and optimal full propensity matching. N200, P300, and correct-related negativity (CRN) components were extracted and analyzed to index conflict monitoring, conflict resolution, and performance monitoring, respectively, in response to stop signals and their absence. Our results revealed that HCs exhibited larger stop-P300 amplitudes than MDD and COM (η2 = 0.068); females had smaller stop-N200 amplitudes than males (η2 = 0.027); MDD/COM participants taking a serotonergic antidepressant exhibited less negative N200 amplitudes than those who were not (LME, B = 1.95; η2 = 0.044; ATE, B = 2.47). Our findings suggest being treated with serotonergic antidepressants are associated with neural differences in the conflict monitoring of inhibitory control in pure and comorbid depression.

title: Peripheral molecular signatures of major depressive disorder: a systematic review of blood-derived biomarkers for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment response.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is biologically heterogeneous, yet diagnosis and treatment selection remain largely symptom-based. Blood-derived molecular biomarkers may offer scalable tools for biomarker discovery, biological stratification, and treatment-response research, but their clinical readiness remains uncertain. This PRISMA-compliant systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261379864). PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from 2014 to 27 April 2026 for human studies evaluating blood-derived molecular biomarkers in MDD or clinically defined depressive phenotypes with extractable depression-relevant data. Eligible domains included transcriptomics, DNA methylation, non-coding RNA, immune-inflammatory, mitochondrial/metabolic, neurotrophic/neuroendocrine, multi-omics, and machine-learning biomarker studies. Owing to methodological and platform heterogeneity, a structured narrative synthesis was performed rather than quantitative meta-analysis. Methodological quality was assessed using a modified QUADOMICS framework, prediction-model studies were additionally assessed using PROBAST, and certainty was judged using a modified GRADE approach. Of 9,354 records identified, 25 reports met the eligibility criteria, representing 24 independent participant datasets because two methylation analyses used the same underlying NESDA cohort. Included studies used whole blood, PBMCs, leukocytes, monocytes, serum, plasma, and cell-free RNA across diverse molecular platforms. Individual biomarkers were heterogeneous, but recurrent pathway-level signals involved immune-inflammatory and interferon-related pathways, NF-κB signalling, mitochondrial and energy metabolism, DNA methylation and epigenetic regulation, neurodevelopmental/synaptic pathways, stress-response signalling, autophagy, and non-coding RNA regulation. Multi-marker and multi-omics panels showed promising apparent diagnostic or treatment-response relevance, but most were internally validated, cohort-specific, or exploratory. Modified GRADE certainty was low to very low across biomarker domains. Blood-derived molecular signatures in MDD show stronger convergence at the pathway level than at the individual-biomarker level. Current evidence supports hypothesis generation and biological stratification, but no blood-derived biomarker or panel is ready for routine diagnosis or treatment selection.

title: Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with antidepressants in major depressive disorder: a randomized, double-blind, single-center, sham-controlled trial.
text: Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (DMPFC-rTMS) has shown some evidence of an antidepressant effect. This study aimed to examine the efficacy and safety of DMPFC-rTMS as a combination strategy with concurrently initiated selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) compared with conventional high-frequency left-prefrontal rTMS (HF-rTMS) + SSRI or sham stimulation + SSRI. In this prospective, single-center, six-week, randomized, three-arm, double-blind, sham- and active-comparator-controlled trial, patients with a current episode of major depressive disorder (MDD) were randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive either DMPFC-rTMS (20 sessions, 110% motor threshold, 2000 pulses), HF-rTMS (20 sessions, 110% motor threshold, 2000 pulses), or sham stimulation, all in combination with a concurrently initiated SSRI. The primary outcome was the change in the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) score at week six of the study. The secondary outcomes included changes in subjective assessment; response, remission, and dropout rates; and side effects of both rTMS and antidepressant treatment. Sixty patients (20 per group) were randomized and included in the analysis. The mean change in the MADRS total score from baseline to week 6 was -14.3 points (95% confidence interval [CI]: -18.3, -10.3) in the DMPFC-rTMS group, -8.2 points (95% CI: -11.7, -4.7) in the HF-rTMS group, and -12.6 points (95% CI: -16.1, -9.0) in the sham group. However, no pairwise comparisons between these groups reached statistical significance. The response/remission rates (DMPFC-rTMS: 35%/20%; HF-rTMS: 30%/15%; sham: 55%/45%) and the dropout rates (45%, 25%, and 25%, respectively) did not differ significantly between the groups. No serious adverse events occurred. This study did not demonstrate superior efficacy of DMPFC-rTMS or HF-rTMS over sham stimulation when initiated concurrently with SSRIs. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory. The trial was underpowered to detect the likely incremental effect of adding rTMS to a concurrently initiated SSRI and was further limited by a high sham response and differential attrition in the DMPFC-rTMS arm. Optimal stimulation parameters and patient selection require further validation. ISRCTN26184028 (Registered retrospectively, July 26, 2022).

title: Effect of electroconvulsive therapy on anhedonia in adults with major depressive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Anhedonia is a core symptom of major depressive disorder (MDD) and may persist despite otherwise effective treatment. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a widely used and effective intervention for severe and treatment-resistant depression, however, its specific effects on anhedonia remain poorly characterized. To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis examining ECT-associated changes in anhedonia in adults with MDD. A systematic search was conducted across Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Scopus. Studies were eligible if they included adults with MDD, administered ECT as a treatment, and assessed anhedonia using a validated scale. Standardized mean change ratios (SMCs) were calculated and pooled using a random-effects model. Eleven studies were included in the systematic review, of which five provided quantitative data for meta-analysis. Across 132 participants, ECT was associated with a significant improvement in anhedonia severity (SMC = 1.02; 95% CI, 0.63-1.42). ECT was associated with a statistically significant improvement in anhedonia among adults with MDD. However, given the small number of included studies and non-randomized pre-post designs, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future ECT studies should assess anhedonia as an outcome, while using a validated anhedonia measure.

title: Electroconvulsive therapy for trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with major depressive disorder: A case series of three elderly women.
text: Severe cenesthopathy associated with major depressive disorder (MDD) may cause malnutrition and functional decline. We report three elderly women with trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with MDD who improved markedly following electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Case A: A woman in her 60s developed MDD while caring for her mother with dementia. Despite pharmacological treatment, trunk, limb, and oral cenesthopathy developed 6 months later, resulting in reduced food intake and physical deterioration. Symptoms improved after six ECT sessions, nearly resolved after 12, and ECT was completed after 15 sessions without recurrence. Case B: A woman in her 70s developed MDD after prolonged caregiving stress. Despite pharmacological treatment, she developed trunk and visceral cenesthopathy with organ displacement sensations, dyspnea, speech disturbance, and loss of appetite. Cenesthopathy resolved after three ECT sessions; dyspnea and speech disturbance improved after 10. ECT was completed after 13 sessions. After recurrence, a second acute ECT course followed by maintenance ECT maintained clinical stability. Case C: A woman in her 70s with longstanding MDD developed visceral and oral cenesthopathy after discontinuing antidepressants. Despite pharmacological treatment, she became unable to eat or drink. Cenesthopathy resolved after four ECT sessions, restoring oral intake. ECT was completed after eight sessions without recurrence. ECT may be an effective treatment for trunk and visceral cenesthopathy associated with MDD. Early consideration of ECT may be warranted when malnutrition or physical deterioration necessitates rapid symptom control.
source: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

title: Oxidative stress in major depressive disorder: from experimental models to clinical therapeutic perspectives.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a highly prevalent psychiatric condition with complex and multifactorial pathophysiology. Increasing evidence suggests that oxidative stress, defined as an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defense systems, plays a central role in the onset and progression of MDD. This narrative review integrates findings from preclinical animal models, clinical studies and therapeutic interventions to provide a comprehensive overview of oxidative stress in MDD. Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD consistently exhibit increased lipid peroxidation products, protein and DNA oxidation markers, and altered antioxidant defenses, including glutathione and superoxide dismutase. Animal models including chronic unpredictable mild stress, chronic social defeat stress, and lipopolysaccharide administration consistently demonstrate that oxidative stress drives depressive-like behaviors through mechanisms affecting dendritic spine density, glutamatergic function, and hippocampal neurogenesis. Additionally, oxidative stress is closely linked to inflammatory signaling and redox-regulatory signaling pathways, such as NF-κB and Nrf2/Keap1, highlighting its function as a major modulator of neuronal dysfunction in MDD. Therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and spanning from conventional antidepressants to antioxidant compounds, stem cell therapies, natural products, and physical exercise demonstrate promising potential in restoring redox balance and improving depressive symptoms, although high heterogeneity across studies has been reported. Collectively, these findings support oxidative stress as a unifying mechanism in MDD pathophysiology and a promising target for novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

title: Plasma Lipidomic Features of Adolescent Major Depressive Disorder and Lipid Changes After Fluoxetine Treatment.
text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a major public health concern, yet objective biological markers and treatment-related metabolic changes remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize plasma lipidomic alterations in adolescent MDD and explore lipid changes associated with fluoxetine treatment. This study enrolled 75 adolescents with MDD and 75 matched healthy controls (HCs). Among the adolescents with MDD, 44 had paired baseline and week-8 plasma samples available and were included in the longitudinal analysis. Plasma lipidomic profiles were analyzed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). A total of 865 lipid species were detected. Compared with HCs, adolescents with MDD showed distinct plasma lipidomic profiles, with 82 differentially abundant lipid species identified, primarily involving triglycerides, lysophospholipids, free fatty acids, membrane phospholipids, and sphingolipids. Among the machine-learning models, logistic regression showed the highest discriminative performance, with a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79-0.91). Longitudinal analysis identified 21 lipid species meeting the differential criteria following fluoxetine treatment, mainly involving triglycerides and bile acid-related metabolites. Integrative pathway and target analyses suggested that fluoxetine-associated lipid changes may involve neurotransmitter signaling, inflammatory lipid metabolism, PI3K-Akt signaling, and nuclear receptor-related pathways. This study characterizes alterations in plasma lipid metabolism in adolescent MDD and the lipidomic changes following fluoxetine treatment, providing new lipidomic evidence for candidate lipid signatures and potential treatment-associated biological pathways. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05814640. Registered 20 February 2023, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05814640.

title: Baseline alexithymia and recovery from major depressive disorder: a longitudinal study.
text: To investigate whether alexithymia is associated with baseline symptom severity or longitudinal treatment outcomes in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). The sample comprised 258 outpatients with MDD (mean age = 31.77, SD = 11.30) followed for six months. Alexithymia was assessed with the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20), depressive symptoms with the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and psychopathology with the SCL-90-R. The prevalence of alexithymia was 27.9% (n = 72) at baseline, 18.4% (n = 29) at 3 months, and 16.1% (n = 23) at 6 months. Among patients with baseline alexithymia, 40.3% remained alexithymic at 3 months and 31.9% at 6 months. At baseline, alexithymic patients had significantly higher BDI scores and scores on all TAS-20 subscales and SCL-90-R domains. Depressive symptoms decreased significantly during follow-up, with the greatest improvement during the first 3 months. Although alexithymic patients had consistently higher depressive symptom levels, the time × group interaction was not significant, indicating similar improvement in both groups. However, participants with baseline alexithymia were significantly more likely to be lost to follow-up than those without alexithymia. Alexithymia was associated with greater baseline psychopathology and persistently higher depressive symptom levels. However, alexithymic and non-alexithymic patients showed similar trajectories of symptom reduction, suggesting that alexithymia does not limit improvement in depressive symptoms.

title: Resistance training volume for major depressive disorder: the MoveMind randomized controlled trial protocol.
text: This randomized controlled trial aims to investigate the effects of resistance training (RT) volume (high vs. low) and non-exercise group on depressive symptoms, remission rates, adherence and the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms underlying these effects in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). A total of 150 adults (18-59 years) diagnosed with MDD will be randomized into three groups: high-volume RT (HV, n=50; 4 sets of 10-12 repetition maximum [RM]), low-volume RT (LV, n=50; 2 sets of 10-12 RM), and a non-exercise control group (CG, n=50). Participants in the intervention groups will train three non-consecutive days per week for 8 weeks. The primary outcome, depressive symptoms, will be assessed by a psychiatrist using the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale. Secondary outcomes will include potential psychological mechanisms (perceived self-efficacy, affective responses to exercise, and well-being), assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and at the 3-month follow-up, and neurobiological mechanisms assessed by inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers related to MDD pathophysiology, including TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1β, CRP, IGF-1, BDNF, insulin, glucose, and cortisol, measured before and after the intervention. Tertiary outcomes will include dietary intake and ultra-processed food consumption (24-hour dietary recall), body composition (DXA), muscular strength, and sleep quality. Intervention efficacy will be analyzed using intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models. The findings may contribute to more effective, personalized, and sustainable RT prescriptions that improve adherence and complement conventional treatments for MDD. https://ensaiosclinicos.gov.br/rg/, identifier RBR-9tn4ncp.

title: Reduced Serum Apelin-13 Levels in Medication-free Adults with Major Depressive Disorder.
text: The apelinergic system has been implicated in neuroinflammatory and neuroplastic mechanisms related to depressive disorders. Apelin-13, the most biologically active isoform of apelin, has demonstrated antidepressant-like effects in preclinical studies; however, clinical evidence remains limited. This study aimed to investigate serum Apelin-13 levels in medication-free adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and assess their clinical relevance. This cross-sectional, case-control study included 80 medication-free adults diagnosed with MDD and 81 healthy control subjects matched for age, sex, and body mass index. Psychiatric diagnoses were established using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5. Depression severity was assessed using the 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Serum Apelin-13 concentrations were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Between-group comparisons, correlation analyses, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses, and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed. Serum Apelin-13 levels were significantly lower in patients with MDD than in healthy controls (p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis demonstrated a moderate discriminative ability of serum Apelin-13 levels, with an area under the curve of 0.719. Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that lower serum Apelin-13 levels were independently associated with MDD after adjustment for relevant confounding variables (p < 0.001). No significant association was observed between serum Apelin-13 levels and depression severity. These findings indicate that serum Apelin-13 levels are reduced in medication-free adults with MDD and may reflect an underlying biological vulnerability rather than current symptom severity. Apelin-13 may represent a trait-related biomarker contributing to the biological characterization of depressive disorders.
source: Clinical psychopharmacology and neuroscience : the official scientific journal of the Korean College of Neuropsychopharmacology

title: Identifying Distinct Patient Preference Patterns in Second-Line Treatment for Type 2 Diabetes: A Latent Class Analysis of a Discrete Choice Experiment.
text: Treatment decisions in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) require knowledge of patient preferences. The German National Health Care Guideline emphasizes preference-based decision making, with treatment goals negotiated in light of individual risk profiles, therapy-related effects, and life circumstances. Systematic preference heterogeneity suggests these contextual factors shape how patients prioritize attributes, posing a central challenge for medical decision making. Latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to data from a discrete choice experiment (DCE) conducted between August and November 2023 among 583 individuals with T2D in Germany. Participants completed 12 choice tasks using a partial profile design. Treatment options were described by risks of myocardial infarction, stroke, neuropathy, nausea, and severe hypoglycemia as well as weight change, intake mode, and schedule. Analyses were conducted for the overall sample and stratified by treatment experience (population 1: monotherapy, n = 292; population 2: second line, n = 291). In a 3-class solution (N = 583), one class (28%) strongly prioritized weight outcomes, while remaining classes prioritized nausea risk. Stratified 2-class solutions revealed significant differences in preferences for weight change, administration schedule, and nausea risk, with professional status and weight-related factors corresponding to class membership as contextual factors. LCA findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating representations of distinct decision logics. Furthermore, limitations inherent to the DCE design, including attribute reduction and partial profile approach, as well as potential variance in response behavior, were carefully considered and addressed. Patients with T2D exhibit distinct preference structures rather than uniform tradeoffs, differing fundamentally in whether disease-related, treatment-related, or administration attributes dominate their evaluations. Identifying latent preference patterns may enhance the transparency of tradeoffs in participatory treatment deliberation and support structured, guideline-aligned medical decision making.

title: Smart blood glucose management experience and needs in community-dwelling older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and excess adiposity: A qualitative study.
text: To explore the experiences and needs of community-dwelling older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and excess adiposity regarding smart blood glucose management tools, and to understand their challenges and support needs in community-based digital health management. A descriptive qualitative study was conducted using purposive sampling. From October 2025 to February 2026, 19 eligible older adults were recruited from a community in Hangzhou, China. Data were collected through face-to-face semi-structured interviews and analyzed using a thematic analysis approach with NVivo 15.0 software until data saturation was achieved. Smart blood glucose management tools included home blood glucose monitoring devices and digital platforms or applications used for blood glucose tracking and diabetes management. Thematic analysis generated five core themes and 15 subthemes: (1) dynamic motivation in disease risk perception; (2) digital health information: empowerment and cognitive burden; (3) use of digital monitoring tools: convenience, barriers, and trust; (4) community healthcare context: support and selective engagement; and (5) emotional-behavioral responses to monitoring results. Blood glucose monitoring was characterized as a dynamic process shaped by the interaction of cognitive, technological, contextual, and emotional factors. While risk perception and abnormal monitoring results may enhance short-term engagement, long-term adherence was constrained by limited disease understanding, information overload, usability challenges, trust issues, and gaps between healthcare accessibility and effective utilization. Smart blood glucose management among community-dwelling older adults with T2DM and excess adiposity is shaped by interacting cognitive, technological, contextual, and emotional factors. Future interventions should consider these multifaceted factors to better support sustained self-management among older adults with T2DM and excess adiposity.

title: Serum glypican-4 and visfatin in patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus: associations with insulin resistance and discriminatory performance.
text: Insulin resistance and an altered pattern of adipokine secretion are defining features of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). In this context association of two recently described adipokines, glypican-4 (GPC4) and visfatin, with insulin resistance is insufficiently characterized especially among Middle-Eastern populations. The present work assessed circulating GPC4 and visfatin, their relationship with insulin resistance, and their discriminatory performance in patients with newly diagnosed T2DM. Ninety patients with newly diagnosed T2DM (diagnosed 1-6 months earlier and receiving metformin 500 mg/day) and 60 conditionally healthy controls, all older than 40 years, took part in this case-control study. Circulating GPC4 and visfatin were quantified by ELISA and glycemic indices, HOMA-IR, the lipid profile and renal function were determined. After normality had been verified with the Shapiro-Wilk test, groups were contrasted with Student's t-test, relationships examined with Pearson's correlation, independence from age and body mass index (BMI) checked through multiple linear regression and discriminatory ability appraised by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with areas under the curve (AUC) compared by DeLong's test. Circulating GPC4 (788.02±151.66 pg/ml vs 592.69±97.94 pg/ml) and visfatin (3.93±0.78 ng/ml vs 2.36±0.47 ng/ml) were markedly higher in the patient group than in controls (p < 0.001); patients also had a more atherogenic lipid profile, whereas renal function was comparable. Each adipokine was positively associated with HOMA-IR (GPC4: r = 0.499; visfatin: r = 0.293; p < 0.01). In multiple linear regression, group membership - rather than age or BMI - was the only independent correlate of both adipokines (standardised β = 0.584 and 0.752, respectively; p < 0.001), the models explaining 35% and 57% of the variance (R2 = 0.346 and 0.571). Visfatin and GPC4 discriminated diabetic patients from controls with AUCs of 0.950 and 0.852, respectively, the AUC of visfatin being significantly greater (p = 0.004). In patients with newly diagnosed T2DM, serum GPC4 and visfatin were already elevated at diagnosis and were associated with insulin resistance, independently of age and adiposity. However, a contribution of metformin therapy cannot be excluded. Both adipokines merit further, preferably treatment-naive, investigation as correlates of the insulin-resistant state.

title: Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Older Adults.
text: Older adults with type 2 diabetes are a highly heterogeneous population requiring individualized, safety-focused care. Management should consider diabetes phenotype, functional status, comorbidities, complications, life expectancy, treatment burden, costs, and social determinants of health. Glycemic targets should be personalized, with tighter goals for healthy older adults and relaxed goals for frail individuals or those with limited life expectancy. Medication selection should prioritize low hypoglycemia risk, cardiovascular and renal benefits, regimen simplicity, and avoidance of polypharmacy. Insulin therapy, technology, nutrition, exercise, screening for complications, and caregiver education should be tailored to preserve independence, prevent hypoglycemia, and maintain quality of life.

title: Low-glycemic load diet enhances pancreatic β-cell function through the fucose-Rnf183 axis in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: Our previous studies demonstrated that low-glycemic load (GL) diets reduced diabetes risk and promoted remission in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Serum samples from newly diagnosed T2DM patients with random 3-month low-GL dietary intervention or conventional energy-restricted diet were analyzed using LC-MS-based metabolomics. High glucose (HG)-treated MIN6 cells with or without fucose were used to assess β-cell function, apoptosis, and transcriptomic sequencing. Rnf183 was knocked down in MIN6 cells. Metabolomic analysis revealed that metabolites identified by LC-MS were mostly classified as carboxylic acids and derivatives, fatty acyls, and glycerophospholipids. Fucose exhibited the highest VIP score among all differential metabolites and was significantly upregulated in T2DM patients with a low-GL diet compared to those without a low-GL diet. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that fucose-associated fructose and mannose metabolism was affected by the low-GL diet. Fucose enhanced the expression of key β-cell functional genes (Pdx1, Nkx6.1, Mafa, and Insulin2) and attenuated HG-induced apoptosis in MIN6 cells. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that fucose regulated T2DM progression-related pathways (Notch signaling and insulin secretion) and protein ubiquitination in HG-induced MIN6 cells. Correspondingly, fucose reduced global ubiquitination of MIN6 cells and downregulated ubiquitination regulator Rnf183. Rnf183 knockdown increased expression levels of key β-cell functional genes in HG-treated MIN6 cells. Low-GL diet reshapes the serum metabolome of T2DM patients and increases fucose abundance. Fucose enhances pancreatic β-cell function, partly through suppression of ubiquitination and Rnf183. These findings provide mechanistic insights into dietary interventions for diabetes management.

title: Tirzepatide and risk of nutritional deficiency anemia compared with GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.
text: Nutritional deficiency anemia (NDA) is a potential concern during incretin-based treatment, but its comparative occurrence with tirzepatide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX database. Adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity who initiated tirzepatide or a GLP-1RA between January 1, 2022, and August 31, 2026, were identified. Patients with prior use of either treatment, NDA, type 1 diabetes, or bariatric surgery were excluded. After 1:1 propensity score matching, outcomes were assessed from day 1 through day 365. The primary outcome was a composite of iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency anemia. The matched cohorts included 67,608 patients each. NDA occurred in 1,440 tirzepatide users (2.13%) and 1,917 GLP-1RA users (2.84%; hazard ratio [HR], 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83-0.95). Tirzepatide was associated with less iron deficiency anemia (HR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.81-0.93), whereas estimates for vitamin B12 deficiency anemia (1.07; 0.83-1.38) and folate deficiency anemia (0.98; 0.56-1.71) were inconclusive. Tirzepatide initiation was associated with a modestly lower hazard of diagnosed NDA, predominantly iron deficiency anemia, than GLP-1RA initiation. Residual confounding and differences in follow-up and ascertainment limit causal interpretation.

title: Economic, Psychological, Political, and Systemic Barriers to Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes: Evidence From a Conflict-Affected Healthcare System.
text: IntroductionPolitical instability, economic hardship, and limited healthcare infrastructure exacerbate barriers to effective management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. This study was designed to identify and analyze the barriers to insulin therapy among patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus in conflict-affected settings.MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 377 adult patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Participants were recruited from governmental hospitals, diabetes clinics, and community health centers using a multi-site convenience sampling approach.ResultsGlycemic control was poor, with 83.6% of patients having glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 7%. Economic barriers were highly prevalent as 61.3% of patients reported insulin as unaffordable and 74.0% experienced supply shortages. Psychological barriers included fear of hypoglycemia (55.4%), stigma (32.1%), and lack of motivation (69.2%). Healthcare system barriers were striking, with 81.7% perceiving providers as inadequately qualified and 74.0% lacking regular access to professionals. Political instability further compounded challenges, with 85.9% reporting restricted access and 74.0% missing doses due to conflict-related disruptions. Patients with low income were more likely to report difficulty adhering to insulin therapy due to political circumstances (OR = 9.8, 95% CI: 3.6-26.3).ConclusionBarriers to insulin therapy among Palestinian patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are multifactorial, spanning economic, psychological, healthcare system, social, and political domains. Interventions must prioritize low-income and less-educated patients, strengthen healthcare provider training, and address systemic disruptions caused by political instability. Tailored strategies are urgently needed to improve insulin adherence, reduce complications, and enhance diabetes outcomes in resource-constrained and conflict-affected settings.
source: Inquiry : a journal of medical care organization, provision and financing

title: Nine-Year Trends in Treatment Patterns, Comorbidities, and Healthcare Utilization in Type 2 Diabetes in France: Insights From Integrated Health Data.
text: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a chronic condition with multimorbidity. Treatment strategies have evolved gradually over the past decades. We described longitudinal treatments, comorbidities, and healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) among adults with T2D in France between 2015 and 2023. The OREOT cohort included adults with T2D identified between 2015 and 2018 in IQVIA Electronic Medical Records and linked to the French National Health Data System. Patients were followed until 31 December 2023. Baseline characteristics, longitudinal clinical data, treatment patterns, incident comorbidities, and HCRU were assessed. Treatment trajectories were reconstructed using state sequence analysis. Among 236,305 patients, 57% were men, and the median age was 67 years. At baseline, 77% of patients had hypertension, 62% had dyslipidemia, and 57% had cardiovascular disease. Over a median follow-up of 8.7 years, body mass index and HbA1c remained stable, whereas renal markers worsened (mean eGFR -7 mL/min/1.73 m2). Incident comorbidities were frequent, particularly cancer (21%) and chronic kidney disease (11%). Metformin use declined (from 73% to 65%), while use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (from 5% to 18%), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (from 0% to 17%), and insulin (from 16% to 22%) increased, alongside growing regimen complexity. Healthcare utilization was characterized by frequent primary care visits (median 49 GP visits), with limited endocrinology (21%) and nephrology (5%) involvement, and regular HbA1c monitoring, with a median of three tests per year. Overall, 20% of patients died during follow-up. Between 2015 and 2023, T2D management in France shifted toward newer and more complex therapies, while a high burden of comorbidities and progressive renal decline persisted, highlighting the need for coordinated care and long-term real-world evaluation of newer glucose-lowering therapies.

title: Association of glycemic coefficient of variation with reduced appendicular skeletal muscle mass index among patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a cross‑sectional study.
text: The coefficient of variation (CV) of glycemia, calculated from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data, quantifies intraday glycemic variability. However, its association with reduced appendicular skeletal muscle mass in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association between glycemic CV and reduced ASMI. This retrospective cross-sectional study enrolled 1453 hospitalized T2DM patients aged ≥18 years who required intensive insulin pump therapy. Baseline clinical and laboratory data were collected, and glycemic CV was computed from CGM records. ASMI was measured using bioelectrical impedance analysis. Participants were categorized into the reduced ASMI group (n = 341) and normal muscle mass group (n = 1112) according to ASMI values, and further stratified by quartiles of glycemic CV. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to examine the independent association between glycemic CV and reduced ASMI. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) models were constructed to characterize the shape of this association. Subgroup analyses and multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted to verify the robustness of findings. Glycemic CV was significantly higher in participants with reduced ASMI. In the fully adjusted multivariable model, elevated glycemic CV was independently associated with increased odds of reduced ASMI (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.04-1.31, P = 0.008). RCS analysis indicated a statistically significant overall association, with no statistically significant nonlinearity (P = 0.148). Subgroup analyses revealed no significant interactions across strata of age, diabetes duration, gender, HbA1c, and visceral fat area. Sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the association between glycemic CV and reduced ASMI disappeared after additional adjustment for BMI (OR = 0.96, 95% CI: 0.52-1.82, P = 0.902), suggesting that the association was sensitive to adjustment for BMI. In hospitalized patients with type 2 diabetes receiving intensive insulin pump therapy, elevated glycemic variability was associated with reduced ASMI in the primary model; however, this association was no longer statistically significant after additional adjustment for BMI, indicating that the association was sensitive to adjustment for BMI. Intra-day glycemic variability may provide clues for exploring the mechanisms underlying skeletal muscle mass maintenance in this population.

title: LPA genetic variation is associated with type 2 diabetes after adjustment for lipoprotein(a) concentration: results of the Aragon Workers' Health Study.
text: Epidemiological and Mendelian randomization studies have reported an inverse relationship between lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] concentration and type 2 diabetes (T2D), although findings have not been uniform across studies. We hypothesized that genetic variation at the LPA locus may contribute to T2D development beyond circulating Lp(a) concentration alone, and therefore aimed to investigate the association between common LPA variation and incident T2D. We analysed 5058 male participants from the Aragon Workers' Health Study with approximately 15 years of follow-up. T2D was defined as the presence of antidiabetic treatment or HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Common LPA single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with a minor allele frequency ≥ 1% were selected. Several weighted LPA genetic scores were constructed, with the 15-SNV score defined as the primary LPA genetic score and alternative and more restricted scores evaluated in sensitivity analyses. Associations of single LPA variants and LPA genetic scores with incident T2D were assessed using multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age, body mass index, ln-transformed Lp(a), and a T2D polygenic risk score. False discovery rate correction was applied to account for multiple testing. Robustness was assessed using leave-one-out analyses and Cox proportional hazards models. Among 4744 participants free of T2D at baseline, 578 (12.2%) developed incident T2D. Baseline Lp(a) concentrations were lower in participants who developed incident T2D than in those who remained free of T2D (12.6 [5.0-32.5] versus 17.0 [6.1-40.0] mg/dL; p < 0.001). No individual LPA SNV remained significantly associated with incident T2D. In contrast, the primary 15-SNV LPA genetic score was associated with incident T2D after adjustment for measured baseline Lp(a) concentration (odds ratio per one-standard-deviation increase 1.17, 95% confidence interval 1.07-1.29; p = 0.001). The 13-SNV, 12-SNV, 10-SNV coding/splice-related, and 2-SNV Lp(a)-raising scores were also significantly associated with incident T2D after false discovery rate correction. The association with the 15-SNV LPA genetic score was supported by leave-one-out and Cox analyses. A 15-SNV LPA genetic score was associated with incident T2D after adjustment for measured baseline Lp(a) concentration and a T2D polygenic risk score. These findings suggest that common LPA variation represented by the 15-SNV genetic score may contribute to T2D risk through mechanisms not fully captured by circulating Lp(a) concentration alone.

title: The MUSCLE-GLP1-CKD study: design and rationale of a prospective real-world cohort evaluating muscle health after subcutaneous semaglutide initiation in chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes.
text: Sarcopenia and impaired physical function are clinically relevant complications of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are particularly vulnerable to muscle impairment. Semaglutide has established metabolic, cardiovascular and kidney benefits, but its effects on skeletal muscle quantity and function in moderate-to-advanced CKD remain insufficiently characterized.
