MUSCLE-GLP1-CKD is a multicenter, prospective, real-world observational cohort study conducted in two tertiary nephrology departments in Tenerife, Spain. Adults with CKD stages 3a-4 and T2DM who are clinically eligible for semaglutide will be followed for 12 months. The primary comparison will include new users initiating subcutaneous semaglutide at the index date and eligible comparable patients who do not initiate any GLP-1 receptor agonist at that date. Patients treated with other GLP-1RA will be included in broader secondary or sensitivity analyses. Assessments at baseline, 6 months and 12 months will include multifrequency segmental bioelectrical impedance analysis, handgrip dynamometry, the Short Physical Performance Battery, gait speed, physical-activity and nutritional questionnaires, and routine renal and metabolic data. The primary outcome is the adjusted between-group difference in mean change in appendicular skeletal muscle mass index from baseline to 12 months, reported with a 95% confidence interval. Secondary outcomes include changes in muscle strength, physical performance, phase angle, sarcopenia status, body composition, kidney function, albuminuria and cardiometabolic variables. Kidney outcomes, cardiovascular events and treatment-related adverse events will be exploratory. This study will provide prospective real-world evidence on muscle-health trajectories after semaglutide initiation in CKD and T2DM. A contemporaneous non-initiator comparator, a symmetrical index date and prespecified confounding-control and sensitivity analyses are intended to improve interpretability while acknowledging the limitations of observational treatment comparisons. The study was submitted for registration in the Spanish Registry of Clinical Studies (REec) through the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS) GESTO platform on 16 August 2026 (GESTO identifier: 0116-2026-OBS; AEMPS No. 26-00131).

title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Different Triple Oral Antidiabetic Therapy Regimens and Insulin-Based Therapy Regimens Following Dual Therapy Failure in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
text: The aim of this systematic review and network meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of triple oral antidiabetic therapy (3OADs) and insulin-based therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes after dual therapy failure. Medline (PubMed), Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were systematically searched (from inception to September 1, 2023). The network meta-analysis included randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of 3OADs and/or insulin-based therapies after dual therapy failure. Mean difference (MD) was extracted for changes in HbA1c and body weight; odds ratio (OR) was extracted for hypoglycemia and adverse events. Forty-two articles (13,911 adult patients) were analysed. 3OADs versus insulin-based therapy showed comparable HbA1c reduction (MD 0.01%; 95% CI, -0.56 to 0.58), weight change (MD -1.59 kg; 95% CI, -3.67 to 0.48), hypoglycemia (OR 0.70; 95% CI, 0.37-1.30), and adverse events (OR 1.68; 95% CI, 1.00-2.82) at 22-36 weeks. Sensitivity analysis revealed that 3OADs significantly reduced weight compared with insulin-based therapy (MD -3.30 kg; 95% CI, -5.56 to -1.05). No significant differences in HbA1c reduction, hypoglycemia incidence, or adverse events were observed between metformin (Met) + dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) + sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT-2i) and other 3OAD regimens. Meanwhile, Met + DPP-4i + SGLT-2i had the highest probability of achieving the greatest weight reduction. Compared with insulin-based therapy, 3OADs demonstrated comparable glucose-lowering effects and safety profiles, with a significant weight-sparing benefit observed in sensitivity analysis. Among all 3OAD combinations, Met + DPP-4i + SGLT-2i ranked first for weight loss, without increasing hypoglycemia risk.

title: EHR integrated triage-tool and closed-loop referral system to address social needs among patients with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes in the USA: protocol for a pilot type 3 hybrid implementation-effectiveness randomised trial.
text: Health-related social needs (HRSNs), including food insecurity, housing instability and transportation barriers, can directly affect diabetes self-management. Although HRSN screening has become increasingly common in clinical settings, existing approaches are often limited by the absence of structured triage, incomplete integration of referral processes with clinical workflows, weak community-based organisation (CBO) partnerships and lack of closed-loop systems to confirm service receipt. This study evaluates whether a system-integrated HRSN screening and referral model that triages patients and coordinates technology-facilitated CBO partnerships improves connection to social services and glycaemic control among adults with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in a safety-net primary care setting. This study employs a type 3 hybrid implementation-effectiveness design to assess an intervention aimed at enhancing an existing electronic health record (EHR)-integrated social needs screening and referral programme. A data-driven triage tool incorporating clinical, social and self-efficacy proxy indicators classifies eligible patients into low-support or high-support strata. Patients with uncontrolled T2DM (haemoglobin A1c ≥9%) who have screened positive for at least one HRSN during routine care are then randomised within triage strata to either the control (standard of care) or intervention arm. Triage classification determines the intensity of referral and navigation support for intervention participants but does not alter care for control participants. Intervention participants in the low-support stratum receive a direct referral to a matched CBO through the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)-protected, EHR-integrated platform, with no additional patient outreach. Intervention participants in the high-support stratum receive direct outreach to clarify needs and identify the most appropriate CBO match, followed by referral and sustained navigation to support referral completion. For all intervention patients, a Clinical-Community-Patient Link working group conducts monthly interdisciplinary case reviews to identify and address barriers to service connection. Primary analysis is based on intention-to-treat; secondary analysis is per-protocol. Outcomes include connection to CBOs and changes in glycaemic control, as well as process measures such as feasibility and other implementation metrics. The Boston Medical Center/Boston University IRB approved this pragmatic trial (H-45851) as no more than minimal risk. It granted waivers of informed consent (45 CFR 46.116(f)) and HIPAA authorisation (45 CFR 164.512(i)(2)(ii)) after determining that all regulatory criteria were met. The intervention involves no medications, procedures or experimental treatments. It reorganises existing social needs services, and no care is withheld from either arm. Patients may decline any service at any time without affecting their care. A prospective consent process would have delayed services and would likely have excluded the harder-to-reach patients the study aims to serve. Data will be stored in secure, HIPAA-compliant systems with access restricted to authorised personnel. Findings will be shared through peer-reviewed publications, conferences and partner CBOs using only aggregate or de-identified data. NCT07043426.

title: What keeps healthcare professionals from working as one team in type 2 diabetes care? A qualitative descriptive study in community health centres in North Toraja, Indonesia.
text: This study aimed to explore healthcare professionals’ experiences of implementing interprofessional collaborative practice in community-based type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) management, including factors that facilitate or constrain integrated care. Qualitative descriptive study using an inductive content analysis approach. Three community health centres in North Toraja Regency, Indonesia. 21 healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, nutritionists and pharmacists, were recruited using purposive sampling until code saturation was achieved across the full multidisciplinary sample. The analysis generated five main themes: (1) fragmentation of T2DM services, (2) an incomplete interprofessional collaboration structure, (3) suboptimal implementation of patient-centred care, (4) barriers to patient adherence and (5) technology needs and challenges for integrated T2DM care. Interprofessional collaboration (IPC) remained largely parallel, with limited structured communication and shared care planning. Simple and familiar digital tools, including WhatsApp, were perceived as potentially useful for coordination and continuity of care. This study describes fragmented services, incomplete interprofessional collaboration structures and suboptimal implementation of patient-centred care in community-based T2DM management. Healthcare professionals also identified barriers to patient adherence and limited use of technology for monitoring and follow-up. These findings highlight areas that may be considered in developing more integrated community-based T2DM care, including interprofessional collaboration, patient-centred care and contextually appropriate use of technology.

title: Non-Pharmacological Interventions for Managing Frailty Syndrome Among Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review.
text: Frailty is a multidimensional condition commonly observed in older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and is associated with functional decline, disability, hospitalization, and increased mortality. Although non-pharmacological interventions have been widely investigated, their effects on frailty and related outcomes in this population remain unclear. To synthesize current evidence on non-pharmacological interventions to manage frailty syndrome among older adults with T2DM. This systematic review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. A comprehensive literature search was performed across five electronic databases and platforms: PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, EBSCOhost (CINAHL), and Taylor and Francis Online. Studies were selected according to predefined eligibility criteria structured using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) framework. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools. Given the heterogeneity of intervention characteristics and outcome measures across the included studies, the findings were synthesised narratively. Nine eligible studies were included. Three categories of interventions were identified: (1) exercise-based interventions, (2) behavioural and lifestyle-based interventions, and (3) multimodal interventions. Exercise-based interventions were associated with reported improvements in selected physical and functional outcomes, whereas behavioural and lifestyle-based interventions showed varying findings across metabolic outcomes. Multimodal interventions addressed multiple domains, including physical, metabolic, and psychosocial outcomes. However, differences in study populations, intervention characteristics, and outcome measures limited direct comparisons across categories. The available evidence suggests that non-pharmacological interventions may be relevant to the management of frailty and related outcomes among older adults with T2DM. However, heterogeneity in the included publications, moderate methodological quality, and the inclusion of studies that did not directly assess frailty limit definitive conclusions about intervention effectiveness. The superiority of any intervention category has not been established. Future research should use clearly defined frailty criteria, standardized or clearly specified outcome measures, and transparent reporting of intervention and follow-up periods.

title: Examining treatment burden in relation to comorbidity among adults with type 2 diabetes: A cross-sectional study in a clinical setting in south India.
text: This study examines whether treatment burden differs between people living with diabetes alone and those with additional comorbidities. We interviewed 3,806 adults visiting Dr. Mohan's Diabetes Specialities Centre in Chennai between 24 January 2024 and 13 January 2025. Comorbidities were assessed using a comprehensive list of 69 chronic conditions, developed through multiple rounds of clinician consultation and piloting. Treatment burden was measured using the 13-item Multimorbidity Treatment Burden Questionnaire, translated into the local language and pilot-tested before administration. The global score (0-100) was categorized as none (score=0), low (0<score<10), medium (10≤ score< 22) and high (score≥22). The association between treatment burden and the presence of any comorbidity was examined using proportional odds logistic regression, adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, behavioural, and clinical factors. Overall, 95.2% of participants had at least one comorbidity in addition to diabetes, while 4.8% had diabetes alone. Seven percent reported high treatment burden, and 34% reported medium-to-high burden. Monitoring/self-management (e.g., lifestyle changes, condition monitoring) and accessing social support were the most burdensome domains, particularly for those with comorbidities. Participants with one or more comorbidities had significantly higher odds of reporting greater treatment burden than those without comorbidities (adjusted odds ratio=2.26, 95% CI=1.69-3.01, p-value<0.001). Findings were consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses. Treatment burden is substantial among adults with diabetes in India, particularly for those with comorbidity. These findings highlight the need for patient-centred care models that explicitly account for multimorbidity-related workload and provide targeted support for lifestyle modifications and self-management, especially in resource-constrained settings.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Anagliptin Added to Metformin and Empagliflozin 10 mg in Korean Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Multicentre, Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Phase III Trial.
text: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of anagliptin added to metformin and empagliflozin 10 mg in adults with Type 2 diabetes (T2D) with inadequate glycaemic control. In this multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial, participants receiving metformin (≥ 1000 mg/day) plus empagliflozin 10 mg/day were randomised 1:1 to anagliptin 100 mg twice daily or placebo for 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was change in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) at Week 24 in the full analysis set, analysed using a mixed-effects model for repeated measures. Secondary endpoints included fasting plasma glucose (FPG), HbA1c target attainment, HOMA-β and safety. Glycaemic responder analyses were conducted post hoc. The full analysis set included 195 participants (anagliptin, n = 97; placebo, n = 98). At Week 24, LS mean HbA1c changes were -0.81% and -0.24%, respectively, yielding a treatment difference of -0.57% (95% CI -0.74 to -0.40; p < 0.0001). FPG was also significantly reduced (between-group difference -12.15 mg/dL, 95% CI -19.18 to -5.12; p = 0.0008). HbA1c ≤ 7.0% was achieved by 55.7% versus 25.5% of participants. HbA1c reductions ≥ 0.5% occurred in 68.0% versus 27.6%, and reductions ≥ 1.0% in 33.0% versus 9.2%. HOMA-β improved significantly with anagliptin (between-group difference 14.35, 95% CI 7.37-21.32; p < 0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 22.7% and 17.2%, respectively; no hypoglycaemic events or deaths were reported. Anagliptin added to metformin and empagliflozin 10 mg provided confirmatory evidence of additional glycaemic efficacy in a separately randomised Korean population, increased glycaemic responder rates and improved estimated β-cell function, with acceptable short-term tolerability. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05814406.

title: Berberine and type 2 diabetes mellitus: a natural alkaloid with therapeutic benefits?
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a major and widespread metabolic disorder affecting millions of people worldwide. A key mechanism underlying the onset and progression of T2DM is insulin resistance.The main causes of insulin resistance are a sedentary lifestyle and obesity. Obesity promotes adipose tissue inflammation by increasing immune cell infiltration and inflammatory mediator production, alters gut microbiota toward a pro-inflammatory profile, and induces metabolic endotoxemia, resulting in low-grade systemic inflammation. Together with oxidative stress and elevated free fatty acids, these processes promote insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and pancreatic β-cell dysfunction, thereby exacerbating T2DM. Interestingly, berberine, which is a natural alkaloid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, affects all of the aforementioned events, thereby potentially contributing to the alleviation of insulin resistance and improvement of T2DM. This article provides a thorough narrative review of the available mechanistic and clinical evidence regarding the potential effects of berberine on T2DM by integrating findings from in vitro, animal, and clinical studies. In addition, this review critically examines the limitations, and translational relevance of the existing evidence. It also discusses the current status of berberine-containing pharmaceutical and nutraceutical formulations and highlights key pharmaceutical and translational challenges. The available evidence indicates that berberine has the potential to influence multiple pathogenic pathways implicated in T2DM and may thereby improve insulin sensitivity. Nevertheless, most mechanistic evidence remains preclinical, and further formulation standardization together with well-designed clinical trials are required to define its efficacy, safety, and optimal dosing before routine clinical use.

title: Biases in computable phenotypes for identifying patients with type 2 diabetes.
text: We leveraged real-world data from the OneFlorida+ Data Trust to examine sociodemographic biases associated with computable phenotypes (CPs) for type 2 diabetes (T2D) that incorporate prescription and laboratory information. Medical record review was used as a gold-standard to evaluate the discriminative ability of each CP. CPs identified patients ≥ 18 years from OneFlorida+ electronic health records (9/1/2018 - 2/29/2020). To clarify the relationships among the partially overlapping CP definitions, we defined four mutually exclusive (ME) groups of individuals: 1) T2D diagnosis only (ME_Claims); 2) T2D diagnosis and antidiabetic prescription (ME_Meds); 3) T2D diagnosis and HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (ME_Labs); and 4) Antidiabetic prescription and HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (ME_Meds_Labs). A split sampling approach and multinomial models were used to examine whether sociodemographic factors were associated with ME category membership. In a substudy, physicians reviewed medical records to verify T2D status, and the discriminative ability of each CP definition was assessed. In urban locations, compared to NH-White persons, Hispanic persons had lower odds of identification when CPs incorporated prescription or laboratory information relative to the ME_Claims definition [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.50 (0.46, 0.53), ME_Labs: 0.85 (0.79, 0.93), ME_Meds_Labs: 0.40 (0.36, 0.44)]. In rural locations, compared to NH-White persons, there were lower odds of identification by CPs incorporating prescription or laboratory information relative to the ME_Claims definition among NH-Black persons [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.72 (0.64, 0.82), ME_Labs: 0.52 (0.40, 0.68), and ME_Meds_Labs: 0.55 (0.46, 0.65)] and Other persons [OR (95% CI): ME_Meds: 0.59 (0.45, 0.77), ME_Labs: 0.48 (0.26, 0.87), and ME_Meds_Labs: 0.45 (0.31, 0.67)]. The medical record substudy revealed that the CP requiring a T2D diagnosis and laboratory results had the highest discriminative ability (adjusted AUC = 0.818) and specificity (1.000), while the CP requiring only a T2D diagnosis had the highest sensitivity (0.896). CPs have varying discriminative ability and may introduce measurement bias by excluding patients with less access to care. The interaction between race-ethnicity and rurality illustrates how CPs using prescriptions and laboratory information may omit certain populations. Differences in sensitivity and specificity highlight the varying utility of CPs across research contexts, such as surveillance studies versus cohort discovery.

title: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of FreeStyle Libre Real-Time Continuous Glucose Monitoring System Compared With Self-Monitoring of Blood Glucose in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes on Basal Insulin Plus SGLT2 Inhibitor and/or GLP-1 Agonists in the United Kingdom.
text: We previously showed that FreeStyle Libre (FSL) real-time continuous glucose monitoring system (rtCGM) reduces glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) at 16 and 32 weeks compared with capillary self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) in adults with Type 2 diabetes and above target glucose levels, managed with basal insulin and SGLT-2 inhibitor and/or GLP-1 agonist therapy. We assess the cost-effectiveness of rtCGM compared with SMBG. Participant-level baseline and follow-up health status (Euroqol-5-dimensions-5-levels) and within-trial healthcare resource-use data were collected. We estimated quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) and participant-level costs at 16 and 32 weeks. Long-term cost-effectiveness from the United Kingdom National Health Service perspective was evaluated using the IQVIA CORE Diabetes Model with a 3.5% discount rate. Sensitivity analyses assessed structural and parameter uncertainty. Within-trial analyses found no significant difference at 32 weeks between rtCGM and SMBG in QALYs or healthcare costs. At 32 weeks, adjusted incremental QALYs were -0.015 (95% CI: -0.031 to 0.003) and incremental costs were £254 (95% CI: -£587 to £1070). The lifetime projected incremental QALYs were 0.730 (95% CI: 0.688-0.773) and incremental costs were £4341 (95% CI: 3558-5125), generating an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of £5943 per QALY. At least 4 years of maintained glycaemic benefits are required for rtCGM to be cost-effective. Sensitivity analyses were robust to the base-case results. Benefits of FSL rtCGM in lowering HbA1c in people with Type 2 diabetes on basal insulin plus SGLT-2 inhibitor and/or GLP-1 agonist therapy is likely to justify costs through improved health outcomes and reduced long-term costs of diabetes-related complications.

title: Effects of a Helicobacter pylori-directed treatment regimen combined with metformin on glycemic control and metabolic and inflammatory status in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: ObjectiveTo compare glycemic and metabolic-inflammatory outcomes associated with assignment to a Helicobacter pylori eradication-treatment regimen, metformin, or their combination in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and Helicobacter pylori infection.MethodsThis single-center, three-arm, parallel-group, open-label randomized controlled trial enrolled 120 adult outpatients, randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to a Helicobacter pylori eradication-treatment regimen, metformin, or combined treatment (n = 40 per group). The primary outcome was the change in glycated hemoglobin from baseline to 6 months. Only archived group-by-time cell means, SDs, and sample sizes were available for the present analysis. Longitudinal cell means were analyzed using covariance-adjusted generalized least squares, with sensitivity analyses assuming within-participant correlations of 0.30-0.70.ResultsUnder the summary-data generalized least-squares model with an assumed within-participant correlation of 0.50, glycated hemoglobin showed significant group, time, and group × time effects (P = 1.37e-11, 9.24e-250, and 1.50e-30, respectively). Compared with assignment to the eradication-treatment regimen alone and metformin alone, assignment to combined treatment was associated with greater baseline-to-6-month glycated hemoglobin reductions of 1.76 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 1.43 to 2.09; Holm-adjusted P = 1.78e-25) and 1.77 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 1.41 to 2.13; Holm-adjusted P = 1.49e-22), respectively. Differential longitudinal patterns were also observed for several secondary outcomes. Complication incidence did not differ significantly among groups (P = 0.114).ConclusionsAssignment to the Helicobacter pylori eradication-treatment regimen combined with metformin was associated with greater short-term glycated hemoglobin improvement than assignment to either regimen alone. Because participant-level longitudinal data and post-treatment confirmation of Helicobacter pylori clearance were unavailable, these findings should be interpreted as summary-data associations with treatment-regimen assignment rather than as evidence of an effect mediated by successful eradication.
source: The Journal of international medical research

title: Clinical inertia among patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus in upper-middle-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Despite its critical importance, there has been no comprehensive quantitative synthesis focused specifically on clinical inertia in upper-middle-income countries. Without pooled prevalence estimates, identification of common predictors, and contextual insights into consequences, policymakers and clinicians in these settings are limited in their capacity to design targeted interventions. This study aimed to estimate the pooled estimate of clinical inertia among adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus in upper-middle-income countries. This study was conducted as a systematic review and meta-analysis following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. A comprehensive search was conducted using electronic databases such as PubMed, Science Direct, African Journals Online, and Google Scholar. All retrieved records were imported into EndNote reference manager, and duplicates were removed. The methodological quality of included observational cross-sectional studies was assessed using the Modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional and cohort studies. Data were extracted from all studies that met the inclusion criteria using the Joanna Briggs Institute standardized data extraction form in Microsoft Excel. Quantitative data were analyzed using STATA software version 17. Heterogeneity between studies was assessed using the Cochran's Q test and quantified with the Higgins (I 2) statistic. Ultimately, 13 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final review. In this study, the pooled effect size using the random-effects model was estimated to be 45.56% (95% CI: 32.87-58.25). The pooled prevalence should be interpreted as a summary measure reflecting the overall body of evidence, as substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 99.8%). Diabetes complications and comorbidities were significantly associated with clinical inertia. The findings highlight considerable variability in the reported prevalence of clinical inertia across upper-middle-income countries, suggesting important contextual and methodological differences between studies. This meta-analysis demonstrates that diabetes complications and comorbidities are significantly associated with clinical inertia. Overall, these findings highlight that clinical inertia remains a pervasive barrier to optimal chronic disease management. Health systems should prioritize patients with diabetes complications and multiple comorbidities for timely monitoring and treatment adjustments. CRD420251231712. Factors behind slow treatment decisions in type 2 diabetes in upper-middle-income countries This study looked at why doctors sometimes delay changing or intensifying treatment for people with type 2 diabetes in upper-middle-income countries. Delays in treatment, also called clinical inertia, can lead to higher blood sugar levels and increase the risk of complications such as heart disease, kidney problems, and vision loss. We reviewed and combined results from multiple studies to better understand how common clinical inertia is and what factors contribute to it. Our findings show that both patient-related factors (like not following advice or missing appointments) and healthcare-related factors (like limited resources, lack of guidelines, or busy clinics) can lead to delays in treatment. Understanding these reasons is important because it can help improve diabetes care, reduce complications, and help patients live healthier lives.

title: Efficacy and safety of teneligliptin as add-on therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes treated with empagliflozin and metformin: A 24-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial.
text: This study investigated the efficacy and safety of teneligliptin as an add-on therapy in Korean patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with empagliflozin and metformin. In this multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, participants with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) levels 7.0-10.5% treated with empagliflozin 10 mg plus metformin (≥1,000 mg/day) were randomly assigned to receive teneligliptin 20 mg once daily (n = 116) or placebo (n = 119). The primary endpoint was the change in HbA1c from baseline at week 24, and secondary endpoints included changes in fasting plasma glucose (FPG), achievement rate of target HbA1c, and metabolic parameters. At week 24, the teneligliptin group showed a significant reduction in HbA1c compared with the placebo group (least-squares mean difference -0.69%; 95% confidence interval -0.83 to -0.54; P < 0.0001). The proportion of participants achieving HbA1c < 7.0% was significantly higher in the teneligliptin group (59.5% vs 21.9%; P < 0.0001). Teneligliptin also resulted in significant reductions in FPG and glycated albumin compared with placebo. The treatment was well tolerated, with no significant difference in the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events between the groups. The addition of teneligliptin to empagliflozin and metformin therapy resulted in a significant improvement in glycemic control with a favorable safety profile in Korean patients with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled with the dual therapy. Teneligliptin can be a viable option for patients who do not achieve adequate glycemic control with empagliflozin and metformin.

title: Assessment of efficacy and safety of SlimSEB® for weight reduction in overweight and obese subjects at risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus: a prospective, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, controlled, interventional clinical study.
text: The current clinical study intended to explore the clinical efficacy and safety of SlimSEB® for weight reduction in overweight and obese subjects with the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Eighty-seven subjects (43 overweight and 44 obese) were enrolled in this prospective, interventional, randomized, double-blind, parallel, controlled, clinical study. Subjects were randomized for daily administration of SlimSEB® or placebo for 84 days. The change in anthropometric parameters (body weight, BMI and waist circumference), glucose and insulin related factors (fasting plasma glucose, fasting insulin, hemoglobin A1c, homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance, homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function, disposition index, and quantitative insulin sensitivity check index), and lipid profile and biomarkers (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, and CRP) were assessed. Additional outcomes included changes in visual analogue scale and tolerance to SlimSEB®, and the incidences of adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs). The oral supplementation of SlimSEB® was associated with greater reductions in anthropometric, glycemic, lipid and metabolic parameters than placebo. The body weight, BMI and waist circumference showed significantly greater reductions with SlimSEB® than placebo, with adjusted least square mean differences of -2.60 kg and -4.51 kg (p = 0.0045, p < 0.0001), -0.92 kg/m² and -1.80 kg/m² (p = 0.0063, p < 0.0001), and -3.86 cm and -11.03 cm (p = 0.0169, p = 0.0014) in overweight and obese subjects, respectively. Significant adjusted improvements were also observed with SlimSEB® for fasting plasma glucose (-0.45 mmol/L, -0.45 mmol/L; p = 0.0124 and p = 0.0068), HbA1c (-0.65% and -0.67%; p = 0.0199 and p = 0.003), HOMA-IR (-0.47, -0.69; p = 0.0205 and p = 0.002) in overweight and obese subjects. The lipid parameter analyses showed significant adjusted reductions in total cholesterol by 14.21 and 16% with SlimSEB® in overweight and obese subjects, compared with 3.85% reduction and 8.65% increase in placebo (p = 0.0089 and p < 0.0006). The LDL cholesterol also decreased in overweight and obese subjects by 11.61 and 14.63% over 0.88% reduction and 13.39% increase in placebo (p = 0.0154 and p = 0.0002). CRP levels decreased by 13.6 and 17.3% with SlimSEB® in overweight and obese subjects, respectively, with a significant inter-group difference in obese subjects (p = 0.0001). SlimSEB® was well tolerated at the studied dose, with eight mild AEs reported, none of which was considered related to SlimSEB®, and no SAEs were reported. Daily intake of SlimSEB® resulted in a reduction in body weight, BMI and waist circumference, and showed beneficial changes in selected glucose and lipid parameters, and promote a healthy inflammatory response. These findings suggest that SlimSEB® may support weight management and metabolic health. Further well-designed clinical trials involving larger study populations and longer intervention periods are needed to understand the underlying mechanisms of action. The current investigation was registered in the Clinical Trial Registry, India (CTRI registration number: CTRI/2023/11/059798), and registered on 14/11/2023 (https://ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=OTM3Mjk=&Enc=&userName=).

title: The osteoclast paradox in type 2 diabetes: low turnover, skeletal fragility, and implications for osteoclast-targeted therapy.
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is increasingly recognized as a skeletal-fragility condition characterized at the population level by lower circulating markers of bone formation and resorption, frequently preserved or increased DXA-derived areal bone mineral density (aBMD), and increased fracture risk. These observations arise from different measurement levels and have not been demonstrated to constitute a single biological phenotype within the same individuals. In this Review, we use the term "osteoclast paradox" as an author-proposed heuristic framework-not a diagnostic entity or an established mechanistic syndrome-to organize apparent dissociations among circulating bone-turnover markers, osteoclast-lineage biology, tissue-level remodeling, matrix properties, and treatment response in T2DM. Direct human evidence linking these levels remains limited. A small exploratory human study suggests a possible dissociation between osteoclast precursor phenotype and mature function, whereas histomorphometry indicates that remodeling can remain coupled despite delayed progression; neither observation establishes generalized preservation or enhancement of mature osteoclast resorptive function. Experimental studies further show context-dependent effects of hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end products, oxidative stress, insulin signaling, inflammation, and the marrow environment on osteoclast differentiation and function. The observed skeletal phenotype is also modified by obesity and body composition, renal and microvascular disease, and glucose-lowering or weight-loss therapies; these overlapping exposures should not be attributed automatically to T2DM itself. Matrix glycation, altered material behavior, osteocyte dysfunction, osteoblast-lineage impairment, and altered basic multicellular unit kinetics may contribute to skeletal fragility despite low circulating turnover markers. Pooled randomized-trial analyses suggest that antiresorptive treatment responses are not obviously attenuated by T2DM, although diabetes-specific fracture estimates are unevenly powered and treatment response should not be interpreted as mechanistic validation of the proposed framework. Osteoanabolic studies demonstrate aBMD, trabecular bone score, and early microarchitectural responses, but diabetes-specific fracture endpoints remain limited. The framework is therefore intended to separate non-equivalent biological and clinical endpoints, identify evidence gaps, and generate testable hypotheses for osteoclast-targeted research. Current treatment should remain fracture risk-based rather than guided by an unvalidated turnover phenotype.

title: Vitamin B12 deficiency in metformin-treated adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus in Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Vitamin B12 deficiency is a clinically important complication of long-term metformin therapy and may contribute to hematological and neurological complications in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Although metformin is widely used in Africa, comprehensive evidence on the prevalence and associated factors of vitamin B12 deficiency among metformin-treated patients remains limited and fragmented. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency and identify factors associated with its occurrence among adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus receiving metformin in Africa. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, AJOL, AIM, DOAJ, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and reference lists from January 1, 2000, to October 18, 2026. Eligible studies reported the prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency in metformin-treated adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Methodological quality was assessed using JBI tools, and pooled prevalence was estimated using a random-effects REML model in Stata 17.0. Nineteen studies involving 3108 adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus from 10 African countries were included. The pooled prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency was 14.7% (95% CI: 9.7-21.6%), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I2 = 94.69%) and a 95% prediction interval of 2.0-59.7%, indicating considerable variation in the expected prevalence across different clinical and population settings. The included studies used heterogeneous study-defined diagnostic criteria and laboratory methods for vitamin B12 deficiency. Therefore, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a summary of the available African studies rather than as a continent-wide prevalence estimate. Narrative synthesis suggested that older age, longer metformin exposure, and higher metformin doses were the most consistently reported factors associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. The available African studies yielded a pooled prevalence of approximately 14.7%, based on study-specific definitions of vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 assessment may be particularly relevant in patients receiving long-term or high-dose metformin, especially when neurological or hematological manifestations are present. PROSPERO (CRD420261463974).

title: Development and psychometric evaluation of a pre-sarcopenia risk assessment scale for sedentary young adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
text: The aim of this study was to develop a self-reported risk-assessment scale for pre-sarcopenia-related behavioral and functional risk in sedentary young adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and to assess its psychometric properties. Following COSMIN guidelines, an initial item pool was generated via literature review and semi-structured interviews, then refined through two Delphi rounds and a pilot survey. A convenience sample of 435 patients (June 2024-February 2025) was recruited; 215 participated in exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and 220 in confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Reliability and validity were evaluated. The final 18-item scale comprises four dimensions: behavioral risk perception, muscle function monitoring, sedentary behavior characteristics, and intervention intention. EFA extracted four factors explaining 81.25% of the total variance. CFA demonstrated good model fit (χ 2/df = 1.583, RMSEA = 0.076, SRMR = 0.038, CFI = 0.965, GFI = 0.917). The scale-level content validity index was 0.92; Cronbach's α was 0.894 and split-half reliability 0.792. The newly developed scale showed satisfactory preliminary reliability and construct validity. It should be regarded as a self-reported risk-assessment instrument for pre-sarcopenia-related behavioral and functional risk, rather than a diagnostic or case-finding tool for pre-sarcopenia. Positive risk identification should be confirmed by objective measures such as handgrip strength, muscle mass, and physical performance.

title: Paeonidin- and Cyanidin-Rich Fractions Ameliorate Gut Microbiota and Serum Metabolites in Rats with Type 2 Diabetes.
text: Dietary intervention could modulate gut microbiota, improve insulin resistance status, and play a key role in blood glucose regulation. This study investigated the regulatory effects of paeonidin- and cyanidin-rich fractions (PCs) on gut microbiota and serum metabolites in high-fat, high-sucrose diet/streptozotocin-induced type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) rats. Following a 14-day intragastric PC administration (25 mg/kg/day), non-targeted metabolomics and 16S rDNA sequencing were performed. PC intervention significantly reduced water intake, and even the effects on lipids were limited. Among 83 differential serum metabolites, PC restored 28, including tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) and lysophosphatidylcholines, while decreasing glycated branched-chain amino acid derivatives. PC-enriched Bifidobacterium, Sediminibacterium, SC-I-84, and Fusicatenibacter, which positively correlated with TUDCA. Additionally, PC upregulated insulin secretion and p53 signaling pathways with increased RYR2 and FAS, while downregulating pentose and glucuronate interconversion enzymes (UxaC, XylB). These findings suggest that the amelioration of glycolipid metabolic disorders and insulin secretion defects by PC may be associated with a synergistic gut microbiota-metabolite-enzyme axis, potentially involving Bifidobacterium-mediated TUDCA elevation and downstream modulation of metabolic enzymes.

title: Relationship Between Lower Urinary Tract Problems and Quality of Life in Women with Type 2 Diabetes.
text: Background: This study aimed to examine the relationship between lower urinary tract symptoms and quality of life in women with type 2 diabetes. Materials and Methods: The population of this descriptive cross-sectional study consisted of women with type 2 diabetes who presented to the Urology, and Endocrinology and Metabolism Diseases outpatient clinics for examination between 15 May and 15 November 2025. In the study sample, 372 women were included. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews in outpatient clinics. Hierarchical multiple linear regression and sensitivity analyses were performed. Results: The mean age of the 372 participants was 53.23 ± 13.13 years, and the mean duration of diabetes was 8.81 years. Overall, 52.2% reported a urinary tract infection within the previous six months. The mean BFLUTS-SF total score was 28.63 ± 16.75. Higher BFLUTS-SF scores were negatively correlated with SF-36 dimensions, particularly social functioning (r = -0.562) and bodily pain (r = -0.559). Hierarchical regression analyses revealed significant negative associations between lower urinary tract symptom burden and quality-of-life dimensions after adjustment for relevant sociodemographic and clinical variables. Sensitivity analyses using the combined BFLUTS-LUTS symptom score supported these findings. Conclusions and Recommendations: Greater lower urinary tract symptom burden was associated with poorer health-related quality of life in women with type 2 diabetes, particularly in social functioning, bodily pain, and physical functioning. These findings highlight the importance of routinely assessing lower urinary tract symptoms alongside glycemic parameters in diabetes management. Early identification and multidisciplinary interventions may help address symptom burden and improve quality of life.

title: Effect of a multi-theory model-based AI-HEALS intervention on self-management among outpatients with multimorbidity involving hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia: a randomised controlled trial protocol.
text: Multimorbidity involving hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia increases the risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. Effective self-management is essential for disease control and prevention of complications. However, existing interventions for patients with multimorbidity often lack individualisation, continuous support and patient engagement. To address these challenges, this study will evaluate a personalised intervention guided by the multi-theory model (MTM) of health behaviour change and delivered through the Artificial Intelligence Health Education Accurately Linking System (AI-HEALS) for patients with multimorbidity involving at least two of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia. This study aims to evaluate the effects of the intervention on physiological indicators, self-management behaviours, psychological status and quality of life. This study is conducted in the outpatient setting of a hospital in Zhejiang province and adopts a single-blind randomised controlled trial design, in which outcome assessors are blinded to group allocation. Adults aged 18 years or older with multimorbidity involving at least two of the following conditions: hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidaemia will be recruited and randomly assigned to either routine care or a 3 month MTM-based AI-HEALS intervention. The primary outcome is the change in systolic blood pressure, assessed at baseline, 3 months and 6 months. Secondary outcomes include diastolic blood pressure, glycated haemoglobin, blood lipid, body mass index, anxiety and depressive states, self-management, medication adherence, self-efficacy, perceived social support, eating behaviour, physical activity and quality of life. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Pujiang County Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine (Approval No. 2026C04). Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants before enrolment. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and academic conferences. ChiCTR2600117853.

title: The Relationship Between Preoperative Hemoglobin, Albumin, Lymphocyte, and Platelet Score and Postoperative Outcomes in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery.
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) significantly increases the risk of morbidity and mortality following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Identifying preoperative prognostic indicators is critical for improving postoperative outcomes in this patient population. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between the preoperative Hemoglobin, Albumin, Lymphocyte, and Platelet (HALP) score and postoperative complications and mortality in T2DM patients undergoing isolated CABG surgery. A total of 675 T2DM patients who underwent isolated CABG surgery between 2018 and 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Patients were grouped according to their preoperative HALP scores. Demographic characteristics, postoperative complications, intensive care and hospital stay durations, revascularization needs, and one-year mortality rates were compared between groups. Patients with lower HALP scores experienced significantly higher rates of postoperative infections, pneumonia, renal dysfunction, longer intensive care unit/hospital stays, and increased one-year mortality (P < 0.001). These findings indicate a strong correlation between nutritional/immune status and surgical outcomes in diabetic patients. Preoperative HALP score may serve as a reliable, cost-effective associated factor of postoperative complications and mortality in T2DM patients undergoing CABG. Incorporating HALP scoring into routine preoperative assessment could enhance risk stratification and perioperative management strategies.

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and lung cancer risk in patients with type 2 diabetes and pulmonary nodules.
text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are associated with lower risk of several cancers in observational studies, whereas randomized-trial meta-analyses indicate little or no effect; lung-cancer-specific evidence is limited. We emulated a target trial in the TriNetX federated network comparing new users of GLP-1RAs versus metformin among adults with type 2 diabetes and a coded pulmonary nodule. Eligibility was assessed on or before the first qualifying prescription, a 12-month washout applied in both arms, and cohorts were 1:1 propensity score matched on 51 covariates. Outcomes were ascertained from day 90 to day 1,095. Drug-target cis-Mendelian randomization (MR) tested genetically proxied GLP1R expression against lung cancer in three GWAS consortia, with colocalization. Among 12,622 matched pairs, lung cancer incidence was 1.60% with GLP-1RAs versus 2.14% with metformin (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64-0.92); distant metastasis (HR 0.58, 0.47-0.71) and systemic anti-cancer therapy (0.58, 0.46-0.74) were also lower with GLP-1RAs. Versus metformin, the lung cancer hazard ratio was 0.72 (0.56-0.92) at a 180-day and 0.77 (0.54-1.09) at a 365-day landmark; it was 0.74 (0.59-0.93) versus DPP-4 and 0.85 (0.69-1.05) versus SGLT2 inhibitors. Negative controls were null. MR showed no association between GLP1R expression and lung cancer; colocalization showed little signal at the locus. GLP-1RA initiation was associated with lower short-term lung cancer incidence versus metformin, but the null SGLT2 comparison and null genetic findings do not support sustained receptor-mediated chemoprevention. These findings caution against interpreting early observational signals as chemoprevention and define what future GLP-1RA-cancer studies should report.
source: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology

title: First recorded hypertension and subsequent cardiovascular and kidney outcomes after newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes: a population-based cohort study.
text: Coexistence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and hypertension is associated with adverse cardiovascular and mortality outcomes. However, whether first recorded hypertension during the course of T2D marks a transition to a higher-risk phase remains uncertain. We examined subsequent outcomes and recorded assessments around hypertension recognition. Using regional electronic health records from Ningbo, China, we included 256,221 adults with a first recorded T2D diagnosis from 2012 through 2024 who had no recorded hypertension or major cardiorenal disease. We fitted Cox models with newly recorded hypertension as a time-varying exposure, adjusting for age, sex, calendar year, healthcare contact, comorbidities, medications, blood pressure, glycemia, lipids, kidney function, and liver enzymes. The primary outcome was the first occurrence of myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, or all-cause death. Secondary outcomes included individual components above and a modified version of three-point major adverse cardiovascular events (3P-MACE), comprising myocardial infarction, stroke, and all-cause death. Among 107,946 patients with first recorded hypertension, assessment records were compared over six months before and after its recognition. Among 256,221 adults, hypertension was first recorded during follow-up in 107,946 (42.13%). During a median follow-up of 4.11 years, 34,371 primary outcomes occurred. Incidence rates were 58.05 and 16.10 per 1,000 person-years during exposed and unexposed time, respectively (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 2.49; 95% CI 2.43-2.55). The adjusted HR for modified 3P-MACE was 2.47 (95% CI 2.40-2.55). The primary association was strongest within 90 days of recognition (HR 3.37; 95% CI 3.10-3.65) and persisted beyond three years (HR 2.15; 95% CI 2.07-2.23). Outpatient-contact density was 17.42 versus 3.73 per person-year during exposed and unexposed time. Recorded urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) assessment increased from 3.35% to 4.15%, and assessment of both kidney function and UACR from 2.94% to 3.72%. First recorded hypertension identified a subsequent period of substantially higher observed cardiorenal and mortality risk, accompanied by limited increases in recorded assessment. New hypertension recognition may offer an opportunity to review existing cardiovascular and kidney assessments. Prospective studies should test whether structured reassessment at recognition improves care and outcomes.

title: Temporal stability of an electronic health record-driven machine learning model predicting type 2 diabetes among patients with mental illness.
text: We previously trained and tested a machine learning model to predict incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) in patients with mental illness using electronic health record (EHR) data from routine clinical practice. This hyperparameter-tuned XGBoost model - based on information on sex, age and mean HbA1c within the past two years - predicts whether a patient will meet criteria for T2D in the two years following each contact to psychiatric services. The performance of such a model may drift over time due to changes in standards of care, baseline risk, registration procedures, etc. Therefore, we set out to examine its temporal stability. In the present study, we fitted the model described above on EHR data from January 1, 2013 to December 31, 2017, and examined its stability in predicting T2D two years into the future for patients with contacts in 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023, respectively. Performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). The model showed good discriminative performance across all years (AUROC for 2018 = 0.84, 2019 = 0.83, 2020 = 0.87, 2021 = 0.80, 2022 = 0.84, 2023 = 0.80), with a linear model estimating a decrease in AUROC for T2D prediction of only 0.004 per year (95%CI: -0.024; 0.016). Secondary analyses suggested that models trained on recent data (past year) may achieve similar or better discrimination than models trained on longer historical periods. The temporal stability of the T2D prediction model supports its potential for clinical implementation, facilitating early detection and tailored interventions, while highlighting the importance of continued evaluation.

title: All-cause mortality and associated factors according to age at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in Finland.
text: To assess all-cause mortality among individuals with type 2 diabetes in Finland and to evaluate the impact of age at diabetes diagnosis and other clinical risk factors using nationwide real-world registry data. This was a retrospective dynamic cohort study. Data on 485 713 patients with type 2 diabetes receiving primary and specialized care were retrieved from the Finnish Diabetes Registry for the period 2018 to 2023. Age- and sex-adjusted mortality ratios (SMRs) were calculated by comparing observed deaths with those expected based on mortality rates in the Finnish population without diabetes. SMRs were calculated for the overall cohort and by age at diabetes diagnosis (≤40, 41–79, and ≥80 years). Multivariable rate ratio (RR) analyses assessed factors associated with all-cause mortality in the overall cohort and by age at diagnosis, including sex, baseline age, diabetes duration, hemoglobin A1c, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, chronic kidney disease (CKD) risk, cardiovascular diseases, other complications, and medication use. Overall SMR was 92 (95% CI 91 to 92), decreasing from 288 (95% CI 273 to 304) in those diagnosed at ≤40 years to 56 (95% CI 55 to 57) at ≥80 years. In the overall cohort, mortality was strongly associated with heart failure (RR 2.07, 95% CI 2.01 to 2.13) and high or very high CKD risk (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.61 to 1.70). Insulin alone and combined with oral glucose-lowering medications or glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists were associated with increased mortality (RR 3.37, 95% CI 3.10 to 3.67 and 1.63, 95% CI 1.52 to 1.75, respectively), whereas non-insulin glucose-lowering, lipid-lowering, and renal-protective medications were associated with lower mortality (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.98; RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.59 and RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.75, respectively). Early-onset type 2 diabetes was associated with markedly increased mortality, whereas mortality among those diagnosed at ≥80 years was lower than in the population without diabetes. Heart failure, CKD, and insulin use were the strongest predictors of mortality, highlighting the need for targeted management of high-risk individuals.

title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial.
text: To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes. Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial. 145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China. 12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study. Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years. The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume. 6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm3, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01). Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311.

title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Pentacyclic Triterpene Derivatives as Intestinal FXR Antagonists for Type 2 Diabetes.
text: Intestinal farnesoid X receptor (FXR) antagonism has emerged as a strategy to enhance endogenous glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) secretion and improve metabolic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Dihydrooleanolic acid methyl ester (DKS26) served as the scaffold for the synthesis of 64 pentacyclic triterpene derivatives modified at the terminal carboxyl group and C-3/C-12 positions. Esterification of the terminal carboxylate emerged as a determinant of FXR antagonism, identifying 4l bearing a tetrazole-containing side chain and C-12 hydroxyl motif. Compound 4l antagonized FXR in a TR-FRET assay (IC50 = 11.79 μM), a fivefold improvement over DKS26. In NCI-H716 cells, 4l reduced NR0B2 (SHP) mRNA expression and markedly stimulated GLP-1 secretion. In HFD/STZ-induced diabetic mice, oral 4l improved glycemia, increased circulating GLP-1 and insulin, and alleviated dyslipidemia and organ injury markers. These findings establish the pentacyclic triterpene scaffold as a platform for FXR antagonism and identify 4l as a lead for further optimization.

title: Discovery of Novel GPR119 Agonists with Improved Kinetic Solubility and Drug-like Properties for Type 2 Diabetes Treatment.
text: GPR119 is a compelling therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes due to its role in promoting glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide (GIP), and glucose-dependent insulin secretion. This study aimed to develop a series of novel GPR119 agonists with exceptional kinetic solubility over a broad pH range featuring an N-alkyl piperidine head and pyrrolidine 2-carboxamide tail. Among the synthesized compounds, 18f demonstrated potent activity, exhibiting nanomolar potency (EC50 = 12.6 nM) in the hGPR119-cAMP functional assay as well as a 33.3% hypoglycemic effect in an oral glucose tolerance test. A significant enhancement (175.9%) of total GLP-1 levels was observed at 10 mg/kg administration of compound 18f. Further, compound 18f outperformed the antidiabetic effect of sitagliptin as the DPP-4 inhibitor in female Zucker Diabetic Fatty rats. Furthermore, the favorable pharmacokinetic profiles of compound 18f underscore its potential as a promising lead compound for type 2 diabetes treatment.

title: Prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus, risk factors, and complications in Middle East and North African region: A systematic review.
text: BackgroundType 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is a rapidly growing health challenge in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, contributing to increasing morbidity and mortality.ObjectivesThis review synthesizes evidence on the prevalence of T2DM, risk factors, and complications in the MENA region.MethodsFollowing PRISMA reporting guidelines and PROSPERO registration (CRD420251111168), systematic searches were conducted for studies published between 2015 and 2025.ResultsAcross the 19 included studies, the prevalence and burden of T2DM varied considerably across the MENA region. Regional data indicated an 85.5% increase in diabetes prevalence between 1990 and 2019, while individual population-based studies reported T2DM prevalence of 32.0% in north-eastern Tunisia and 15.3% in southwestern Iran. In Jordan, age-standardized diabetes prevalence increased from 13.0% in 1994 to 23.7% in 2017. Older age, obesity, physical inactivity, hypertension, central adiposity, family history of diabetes, and socioeconomic factors were commonly associated with T2DM. Among individuals with established T2DM, microvascular and macrovascular complications were reported in 17.7% and 10.7%, respectively, while diabetic neuropathy affected 15.3%-23.0% in selected studies. Suboptimal glycaemic and cardiovascular risk-factor control was also frequently reported.ConclusionT2DM constitutes a substantial and heterogeneous public health challenge across the MENA region. The findings indicate a need for context-specific strategies that integrate prevention, early detection, culturally appropriate lifestyle interventions, and comprehensive long-term disease management. Strengthening multidisciplinary approaches and addressing modifiable risk factors may help reduce the future health burden associated with T2DM across the region.

title: Remote Patient Monitoring for Type 2 Diabetes Management During Pregnancy: A Feasibility Study and Outcomes Analysis within a Medicaid Population.
text: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) during pregnancy is a growing public health concern due to its increasing prevalence and association with adverse maternal and neonatal health outcomes. This study assessed the feasibility of using a Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) iGlucose glucometer to manage T2DM during pregnancy among a cohort of Medicaid women and compared clinical outcomes among RPM users and women using a standard glucometer. Thirty-three pregnant women utilizing Medicaid with T2DM were provided an RPM iGlucose device. Participants completed a pre-post survey and semi-structured interview. To assess clinical outcomes, we created a Connected Device Use group, consisting of participants who used the iGlucose device or a continuous glucose monitoring device, and a Standard Paper Log group, consisting of individuals who used a standard glucometer. A significant decrease between pre-post scores was seen for Appraisal of Diabetes (p=0.0046) and Perceived Stress (p=0.0296). Treatment Self-Efficacy (p=0.0030) and General Self-Efficacy (p=0.0129) significantly increased with iGlucose device use. Overall, perceptions of the iGlucose device were positive with advantages including automatic upload of glucose readings, ease of use, increased self-efficacy, perceived better care, and decreased stress and anxiety. No significant difference in clinical outcomes was seen between groups. By automatically uploading glucose readings, remote patient monitoring significantly lightens the burden for people with chronic conditions. This technology provides healthcare clinicians with accurate, real-time data which can lead to better informed and proactive care decisions.

title: Hedonic hunger and eating-disorder symptoms in relation to glycaemic control across treatment regimens in adults with type 2 diabetes: a cross-sectional study.
text: Eating-related behavioural factors may contribute to the complexity of glycaemic management in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but their relationships with treatment context remain insufficiently understood. This study examined hedonic hunger and eating-disorder symptom dimensions in relation to glycaemic control across different treatment regimens in adults with T2DM. This cross-sectional study included 203 adults with T2DM attending an outpatient diet clinic in southeastern Turkey between March and September 2025. Participants were receiving oral antidiabetic medication only (n = 108), insulin only (n = 32), or combined oral medication plus insulin therapy (n = 63). Hedonic hunger was assessed using the Power of Food Scale (PFS), and eating-disorder symptom dimensions using the 13-item Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire-Short Form (EDE-Q-13). Anthropometric measurements, 24-h dietary recall data, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) were obtained. Hierarchical linear regression was used to examine factors associated with HbA1c. HbA1c differed substantially across treatment groups and was highest in the insulin-only group (p < 0.001). Several PFS subscales and EDE-Q-13 symptom dimensions also differed between groups, although their effect sizes were small. Selected PFS dimensions were weakly positively correlated with glycaemic indicators, whereas the EDE-Q-13 eating-restraint subscale and total score showed weak inverse correlations with HbA1c. In the fully adjusted model, insulin-only and combination therapy were associated with higher HbA1c compared with oral medication only, while body mass index (BMI) was inversely associated with HbA1c. Neither the PFS food available subscale nor the EDE-Q-13 total score remained independently associated with HbA1c. The final model explained 27.2% of the variance in HbA1c (adjusted r 2 = 0.230). Treatment context was more strongly related to glycaemic status than the behavioural measures assessed, although modest differences in hedonic hunger and eating-disorder symptom dimensions were evident across treatment regimens. These findings suggest that eating-related behavioural characteristics may provide complementary information in nutritional assessment and should be interpreted alongside the broader clinical context of T2DM management.

title: Feasibility and acceptability of a culturally adapted medical nutrition therapy intervention for adults with type 2 diabetes in Benin: a single-arm mixed-method study.
text: Medical nutrition therapy (MNT) is a cornerstone of type 2 diabetes (T2D) management, but access to culturally appropriate nutrition care remains limited in many low-resource settings. We evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of OSanDiaBé, a culturally adapted MNT intervention for adults with T2D in Cotonou, Benin, West Africa. Guided by the Obesity-Related Behavioral Intervention Trials (ORBIT) framework, we conducted an ORBIT Phase IIa single-arm, pre-post mixed-methods feasibility study among adults aged 40-65 years with T2D. The intervention combined two individualized nutrition counseling sessions with eight group sessions delivered by trained dietitians and nutritionists in community settings over 12 weeks. Primary outcomes were recruitment, retention, attendance, intervention fidelity, and acceptability. Secondary exploratory outcomes included diabetes knowledge, diet quality, physical activity, diabetes self-efficacy, anthropometry, blood pressure, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and using paired comparisons, while qualitative data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Among 42 adults screened, 36 were enrolled (85.7%), and 30 completed the 12-week follow-up (83.3% retention). Mean attendance was 7.2 of 8 group sessions, and intervention fidelity exceeded 85%. The prespecified acceptability progression criterion was met, with a mean overall satisfaction rating of 4.87 ± 0.35, exceeding the prespecified threshold of ≥4.0. Exploratory improvements were observed in overall diabetes knowledge (50.0-83.3%), diet quality (+9.29 points), regular physical activity participation (26.7-86.7%), and diabetes self-efficacy (+15.45 points). Mean HbA1c decreased by 0.58 percentage points (95% CI -1.12 to -0.04), with modest reductions also observed in body weight and body mass index. Qualitative findings identified culturally tailored educational materials, practical tools, peer support, and community-based delivery as important factors supporting participant engagement and intervention acceptability. OSanDiaBé was feasible to implement and highly acceptable among adults with T2D in urban Benin. These findings support progression to a pilot randomized controlled trial to further evaluate the intervention and generate preliminary estimates to inform subsequent effectiveness, implementation, economic, and scalability research.

title: Association of longitudinal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D trajectories with subsequent liver stiffness increase in patients with early-onset type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.
text: A single serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] measurement may not adequately reflect long-term vitamin D exposure. We evaluated the associations of longitudinal 25(OH)D trajectories with subsequent liver stiffness measurement (LSM) increases in patients with early-onset type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. This retrospective study included 286 patients managed between 2022 and 2025. Latent class mixed-effects modeling identified 25(OH)D trajectories before a 1-year landmark. The primary outcome was a follow-up LSM value that was both at least 20% (relative) and at least 2.0 kPa (absolute) higher than the landmark value; the conservative sensitivity outcome required increases of at least 30% and at least 3.0 kPa, respectively. Logistic regression models were fitted across 50 pseudo-class draws and pooled using Rubin's rules. Follow-up LSM was analyzed by analysis of covariance adjusted for landmark LSM and prespecified covariates. A segmented linear mixed-effects model compared LSM slopes before and after the landmark. Three trajectories were identified: persistently low (n = 95), increasing (n = 84), and stable high (n = 107). The primary-outcome rates were 54.7%, 33.3%, and 18.7%, respectively. Compared with the stable-high trajectory, the odds ratios in the prespecified primary model were 3.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.68-6.61) for the persistently low trajectory and 1.98 (95% CI, 1.03-3.82) for the increasing trajectory. After additional adjustment for vitamin D supplementation, cumulative dose, metabolic factors, and medications, the corresponding odds ratios were 2.87 (95% CI, 1.38-5.96) and 1.84 (95% CI, 0.91-3.72). Under the conservative outcome definition, the corresponding odds ratios were 3.18 (95% CI, 1.39-7.27) and 1.71 (95% CI, 0.76-3.84). Adjusted follow-up LSM was higher by 1.07 kPa (95% CI, 0.66-1.48) and 0.52 kPa (95% CI, 0.10-0.94), respectively. The post-landmark LSM slope exceeded the pre-landmark slope by 0.98 kPa/year (95% CI, 0.80-1.16). The persistently low 25(OH)D trajectory showed the most consistent association with subsequent LSM increase. The increasing trajectory showed weaker, outcome-definition-dependent associations and coincided with more frequent vitamin D supplementation and a greater reduction in body mass index. These findings should be interpreted as longitudinal associations rather than causal effects or evidence of validated individual-level predictive performance.

title: Associations of health literacy, dietary decisional balance, and dietary self-efficacy with dietary self-management behaviors in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a cross-sectional study.
text: Dietary self-management is essential for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet the factors associated with it and their interrelationships remain underexplored. To examine the associations of health literacy, dietary decisional balance, and dietary self-efficacy with dietary self-management behaviors in patients with T2DM. This was a cross-sectional study conducted in four endocrinology departments of four tertiary hospitals in Guangdong province from September 2022 to January 2023. A total of 387 inpatients diagnosed as T2DM were consecutively sampled. Health literacy was measured using the Health Literacy Scale (FCCHL). Dietary decisional balance was assessed using the Dietary Decisional Balance Scale, dietary self-efficacy using the diet-specific subscale of the Stanford Self-efficacy for Diabetes scale, and dietary self-management behaviors using the general diet domain of the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities scale. The primary model was estimated using structural equation modeling in Mplus 7.0 with the robust maximum likelihood estimator (MLR). For inference on the indirect associations, the primary model was re-estimated using maximum likelihood (ML) with 5, 000 bootstrap draws, and bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were obtained. A covariate-adjusted SEM was further estimated by including sociodemographic and clinical characteristics (age, sex, marital status, education, residence, occupation, income, smoking, disease duration, complications, and hospital). Both the primary and dimension-specific SEMs showed good fit. A higher level of health literacy, dietary decisional balance, and dietary self-efficacy was associated with better dietary self-management behaviors. Health literacy showed a significant indirect association with dietary self-management behaviors through dietary self-efficacy (β = 0.077, 95% CI: 0.017 - 0.137, p = 0.012), but the indirect association through dietary decisional balance was not significant (β = 0.028, 95% CI: -0.006 - 0.062, p = 0.101). Dimension-specific analyses further showed that communicative health literacy was positively associated with dietary self-efficacy (β = 0.162, p = 0.034) and dietary self-management behaviors (β = 0.135, p = 0.043), whereas critical health literacy was positively associated with perceived benefits (β = 0.332, p < 0.01), and perceived barriers were negatively associated with dietary self-management behaviors (β = -0.166, p = 0.001). Diabetes care should move beyond knowledge transmission by supporting patients' communicative and critical health literacy, strengthening dietary self-efficacy, and identifying and addressing perceived dietary barriers to support dietary self-management behaviors in patients with T2DM.

title: Effect of social media-based diabetes self-management education and support on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Digital interventions are being used for diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES), but evidence of their effectiveness is limited. This review and meta-analysis examined the impact of social media-based DSMES on glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), and an exploratory post hoc analysis assessed the effect of intervention duration on outcomes. A PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was conducted using PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PsycINFO, with 789 records screened and one additional record identified through a saved search (total of 790). Eligible studies were English-language articles published over a just-over-ten-year period. These studies focused on adults with T2DM, reported HbA1c outcomes, and utilized social media for DSMES interventions. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). A random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled mean differences (MD) in HbA1c percentage points, with subgroup analyses by intervention duration; heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. This systematic review identified 13 studies, including 11 RCTs for the meta-analysis. The pooled analysis demonstrated a statistically significant overall effect favoring the intervention (MD = -0.44 HbA1c percentage points, 95% CI -0.87 to -0.00, p = 0.05). Substantial between-study heterogeneity was observed (I² = 91%), and the 95% prediction interval ranged from -2.08 to 1.20. Interventions of 3 months or less showed no significant effect (MD = -0.12, 95%CI -0.51 to 0.28, p = .56), whereas interventions longer than three months showed a large, statistically significant effect (MD = -1.02, 95% CI -1.75 to -0.29, p = 0.01). The test for between-subgroup differences was significant (Q = 4.56, df = 1, p = .03). Social media-based DSMES interventions may be associated with improvements in glycemic outcomes in adults with T2DM. While interventions longer than three months showed greater pooled effects, interpret these post hoc results carefully because of significant heterogeneity (I² = 91%).
