This pooled estimate represents an average effect across heterogeneous interventions and populations and therefore should not be understood as a uniform effect of social media-based DSMES. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/BZR6P, OSF Registries BZR6P.
source: Frontiers in clinical diabetes and healthcare

title: Association of Type 2 diabetes remission with mortality and vascular outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies.
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remission is increasingly recognized as an achievable clinical state. However, its long-term associations with mortality and vascular complications remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies to evaluate the associations of T2DM remission with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, microvascular complications, and macrovascular complications. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to July 20, 2026, without language restrictions. Longitudinal studies were eligible if they included adults with T2DM, assessed remission before outcome ascertainment, compared participants who achieved remission with those who did not achieve or maintain remission, and reported an adjusted effect estimate after at least 12 months of follow-up. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Ten studies met the eligibility criteria, of which nine contributed to the quantitative synthesis. T2DM remission was not significantly associated with all-cause mortality (3 studies; HR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.53-1.21; I² = 65.0%), but pooled estimates suggested lower hazards of cardiovascular events (5 studies; HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.59-0.80; I² = 11.7%) and microvascular complications (5 studies; HR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.38-0.93; I² = 93.4%). In an exploratory analysis of broader macrovascular complications, the pooled estimate also suggested a lower hazard (6 studies; HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.58-0.93; I² = 75.6%), although substantial heterogeneity was observed. Sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the overall direction of the pooled estimates. The certainty of evidence was low for cardiovascular events and very low for all-cause mortality, microvascular complications, and macrovascular complications. T2DM remission was associated with lower pooled hazards of cardiovascular events, while the associations with microvascular and macrovascular complications were less certain due to substantial heterogeneity and limited precision. The association between T2DM remission and all-cause mortality remained uncertain. These findings suggest a favorable long-term prognostic association of T2DM remission, although they should not be interpreted as evidence of causality. Long-term glycemic monitoring, comprehensive risk-factor management, and surveillance for diabetes-related complications should therefore continue after remission.

title: Effect of a lacto-vegetarian diet combined with 14-hour time-restricted eating on metabolic outcomes in women with Type 2 diabetes: a 24-week randomized controlled trial.
text: Women with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) often require interventions that are culturally acceptable, practical, sustainable, and can be easily fit into their daily routine to manage their blood sugar levels. Although plant-based dietary patterns and time-restricted fasting have demonstrated metabolic benefits, limited evidence exists on their combined effects in Indian women with T2DM. This trial evaluated whether a lactovegetarian diet combined with 14-hour time-restricted eating improves glycemic and cardiometabolic outcomes compared with usual diabetes care. 96 women (25-60 years) with T2DM were enrolled in a 24-week, multicenter, randomized, open-label parallel-arm trial; 90 completed the study. The participants were divided into two groups: an intervention group following a structured lacto-vegetarian diet combined with 14-hour fasting, and control group receiving usual diabetes care. The diet contained 15-20% protein, 20-25% fat, and improved carbohydrate quality (50-55% from whole grains/high-fiber foods). Biochemical estimations and anthropometric measurements were taken at baseline and 24 weeks. The study employed an intention-to-treat analysis protocol, and the perceived benefits and safety of the intervention were reported. At 24 weeks, baseline-adjusted between-group comparisons showed significantly greater improvements in the intervention group compared with usual diabetes care. The intervention group had lower adjusted values for body weight, BMI, glycemic, and lipid profiles. The adjusted mean HbA1c was 6.53% in the intervention group compared with 7.65% in the control group, with an adjusted mean difference of -1.12% (95% CI: -1.35 to -0.89; p < 0.001). HOMA-IR was also significantly lower in the intervention group, with an adjusted mean difference of -1.84 (95% CI: -2.27 to -1.41; p < 0.001). Adverse events were mild and transient, while most participants reported improved energy, mood, weight loss, and overall health. A culturally adaptable lacto-vegetarian diet combined with a 14-hour time-restricted fasting regimen safely improves metabolic control and insulin sensitivity in women with Type 2 Diabetes, offering a practical, women-centric strategy that may be implementable within structured clinical nutrition services, although its staffing requirements, cost, and scalability require further evaluation. CTRI/2024/09/073262, Ethical Approval by Institutional Committee: SIU/IEC/781A.

title: Effects of henagliflozin proline tablets versus metformin extended-release tablets on body composition in geriatric patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus (HABIT-GEMs): study protocol for a multicentre, randomised, open-label trial.
text: Older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) frequently present with sarcopenic obesity, characterised by excess adiposity and reduced skeletal muscle mass, which is associated with frailty, falls and increased mortality. Glycaemic control alone may be insufficient to address these concomitant changes in body composition, supporting the importance of therapies that preserve muscle mass while also limiting adverse changes in body composition. SGLT2 (sodium–glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors induce weight loss, but their effects on fat and skeletal muscle mass remain incompletely understood, particularly in older adults. Metformin extended-release (metformin XR), a standard first-line therapy, is generally weight neutral and serves as an appropriate comparator. This non-inferiority randomised controlled trial is designed to compare the effects of henagliflozin and metformin XR on body composition in older adults with newly diagnosed T2DM. HABIT-GEMs is a multicentre, randomised, open-label and blinded-endpoint trial conducted in six tertiary hospitals in China. A total of 116 adults aged 60–85 years with newly diagnosed T2DM and elevated body fat will be randomised 1:1 to receive henagliflozin or metformin XR for 24 weeks. The primary outcome is the change in appendicular skeletal muscle mass index from baseline to week 24, assessed using multifrequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Secondary outcomes include body composition, glycaemic indices, inflammatory markers, physical function and safety outcomes. The study has been approved by the Huadong Hospital Ethics Committee (2025K268) and will be conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. Written informed consent will be obtained from all participants. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07323381) and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500112008). Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific conferences. De-identified data may be shared upon reasonable request, subject to ethics approval. NCT07323381 and ChiCTR2500112008.

title: A personalized glucose-aware meal guidance agent for type 2 diabetes self-management.
text: Type 2 diabetes self-management requires individuals to coordinate meals, glucose monitoring, medications, insulin use, and daily routines outside the clinic. Although personalized postprandial glucose response (PPGR) prediction has advanced, numerical predictions alone do not provide the explanations and practical meal-level guidance needed for everyday decision-making. We developed a Personalized Glucose-aware Meal guidance Agent (PiGMA), to translate individualized PPGR predictions into prediction-linked explanations and meal-level guidance. This retrospective proof-of-concept study used 3857 meal records from 140 individuals with type 2 diabetes across two clinical centers, comprising a development cohort of 130 participants with 3580 meals and a held-out cohort of 10 participants with 277 meals. PiGMA combined a personalized PPGR predictor with an instruction-tuned LLaMA3.1-based guidance module trained for meal scoring, dietary advising, and PPGR interpretation. Evaluation included task-specific quantitative benchmarks, five-run G-Eval assessment, and blinded review by two endocrinologists. Participant-specific fine-tuning reduced mean absolute error in seven of ten held-out participants, with significant improvement using five or more days of personalization data. PiGMA outperformed the base model in meal scoring, achieved higher scores for PPGR interpretation, and outperformed medical-domain language models in dietary advising. In blinded expert evaluation, PiGMA received higher PPGR-interpretation ratings and was preferred in 33 of 40 endocrinologist rater-case judgments. However, character-span-level unsupported content was higher for PiGMA than for the base model in PPGR interpretation (12.29 % vs. 3.60 %). PiGMA provides retrospective proof-of-concept evidence that individualized PPGR predictions can be translated into prediction-linked meal guidance. However, the higher hallucination or unsupported-content rate and absence of prospective patient evaluation indicate a safety-reliability trade-off and preclude conclusions regarding clinical effectiveness, safety, or deployment readiness.

title: Antimicrobial Management Following Positive Pneumococcal Urinary Antigen Testing in Hospitalized Community-Acquired Pneumonia: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Pneumococcal urinary antigen testing (PUAT) rapidly supports pneumococcal etiology in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), but how positive results are incorporated into antimicrobial management in routine care remains uncertain. To characterize antimicrobial stewardship actions implemented after a positive PUAT result became available in hospitalized adults with CAP, identify potential areas for improving guideline-concordant antimicrobial management, and compare clinical outcomes according to individual stewardship measures. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study at a Portuguese tertiary hospital including adults hospitalized with CAP and positive PUAT between January 2020 and December 2024. The primary endpoint was antimicrobial spectrum narrowing. Post-PUAT atypical coverage optimization and intravenous-to-oral switch were analyzed separately. Among 332 episodes, antimicrobial spectrum narrowing occurred in 30 (9.0%), after a median of 3 days (Q1-Q3, 2-4). De-escalation to ampicillin or amoxicillin occurred in 7 episodes (2.1%). Post-PUAT atypical coverage optimization occurred in 158 episodes (47.6%) and intravenous-to-oral switch in 71 (21.4%). Narrowing and intravenous-to-oral switch were associated with shorter length of stay in unadjusted analyses, although these associations were exploratory and potentially influenced by clinical stability. In hospitalized PUAT-positive CAP, antimicrobial spectrum narrowing was uncommon, whereas atypical coverage optimization was the most frequent prescribing change. Structured post-result reassessment pathways may help improve guideline-concordant antimicrobial management.
source: Mediterranean journal of hematology and infectious diseases

title: Case Report: Community-acquired pneumonia due to coinfection with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila.
text: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of CAP, whereas Legionella pneumophila is an important atypical pathogen frequently associated with severe disease and an increased risk of complications. Coinfection with these two microorganisms is less frequently reported and may pose significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We present the case of a 62-year-old non-smoking man with multiple comorbidities, including type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, left bundle branch block, arterial hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia, who presented with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, headache, progressive dyspnea, chest pain, productive cough, and purulent sputum. Chest imaging revealed bilateral bronchopneumonia with pleural effusion. Microbiological investigations confirmed coinfection with Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 by urinary antigen testing and Streptococcus pneumoniae by real-time PCR (BioFire) from sputum, with a bacterial load of 10⁷, consistent with acute infection. The patient received combined antimicrobial therapy targeted at the identified etiological pathogens, together with comprehensive supportive and symptomatic treatment to address the multiple complications that occurred during the course of hospitalization. This therapeutic approach resulted in gradual clinical improvement and complete recovery. This case highlights the importance of considering bacterial coinfection in severe community-acquired pneumonia with multiorgan involvement and the value of combining urinary antigen testing with molecular diagnostics for early etiological diagnosis and timely targeted treatment.

title: Utility of the Acute Illness Observation Scale in Assessing Severity of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Children Aged 2-60 Months: A Prospective Observational Study.
text: Early identification of severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children is difficult in resource-limited settings. The Acute Illness Observation Scale (AIOS) is a bedside score based on observable behavioural and physiological parameters. The authors evaluated its utility for severity assessment in children aged 2-60 mo with CAP. In this prospective observational study, 144 children aged 2-60 mo with CAP admitted to a tertiary-care teaching hospital in Central India (June 2023-November 2024) were classified using IMNCI criteria. AIOS was assessed at admission. ROC analysis used IMNCI-defined severe pneumonia as the outcome; the optimal cut-off was selected by the Youden Index. Severe pneumonia was present in 79.9% of participants. Higher AIOS scores were associated with grunting, inability to drink/feed, lethargy, crepitations, bronchial breathing, hypoxaemia, leukocytosis, abnormal chest radiographs, intravenous fluid and antibiotic requirements, and longer oxygen therapy. AIOS ≥12 had sensitivity 73.9%, specificity 89.7%, PPV 96.6%, NPV 46.4%, accuracy 77.1%, and AUC 0.89. AIOS may complement IMNCI-based severity assessment in tertiary emergency and resource-limited settings. Diagnostic performance should be interpreted cautiously because AIOS and IMNCI contain overlapping clinical features and IMNCI is not an independent gold standard.

title: Neurophysin I in Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Prognostic Value and Association With Renal Function.
text: Neurophysin I (NP-I) is an accurate biomarker for the evaluation of oxytocin (OXT), a hypothalamic hormone with putative anti-inflammatory effects. We aimed to assess whether NP-I measured at the time of diagnosis in patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) could predict adverse outcomes. This was a secondary analysis of the prospective STEP Trial (NCT00973154). Blood samples were collected at inclusion for routine laboratory testing, and demographic data and Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) scores were recorded. Adult patients hospitalized with CAP who had normal serum sodium levels at inclusion and an available blood aliquot for NP-I measurement were included. For the purpose of this exploratory analysis across disease severity, patients were selected to achieve approximately equal numbers in low-intermediate (PSI I-III) and high-risk (PSI IV-V) groups, with similar distributions of age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Sixty-five patients were included (male-to-female ratio, 38/27 (58.5%:41.5%), median age 79 (76-83) years). NP-I levels did not differ between low-intermediate and high-risk groups (P = 0.441), between patients with and without CAP-related complications (336 (190-607) vs. 225 (147-539) pM, P = 0.326), or between survivors and non-survivors (199 (121-429) vs. 304 (174-604) pM, P = 0.259). In univariable logistic regression analysis, PSI was significantly associated with in-hospital mortality (odds ratio (OR), 1.027; 95% CI, 1.008-1.049; P = 0.006), but adding NP-I did not improve predictive performance (DeLong's test P = 0.509 vs. PSI alone). Patients with impaired renal function (n = 28) had higher NP-I levels than those with preserved renal function (n = 37) (446 (278-685) vs. 182 (124-403) pM, P < 0.001) and NP-I was inversely associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in multivariable analysis adjusted for age and sex (β = -9.06, P = 0.038). NP-I is elevated in patients with impaired renal function, likely reflecting reduced renal clearance. NP-I measured shortly after CAP diagnosis appears to provide no prognostic information for adverse outcomes.

title: Clinical Course and Outcomes of Complicated Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Children During a 5-Year Period Including the COVID-19 Pandemic.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a significant cause of morbidity in children. Despite widespread vaccination, the incidence and clinical course of complicated CAP (cCAP) continue to pose diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical course, management, and outcomes of children with cCAP in pediatric clinical practice. This retrospective-prospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary university hospital between December 2019 and December 2024. Children under 18 years of age diagnosed with cCAP were included. A total of 52 children were included, with a median age of 70.5 months; 48.1% were female. Parapneumonic effusion (PPE) was the most common complication (86.5%), followed by empyema (21.2%) and necrotizing pneumonia (7.6%). Bacterial pathogens were identified in a minority of cases. Among the limited number of culture-positive cases, group A Streptococcus and Streptococcus pneumoniae were the most frequently identified organisms (11.5%, n = 6). Chest tube thoracostomy was required in 60% of patients, and surgical intervention in 9.6%. Patients requiring chest tube placement had significantly higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels and longer durations of intravenous (IV) antibiotic therapy. No mortality was observed. Despite extensive vaccination in healthy children, cases of cCAP still occur, and the causative agent is isolated only in a very few cases. The findings are consistent with the fact that vaccine breakthrough infections, including those caused by pneumococcal serotypes 3 and 14, may still contribute to severe cCAP, whereas group A Streptococcus was identified in a minority of culture-positive cases. Elevated CRP levels at admission may serve as a useful predictor for invasive interventions.

title: Bacterial spectrum, age and calendar-quarter distribution, and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of isolates recovered from respiratory specimens of children hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia in Chongqing, China: a three-year retrospective study.
text: Community acquired pneumonia (CAP) continues to be an important cause of admission of children in hospitals. This study focused on bacterial isolates from respiratory samples, age distribution and antibiotic resistance patterns of children below seven years admitted with CAP in Chongqing, China from January 2023 to December 2025. Of the 2,988 patients included in the study, 884 (29.59%) were positive for bacterial culture, with 930 isolates. The predominant species were Haemophilus influenzae (43.01%), Moraxella catarrhalis (22.80%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (14.84%), and Staphylococcus aureus (10.32%). The distribution of recovered isolates differed significantly across age groups (P < 0.01). After adjustment for calendar year, overall culture positivity did not differ significantly across quarters (P = 0.085), although a significant quarter-by-year interaction was observed (P = 0.005), indicating that quarterly patterns varied between years. Year-adjusted quarterly associations were also observed for H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, and S. aureus. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed high non-susceptibility to ampicillin (65.25%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (62.33%) among H. influenzae isolates, and to erythromycin and clindamycin (99.19% for each) among S. pneumoniae isolates. Oxacillin non-susceptibility was observed in 20.25% of tested S. aureus isolates, while imipenem non-susceptibility was uncommon among tested Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates. These findings support continued regional microbiological surveillance and may inform institutional antimicrobial stewardship. Because nasotracheal suction specimens may contain colonizing organisms, culture recovery alone does not establish the bacterial causes of CAP.

title: Community-acquired pneumonia in Europe: heterogeneity, evidence gaps, and priorities for care.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a leading cause of hospital and intensive care admission and infectious death in Europe, particularly among older adults, people with multimorbidity, and immunocompromised patients. This Review argues that persistent uncertainty in CAP evidence largely reflects heterogeneity across eight domains: case definition, host, pathogen ascertainment, severity, inflammatory response, treatment exposure, timing and trajectory, and outcome measurement. We examine how these domains distort incidence estimates, pathogen rankings, diagnostic accuracy, severity classification, and trial findings. Within this framework, we highlight developments relevant to Europe: randomised vaccine trials assessing hospitalisation rather than immunogenicity; national data suggesting a changing, increasingly β-lactam-resistant role for Haemophilus influenzae; evidence suggesting that discordant corticosteroid trials reflect heterogeneity of treatment effect rather than drug or protocol differences; and the first randomised trial of host-response-directed immunotherapy in pneumonia-predominant sepsis. We also examine continuing fragmentation in European adult vaccination policy, surveillance, and diagnostic capacity. We propose a diagnostic approach organised by clinical group, a minimum CAP dataset with explicit governance, and a research agenda separating interventions applicable now, evidence required before implementation, and unresolved questions. This approach connects advances in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment with the methodological and organisational changes needed to generate more reliable, clinically actionable European evidence.

title: Risk factors for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa community-acquired pneumonia at a high-volume transplant center.
text: To validate risk factors for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Retrospective, single-center, cohort study from October 1, 2018, to March 31, 2023. Mayo Clinic Hospital in Phoenix, AZ. Adult patients with CAP, identified using ICD-10 diagnosis codes, receipt of systemic antibiotics for a "respiratory tract infection" within 48 hours of hospitalization, and availability of respiratory cultures. Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with MRSA or P. aeruginosa isolation in respiratory cultures. A total of 1,485 patients met inclusion criteria; 32 (2.2%) had MRSA and 81 (5.5%) had P. aeruginosa isolated from respiratory culture. Multivariate logistic regression analyses identified substance use disorder [aOR 8.29, P < .001], influenza [aOR 7.64, P = .003], lung abscess/empyema [aOR 4.58, P = .031], and peptic ulcer disease (PUD) [aOR 4.09, P = .017] as MRSA risk factors. Bronchiectasis [aOR 3.67, P < .001], PUD [aOR 3.48, P = .006], and COPD [aOR 2.60, P = .005] were independently associated with P. aeruginosa. Immunocompromised conditions, including transplantation (solid organ and hematopoietic stem cell) and malignant tumor were not independently associated with either organism. Our results substantiate previously demonstrated risk factors for MRSA and P. aeruginosa in CAP. We did not observe an independent association between immunosuppressed conditions evaluated and isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa.

title: Respiratory viral detection and severity risk factors in hospitalized children with community-acquired pneumonia following relaxation of COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions: a 20-month retrospective cohort in Guilin, China.
text: After the withdrawal of COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) in China, we characterized the demographic, clinical and virological features of virus-positive community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in children younger than 5 years during the post-NPI period. We conducted a retrospective study using electronic medical records from a tertiary hospital in Guilin, China. We enrolled 1,255 children hospitalized with CAP between December 2022 and July 2024. All participants were tested for five respiratory viruses: respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza virus (PIV), adenovirus (ADV), influenza-A (Flu-A) and influenza-B (Flu-B). Of 1,255 hospitalized CAP cases, 681 (54%) were virus-positive, including 112 (16% of virus-positive cases) who met severe CAP (SCAP) criteria. RSV showed the highest detection rate (23%, 292/1,255), followed by PIV, ADV, Flu-A and Flu-B; detection patterns differed significantly across age groups. Bacterial co-detection was common among virus-positive cases. Multivariable analysis identified bacterial co-detection (OR 1.90, 95% CI [1.12-3.23]), wheeze (OR 1.59, 95% CI [1.02-2.49]), and chronic comorbidities (OR 2.44, 95% CI [1.5 7-3.78]) as independent risk factors for severe disease, whereas rhinorrhoea was associated with reduced severity (OR 0.43, 95% CI [0.27-0.66]). Among virus-positive cases, RSV was the most frequently detected virus in children younger than 5 years hospitalized with CAP during the post-NPI period in Guilin, China. Early identification of independent risk factors for SCAP may help clinicians's recognition high-risk children promptly.

title: Comparative outcomes of influenza, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, and respiratory syncytial virus community-acquired pneumonia: insights from an Italian retrospective cohort study.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Viral pathogens, particularly influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), are increasingly recognized as key contributors to CAP in hospitalized adults. This single-center, retrospective cohort study examined and compared the clinical characteristics and outcomes of adults hospitalized with viral CAP due to influenza, SARS-CoV-2, or respiratory syncytial virus between January 2022 and December 2023 in Milan, Italy. A total of 165 patients with laboratory-confirmed single-virus infection and clinically and radiologically confirmed pneumonia were included. Patients with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia presented with the highest in-hospital mortality (20.9%) and 12-month all-cause mortality (51.9%). Patients with influenza, although younger, showed increased rates of cardiovascular events and intensive care unit admissions. Bacterial coinfections were most common in influenza cases. Immunocompromised status was the second most frequent comorbidity (37.6%) after arterial hypertension. These findings underscore significant differences in clinical trajectory and long-term outcomes among major viral CAP etiologies and support the need for pathogen-specific management strategies.

title: Conflicts of Interest and Broad-Spectrum First-Line Antibiotic Recommendations in Community-Acquired Pneumonia Guidelines: A Meta-epidemiological Study Using the WHO AWaRe Classification.
text: This study aimed to quantify recommendation-level broad-spectrum first-line antibiotic options and explicit escalation criteria in adult community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) guidelines using the WHO AWaRe classification, and to describe findings by recommendation-relevant financial conflicts of interest (COI) and publication period. We conducted a cross-sectional meta-epidemiological study of adult CAP guidelines published from 2015 to 2025 that reported development informed by a systematic review or equivalent evidence review. The analysis unit was the recommendation unit, defined as the smallest structured empiric treatment statement for a distinct clinical subgroup. The primary outcome was broad-spectrum first-line therapy, defined as inclusion of at least one WHO AWaRe Watch or Reserve antibiotic as a first-line option. Seven guidelines were included, providing 30 recommendation units. Of these, 19/30 (63%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 44-80%) included broad-spectrum first-line therapy, and 8/30 (27%; 95% CI 12-46%) contained explicit escalation criteria. In an exploratory descriptive comparison, broad-spectrum first-line therapy appeared more frequent in COI-present units than in COI-absent units (12/13 [92%] vs 7/17 [41%]). Broad-spectrum first-line therapy was observed in 6/8 (75%) pre-2020 units and 13/22 (59%) units published from 2020 onward. Fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines appeared more frequently in COI-present units, and drug-specific COI was most frequent for these classes. Broad-spectrum first-line therapy was common across adult CAP guidelines, but explicit operational boundaries for broader empiric coverage were often not stated in structured recommendations. These exploratory findings warrant further investigation in larger samples.

title: Comparison of Neutrophil-to-Monocyte-Plus-Lymphocyte Ratio and Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index Between Pulmonary Tuberculosis and Community-Acquired Pneumonia Patients.
text: Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) and community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) are significant global health challenges with overlapping clinical manifestations, which often complicates rapid diagnosis in resource-limited settings. This study evaluates the potential of the neutrophil-to-monocyte-plus-lymphocyte ratio (NMLR) and the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) as affordable and accessible hematological markers to help differentiate between these two respiratory infections. A retrospective, cross-sectional observational study was conducted at Ngoerah Hospital, Denpasar, Indonesia, using medical record data from January 2022 to September 2025. The subjects included 25 PTB patients and 24 CAP patients who met the eligibility criteria. Median values of NMLR and SII were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. CAP patients were generally older (mean age 61.0 years) and had a higher male prevalence (75%) compared to PTB patients (mean age 47.4 years; 44% male). All CAP patients (100%) presented with comorbidities, while TB patients showed a lower prevalence of 64%. Although the CAP group exhibited higher median values for NMLR (3.26 vs. 2.63; p=0.082) and SII (1335.77 vs. 1241.45; p=0.280), these differences did not reach statistical significance. No significant differences were found in NMLR and SII values between PTB and CAP patients in the study. This suggests that a high burden of chronic comorbidities, such as heart failure and chronic kidney disease, may mask specific host immune responses to acute and chronic infections. This study stresses the limitations of single inflammatory indices in populations with multiple comorbidities, emphasizing that further investigation into multiparametric diagnostic models is vital for enhancing management precision.

title: CURB-65 score for predicting deep vein thrombosis in severe community-acquired pneumonia: a cohort study.
text: Patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia (SCAP) are at significantly increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE). Traditional VTE risk assessment tools like the Caprini and Padua prediction scores are often underutilized in acute care settings due to their complexity. The CURB-65 score, a routine severity assessment tool for pneumonia, may offer a simplified and integrated approach for VTE risk stratification, but its predictive value for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in SCAP patients requires validation. We retrospectively enrolled 766 adults with SCAP admitted to Beijing Chao-Yang Hospital between January 1, 2015 and August 31, 2024. Baseline characteristics, CURB-65, Caprini, and Padua prediction scores, VTE prophylaxis details, and the occurrence of ultrasound confirmed in-hospital DVT were collected. Multivariable logistic regression was employed to identify independent risk factors for DVT. We further performed a sensitivity analysis restricted to proximal DVT. The predictive performance of the scores was compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Patients were stratified into low-risk (CURB-65 < 3) and high-risk (CURB-65 ≥ 3) groups for further analysis, including Kaplan-Meier survival analysis to compare cumulative DVT incidence. A separate multivariable analysis was conducted in the subgroup of patients who received VTE prophylaxis. The overall incidence of DVT was 30.3% (232/766), with the clinically actionable proximal DVT accounting for 3.0% (23/766) and distal DVT comprising 27.3% (209/766). Multivariable analysis identified a higher CURB-65 score as an independent predictor of DVT (adjusted Odds Ratio [OR] = 1.936, 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 1.503-2.495, P < 0.001). The sensitivity analysis limited to proximal DVT demonstrated that CURB-65 remained an independent predictor (adjusted OR = 1.759, 95%CI:1.431-2.162, P < 0.001). The predictive performance of the CURB-65 score (AUC = 0.717, 95% CI: 0.684-0.749) was statistically higher than that of the Caprini prediction score (AUC = 0.648; raw P = 0.002 for these two curves) and comparable to the Padua prediction score (AUC = 0.680; raw P = 0.052 for these two curves). The high-risk group (CURB-65 ≥ 3, n = 391) had a significantly higher DVT incidence (47.3%) compared to the low-risk group (12.5%, P < 0.001), with Kaplan-Meier curves confirming a higher cumulative incidence (Log-rank P < 0.001). In the prophylaxis subgroup (n = 626), the CURB-65 score remained an independent risk factor for DVT (adjusted OR = 1.953, 95% CI: 1.488-2.562, P < 0.001), and the overall DVT incidence was 30.8% (193/626). The CURB-65 score shows moderate performance in predicting DVT risk among SCAP patients, and retains stable predictive capacity for clinically critical proximal DVT, with discriminative capacity comparable to dedicated VTE assessment tools, though all three scoring systems deliver only fair-to-moderate discrimination. Routine calculation at admission may provide auxiliary clues to preliminarily screen patients with elevated residual DVT risk and facilitate risk-stratified monitoring and individualized thromboprophylaxis. Patients with CURB-65 ≥ 3 remain at substantial residual DVT risk despite standard prophylaxis, supporting the need for future research to optimize preventive strategies in this high-risk population. In addition to pneumonia severity assessment, the CURB-65 score may serve as a convenient auxiliary marker for DVT risk stratification.

title: Infectious diseases clinical pharmacist-led post-prescription review and therapeutic appropriateness in community-acquired pneumonia: an interrupted time-series study in the United Arab Emirates.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a common cause of hospitalization in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Although well-established international clinical guidelines for CAP are available, antimicrobial prescribing practices continue to vary. This variation may contribute to inappropriate antibiotic use and the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance. Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) are shown to improve the quality of antimicrobial prescribing and reduce unnecessary antibiotic exposure. A core component of these programs is post-prescription review, which allows for the assessment of antimicrobial therapy based on clinical guidelines and patient's clinical response. However, evidence evaluating the impact of post-prescription review on the management of CAP in the UAE is limited. This study aimed to assess temporal changes in the appropriateness of antimicrobial therapy following the implementation of a post-prescription review process in adults hospitalized with CAP. This study was conducted using a single-center, quasi-experimental interrupted time series design at a 200-bed tertiary care hospital in Dubai. The study period extended from July 2021 and June 2023. Adult patients aged 18-65 years admitted with CAP were included. Therapeutic appropriateness, assessed across antimicrobial selection, dosing, and duration, was the primary outcome. Length of hospital stay was evaluated as a secondary clinical outcome. Acceptance of clinical pharmacist recommendations during post-prescription review was also analyzed. Post-prescription review was associated with a significant increase in overall therapeutic appropriateness from 24.4% in the pre-intervention phase to 83.3% in the post-intervention phase. Segmented logistic regression demonstrated an immediate step-level increase at the point of intervention (adjusted odds ratio 22.9, 95% CI: 9.8-53.6, p < 0.001), with no significant pre-intervention trend and no significant change in slope post-intervention, indicating a sustained rather than progressive improvement. Acceptance of clinical pharmacist recommendations was high (85.2%). Introduction of post-prescription review was associated with a substantial improvement in therapeutic appropriateness for CAP. This UAE-based study supports strengthening regional antimicrobial stewardship programs through the post-prescription review processes. Larger multicenter trials are warranted. Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: Clinical outcomes of empirical antibiotic strategies in community-acquired pneumonia-associated sepsis: a propensity score-matched cohort study.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) complicated by sepsis remains a life-threatening infectious syndrome associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Although β-lactam-based combination therapy is widely recommended for severe CAP, the optimal empirical antibiotic strategy for septic pneumonia remains uncertain. At the same time, empirical antibiotic selection must balance adequate early treatment against unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic use and the risk of antimicrobial resistance. Evidence specifically targeting this high-risk population is limited. This study aimed to compare the clinical outcomes of β-lactam monotherapy and β-lactam-based combination therapy in patients with CAP-associated sepsis. We conducted a retrospective cohort study at Zhejiang Xiaoshan Hospital from January 2021 to January 2025, including adult patients with CAP-associated sepsis who received empirical β-lactam monotherapy or β-lactam-based combination therapy with macrolides or doxycycline within 48 hours of admission. A total of 100 patients were included before propensity score matching, and 80 patients remained after 1:1 matching. The primary outcome was time to clinical stability (TTCS). Secondary outcomes included mortality, length of hospital stay, antibiotic duration, changes in SOFA score, inflammatory biomarkers, clinical cure, and adverse events. TTCS was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression. Median TTCS was 5.0 days with monotherapy and 4.0 days with combination therapy (P = 0.129). Combination therapy also showed favorable trends in hospitalization duration, clinical cure, inflammatory marker reduction, and organ function recovery. After adjustment for admission SOFA score, combination therapy showed a nonsignificant trend toward earlier clinical stability (adjusted HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.88-2.29; P = 0.151). No significant increase in adverse events was observed. In patients with CAP-associated sepsis, β-lactam-based combination therapy showed a trend toward earlier clinical stability than β-lactam monotherapy, although the difference was not statistically significant. This study addresses an important evidence gap in septic pneumonia management and supports further investigation of individualized antimicrobial strategies guided by disease severity and biological characteristics. The retrospective single-center design and relatively small sample size should be considered when interpreting these findings.
source: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

title: Effect of immunomodulatory therapies on mortality in adults hospitalised with COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 community-acquired pneumonia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the leading infectious cause of morbidity and mortality globally. Severe disease is driven by a dysregulated host inflammatory response, leading to tissue damage. Despite numerous immunomodulatory strategies studied in CAP, their effectiveness remains unclear. To assess the effectiveness of immunomodulatory therapies on 30-day and 90-day mortality in adults hospitalised with CAP. Medline (via Ovid), Embase (via Ovid), Web of Science (Core Collection), Scopus, and Global Health (via Ebscohost) were searched from inception to 9 December 2025. All studies investigating the use of immunomodulatory therapies in adult patients hospitalised with CAP. Adult patients admitted to hospital with CAP. Any immunomodulatory therapy initiated for the management of CAP. RoB2 was used for RCTs and ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies of interventions. Treatments were grouped into pre-specified categories, then analysed in a series of pairwise random-effects meta-analyses. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were undertaken regarding severity, aetiology and individual treatments within selected categories. COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 CAP analyses were performed separately. 196 studies, including 89,117 patients, were included. Nine treatment categories included five or more randomised controlled trials (RCTs) reporting 30-day mortality. Among these, corticosteroids, cytokine inhibitors (predominantly IL-6), and JAK inhibitors were associated with reduced 30-day mortality in COVID-19, with odds ratios of 0.87 (95% CI 0.765-0.999), 0.84 (95% CI 0.76-0.93), and 0.66 (95% CI 0.47-0.93), respectively. The only therapies evaluated in five or more RCTs reporting 90-day mortality were cytokine inhibitors in COVID-19 CAP (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.45-1.03). No therapies were consistently associated with reduced mortality in non-COVID-19 CAP. Cytokine inhibitors reduce 30-day mortality while corticosteroids and JAK inhibitors probably reduce 30-day mortality in adults hospitalised with COVID-19 CAP. Further research is needed to identify effective immunomodulatory strategies for non-COVID-19 CAP. PROSPERO ID - CRD42024565301.
source: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

title: Rural-urban differences in antibiotic duration concordance for community-acquired pneumonia.
text: Outpatient antibiotic prescribing represents a major target for antimicrobial stewardship, yet prolonged treatment durations remain common despite guideline recommendations supporting shorter courses for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Previous studies have reported rural-urban differences in antibiotic prescribing practices; however, little is known about geographic variation in CAP treatment duration within predominantly rural states. To evaluate rural-urban differences in guideline-concordant antibiotic prescribing durations among outpatient providers in North Dakota for community-acquired pneumonia. A cross-sectional study was conducted using linked outpatient prescription and medical claims from the IQVIA database between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2024. Antibiotic prescriptions associated with qualifying CAP diagnoses and identifiable provider ZIP codes were included. Provider rurality was classified using 2020 Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes. Guideline-concordant prescribing was defined as an antibiotic days' supply of ≤7 days, while durations >7 days were considered non-concordant. Rural-urban differences were evaluated using chi-square testing and multivariable logistic regression adjusting for patient age, prescriber type, and study year. A total of 2,085 outpatient CAP-associated antibiotic prescriptions met inclusion criteria, including 1,577 (75.6%) from urban providers and 508 (24.4%) from rural providers. Overall, 1,423 prescriptions (68.2%) were guideline-concordant, while 662 (31.8%) exceeded 7 days. Annual concordance was 67.7%, 65.8%, and 72.4% in 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively. No statistically significant rural-urban differences were observed in any study year (all p>0.05). Similarly, after adjustment for patient age, prescriber type, and study year, provider rurality was not significantly associated with duration concordance (aOR=0.92, 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.17, p=0.492). Approximately two-thirds of outpatient CAP antibiotic prescriptions were guideline-concordant; however, nearly one-third exceeded 7 days despite evidence supporting shorter treatment durations. Provider rurality was not associated with duration concordance, suggesting duration-focused antimicrobial stewardship interventions should be implemented broadly across outpatient settings rather than targeted geographically.
source: Journal of the American Pharmacists Association : JAPhA

title: Time to antibiotics and outcomes for children hospitalized with community acquired pneumonia.
text: It is unclear whether time to antibiotics changes outcomes for hospitalized children with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and whether observation is safe. Our objective was to compare outcomes among children with CAP admitted to the hospital who did and who did not receive antibiotics within 4 h of presentation to the Emergency Department. We conducted a multicenter, retrospective cohort study using data from four hospitals obtained from the Pediatric Health Information System. Children aged 3 months to 18 years, with a chest X-ray, admitted to the hospital from the ED with suspected CAP who received antibiotics were enrolled. Our primary outcome was a composite of escalation of care (escalation in respiratory support, transfer to the intensive care unit, vasopressor use, or chest tube placement). Secondary outcomes were length of stay, duration of oxygen use, and cost of stay. Inverse propensity weighted logistic regression and log gamma regression to evaluate the association of early versus late antibiotics and outcome. There were 758 children hospitalized with CAP who met inclusion criteria, of which 451 (59%) received antibiotics within 4 h. There was no statistical difference in escalation of care between those who received early versus late antibiotics (3% vs. 2%; odds ratio [OR]: 1.46 [95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.57,3.73]). There were no statistical associations with secondary outcomes. This study provides an opportunity for antibiotic stewardship by showing that more time to observe patients with CAP without antibiotics does not change outcomes. This time may identify patients who will improve without antibiotics, limiting side effects.

title: Differentiating Chlamydia psittaci pneumonia from community-acquired pneumonia using clinical features and computed tomography findings.
text: Chlamydia psittaci pneumonia (CPP) is a rare disease that is difficult to diagnose. Its clinical manifestations and chest imaging findings often overlap with those of other types of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), and nonspecific treatment is likely to lead to rapid disease progression. This study aimed to explore the clinical and radiological differences between CPP and CAP. We enrolled 29 patients with non-severe CPP diagnosed using metagenomic next-generation sequencing, as well as 87 with CAP, who had been diagnosed between December 2019 and September 2023. The demographic, clinical, and radiological characteristics of CPP were analyzed and compared with those of CAP. Compared to the patients with CAP, those with non-severe CPP were more likely to experience fever (P = 0.034), headache (P = 0.009), asthenia (P<0.001), abnormal auscultation of the lungs (P = 0.020), and abnormal laboratory examination results-including lymphocyte count (P = 0.002), C-reactive protein (P = 0.001), aspartate aminotransferase (P<0.001), alanine aminotransferase (P<0.001), and creatine kinase levels (P<0.001). Regarding radiological characteristics, CPP predominantly showed unilateral (P = 0.003) and single-lobar (P = 0.004) involvement, whereas CAP commonly exhibited bilateral and multi-lobar involvement. CPP was more likely to be associated with air bronchograms (P = 0.026), interlobular septal thickening (P = 0.001), and bronchovascular bundle thickening (P<0.001) than CAP was. Clinical epidemiology, laboratory examination, and radiological characteristics are useful for diagnosing and differentiating CPP from CAP.

title: Clinical features associated with occult pneumonia among older adults with community-acquired pneumonia: a descriptive retrospective study.
text: Pneumonia is a major global health burden and a substantial threat to older adults. Because pneumonia in this population may present insidiously without typical respiratory symptoms, occult pneumonia can be easily overlooked, resulting in delayed treatment and an increased risk of severe disease and death. This study aimed to identify clinical features associated with occult pneumonia. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of 334 older adults with pulmonary infections admitted to our hospital between January 2023 and January 2025. Patients were randomly assigned to a development cohort (n = 234) and an internal validation cohort (n = 100) at a 7:3 ratio. The development cohort comprised 80 patients with occult pneumonia and 154 with typical pneumonia. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors independently associated with occult pneumonia. LASSO logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation and backward-stepwise logistic regression identified five independent predictors of occult pneumonia: age ≥80 years (OR = 2.584, 95% CI: 1.350-4.948), diabetes mellitus (OR = 3.392, 95% CI: 1.696-6.782), cerebrovascular disease (OR = 2.116, 95% CI: 1.027-4.357), decreased appetite (OR = 4.982, 95% CI: 2.609-9.513), and WBC count (OR = 2.797, 95% CI: 1.290-6.067; all P < 0.05). The association with WBC count was positive and graded: WBC counts were higher in patients with occult than typical pneumonia (median 6.92 vs. 6.06  ×  10⁹/L, P = 0.002), and in sensitivity analyses each 1 × 10⁹/L increase in WBC count was associated with an 18% increase in the odds of occult pneumonia (OR = 1.184, 95% CI: 1.051-1.334) without evidence of non-linearity (P = 0.920). The model achieved AUCs of 0.799 (95% CI: 0.739-0.854) in the development cohort and 0.799 (95% CI: 0.699-0.886) in the internal validation cohort. Calibration was assessed using the calibration intercept, slope, and Brier score, which indicated good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. Age ≥80 years, diabetes mellitus, cerebrovascular disease, decreased appetite, and WBC count were independently associated with occult pneumonia in older adults. These factors characterize the occult presentation phenotype and may help clinicians recognize occult pneumonia among older adults with CAP to support appropriate evaluation and management.

title: Air pollution is associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective multicentre cohort study.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the leading cause of death due to infection worldwide, with its incidence and disease course influenced by air pollution exposure. Little is known about how air pollution influences microbiological findings in patients with CAP. Patients were recruited from a prospective, multicentre study of CAP (CAPNETZ). Air pollution data were collected at the city level considering data up to one month before inclusion. Associations with sputum pathogen detection and cell counts were tested using generalised linear mixed-effects logistic regression models adjusting for clinical confounders, centre-level heterogeneity and meteorological data. Internal validation was performed using an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) approach. Among 4,446 eligible patients with available sputum samples, a potential pathogen was detected in 1,581 patients, while complete sputum-cell-count data were available for 4,014 patients. Detection of Streptococcus pneumoniae was associated with previous higher exposure to sulphur dioxide (SO2) (OR 1.75, p = 0.008) and carbon monoxide (CO) (OR 1.57, p = 0.02). Escherichia coli was more frequently detected in patients who were exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide (NO2) (OR 2.75, p = 0.004) and higher temperature (OR 1.51, p = 0.03), whereas increased fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure (OR 0.37, p = 0.001) was linked to reduced detection. Furthermore, SO2 exposure influenced the likelihood of obtaining a diagnostically relevant sputum culture and was associated with higher odds of detecting a high leucocyte count (OR 1.18, p = 0.02). Results were largely corroborated by EFS, particularly for S. pneumoniae and E. coli detection. Exposure to air pollution was associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in patients with CAP. These findings may have implications for the interpretation of microbiological data in an epidemiological and clinical context and highlight the importance of considering air pollution exposure as a confounding factor. Further validation in cohorts with high-quality environmental, microbiological and antimicrobial resistance data is needed. Registry: German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS-ID: DRKS00005274, Registration date: 2013-09-11.

title: Conversion of VA-to-VV ECMO modes in the management of severe community-acquired pneumonia complicated by septic shock: A case report.
text: In the post-pandemic era, there has been a notable increase in the incidence of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), with an earlier age of onset and more severe clinical symptoms. A subset of these patients requires extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support, either alone or in combination, to maintain hemodynamic and respiratory stability. This paper discusses a case study of a previously healthy middle-aged male who developed severe CAP due to Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp), escalating to septic shock. During his hospitalization, the patient experienced a range of complications, such as septic shock, septic cardiomyopathy, acute kidney injury, lung abscess, empyema, pyopneumothorax, gastrointestinal bleeding, intestinal obstruction, and acquired myasthenia gravis. After undergoing a six-month multidisciplinary treatment regimen that included venoarterial (VA)-venovenous (VV) ECMO mode conversion, invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), and continuous blood purification (CBP), the patient eventually demonstrated clinical improvement. This case report emphasizes the clinical characteristics and management challenges associated with severe CAP and its life-threatening complications, aiming to provide insights into effective therapeutic strategies.
source: Journal of infection and public health

title: Efficacy and Safety of Faropenem in Bangladeshi Adults With Community-Acquired Pneumonia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) causes substantial morbidity, and effective single-agent oral therapies that simplify treatment are needed. Faropenem, an oral penem with broad antibacterial activity, has not previously been compared with standard combination therapy for CAP. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral faropenem, compared with co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin, in adults with mild-to-moderate CAP who did not require hospitalization. In this open-label, randomized controlled trial conducted at two tertiary centers in Dhaka, Bangladesh, adults aged 18-65 years with mild-to-moderate CAP were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to oral faropenem or combination therapy. Patients with severe pneumonia, recent hospitalization, or significant renal or hepatic impairment were excluded 200 mg three times daily or co-amoxiclav 625 mg three times daily plus clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily, each for 7 days with standard care. The primary efficacy outcome was clinical cure at days 10-14, and the primary safety outcome was withdrawal due to adverse events (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06804096). Of 244 patients assessed, 129 were randomized (faropenem, 65; comparator, 64), and all completed follow-up. Clinical cure at days 10-14 was 98.5% with faropenem and 95.3% with the comparator (risk difference +3.1%, 95% confidence interval (CI) -2.8 to +9.1; relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.10). The clinical cure at day 3 was 84.6% versus 78.1%. Adverse events were infrequent (9.2% versus 12.5% in the faropenem and comparator arms, respectively), with no serious adverse events and no treatment withdrawals; altered taste occurred only in the comparator arm. Hepatic and renal parameters showed no clinically meaningful change in either arm. In adults with mild-to-moderate CAP, oral faropenem was non-inferior to co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin. As a single-agent oral therapy, it may offer an alternative when narrower-spectrum first-line regimens are unsuitable. However, larger, blinded, microbiologically well-characterized trials are needed to establish pathogen-specific efficacy. These findings should not be extrapolated to severe or hospitalized CAP or to patients with significant renal or hepatic impairment.

title: Immunomodulatory therapies in bacterial community-acquired pneumonia: Current evidence and future directions.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for more than two million deaths annually. While most patients successfully clear pulmonary infection through an effective host immune response, a subset progress to severe disease characterised by dysregulated and excessive inflammation. This maladaptive immune response drives subsequent organ dysfunction and mortality, prompting increasing interest in immunomodulatory therapies as adjunctive treatments. This article aims to describe the key immunomodulatory strategies investigated for the management of bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, summarise the evidence for their efficacy and limitations, and highlight potential future therapeutic approaches. We conducted a comprehensive literature search of Medline, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus and Global Health, using search terms related to pneumonia and immunomodulatory intervention from database inception to December 8th, 2025. While a broad range of immunomodulatory strategies has been investigated in bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, few have been shown to be reliably beneficial. Corticosteroids are the most extensively studied agents and have been associated with clinically relevant outcomes in selected patient populations, supporting guideline recommendations for their use in severe community-acquired pneumonia. Targeted inhibition of inflammatory cytokines and downstream signalling pathways has been explored to a lesser degree, with limited evidence supporting its use in bacterial community-acquired pneumonia. Other approaches, including passive immunotherapy and immune stimulation, have been investigated, but current evidence supporting their routine use remains inconclusive. Immunomodulation represents an important adjunctive therapeutic strategy in bacterial community-acquired pneumonia. Although progress has been made, particularly with corticosteroids, evidence remains incomplete. Further high-quality research is required to better define patient selection, optimal timing, and the clinical impact of immunomodulatory therapies.
source: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

title: BALF-mNGS-Derived Microbial Detection Profiles and Their Associations with Clinical Severity in Immunocompromised Patients with Community-Acquired Pneumonia.
text: Immunocompromised patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) have heterogeneous pulmonary microbial profiles and frequently experience a severe clinical course. Whether bronchoalveolar lavage fluid metagenomic next-generation sequencing (BALF-mNGS)-derived microbial features are associated with clinical severity in this population remains unclear. To characterize pulmonary microbial features in immunocompromised patients with CAP and evaluate their association with ICU admission and length of hospital stay (LOHS). This multicenter retrospective study included 1072 patients with CAP who underwent BALF-mNGS at five hospitals (August 2021-June 2025), including 362 immunocompromised and 710 immunocompetent patients. Microbial diversity, composition, and differentially enriched taxa were compared by immune status. Among immunocompromised patients, taxon-outcome associations were assessed using adjusted logistic and negative binomial regression, with sensitivity analyses additionally adjusting for antibiotic and antifungal exposure before BALF. Immunocompromised patients had higher alpha diversity (P<0.001), with limited overall community separation. Five taxa were enriched: Burkholderia multivorans, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Candida glabrata, Candida tropicalis, and Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae. In primary analyses, B. multivorans abundance was associated with ICU admission (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.400, 95% CI 1.088-1.801; false discovery rate [FDR]-adjusted P=0.045) and longer LOHS (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.108, 95% CI 1.036-1.186; FDR-adjusted P=0.014). C. glabrata was associated with longer LOHS (aIRR 1.101, 95% CI 1.023-1.185; FDR-adjusted P=0.026). K. pneumoniae showed a nominal ICU association that did not survive FDR correction (FDR-adjusted P=0.084). After additional adjustment for antibiotic and antifungal exposure, the associations of B. multivorans and C. glabrata with longer LOHS remained significant (both FDR-adjusted P=0.044), whereas the association between B. multivorans and ICU admission did not (FDR-adjusted P=0.168). BALF-mNGS-derived microbial features showed limited overall community differences but distinct taxon-specific associations with clinical severity. These exploratory findings require further validation before their prognostic or clinical utility can be established.

title: The Impact of Antibiotic Initiation Timing in Children with Severe Community-Acquired Pneumonia: A Post-Hoc Analysis of an Observational Study.
text: The aim of this study was to examine the association between early antibiotic initiation and clinical outcomes in children admitted to the paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) with severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). We conducted a post-hoc analysis of a multicentre observational study across nine Asian PICUs. Children with severe CAP were categorized into early (≤ 6 h) or late (> 6 h) antibiotic initiation groups (early and late antibiotic groups, respectively) relative to PICU admission. The primary outcome was PICU mortality; secondary outcomes were 28-day ventilation-free days (VFD) and intensive care unit-free days (IFD). Multivariable analyses adjusted for country as fixed effect, age, Paediatric Index of Mortality 3 (PIM 3) score and comorbidities, when feasible. Among the 544 paediatric patients included in the analysis, median age was 14.0 [interquartile range (IQR) 4.0-34.0] months and the PIM 3 score was 0.3 (IQR 0.0-6.8) %. Viral and bacterial pathogens were isolated in 206 (37.9%) and 145 (26.7%) patients, respectively. Almost all patients [537 (98.7%)] received antibiotics, with 475 (87.3%) and 62 (11.4%) patients in the early and late antibiotic groups, respectively. Late antibiotic initiation was associated with higher PICU mortality [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 5.19, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.94-13.88, P < 0.01], septic shock requiring inotropic support (aOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.45-7.28, P < 0.01) and multi-organ failure (aOR 4.60, 95% CI 2.11-10.04, P < 0.01). No significant associations were observed between late antibiotic initiation and VFD or IFD. In critically ill children with severe CAP, initiating antibiotics within 6 h of PICU admission was associated with improved outcomes. This 6-h window may serve as a practical benchmark for quality improvement initiatives.

title: Beyond Digoxin Toxicity: A Fatal Case of BRASH Syndrome Triggered by Community-Acquired Pneumonia.
text: Bradycardia, renal failure, atrioventricular (AV) nodal blockade, shock, and hyperkalemia (BRASH) syndrome is a rare, life-threatening clinical condition caused by the synergistic interaction between hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction, and AV nodal blocking agents, resulting in severe bradycardia and hemodynamic instability. Early recognition is often challenging due to its nonspecific presentation. We report the case of an 82-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, ischemic heart disease, congestive cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease, and chronic digoxin therapy who presented with abdominal pain, confusion, dizziness, hypotension, and profound bradycardia. Investigations demonstrated severe hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury on top of chronic kidney disease, hyponatremia, and electrocardiographic changes consistent with hyperkalemia. Initial differential diagnoses included mesenteric ischemia, adrenal insufficiency, and digoxin toxicity; however, imaging excluded bowel ischemia, cortisol levels were normal, and serum digoxin at the therapeutic level. Community-acquired pneumonia complicated by sepsis was identified as the precipitating trigger for BRASH syndrome. Despite intensive treatment, including hyperkalemia management, isoprenaline infusion, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and supportive care, the patient's condition progressively deteriorated, culminating in multiorgan failure and death shortly afterward. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of BRASH syndrome and emphasizes the importance of early recognition and targeted management to interrupt the vicious cycle and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Evidence-to-Recommendation Framework for 2026 ACE Clinical Guideline on community-acquired pneumonia - assessment, diagnosis and antibiotic prescribing.
text: This Evidence-to-Recommendation (EtR) framework underpins the Agency for Care Effectiveness Clinical Guideline (ACG) for the management of non-severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults, providing the rationale and justification for the guideline recommendations. Pneumonia remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Singapore, accounting for 4.6% of hospitalisations and 23.0% of deaths in 2024. The ACG addresses management gaps that contribute to poor clinical outcomes, including diagnostic uncertainty, inappropriate prescribing and suboptimal treatment. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was followed to develop five evidence-based recommendations covering the assessment, diagnosis and antibiotic management of CAP. This EtR framework summarises the factors that informed the direction and strength of the ACG recommendations, providing the rationale and decisions made by the Expert Group to aid clinicians in understanding and applying the recommendations in the management of CAP. The ACG can be found at https://go.gov.sg/acg-cap.

title: Clinical significance of cytomegalovirus detection in young children with Mycoplasma pneumoniae-associated community-acquired pneumonia: a retrospective cohort study.
text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M. pneumoniae)-associated community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is common in children. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is frequently detected in respiratory samples in this patient population. We aimed to explore the clinical implications of positive CMV DNA in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from immunocompetent children with M. pneumoniae-associated CAP. A retrospective cohort study was conducted for M. pneumoniae-associated CAP children under two years old with CMV DNA test in BALF between January 1, 2022 and September 30, 2025. These children were assigned to the BALF CMV DNA positive group or negative group. Then, the inter-group characteristics were compared. Among the 66 children, 28 and 38 children were assigned to the CMV DNA positive and negative groups, respectively. Children in the BALF CMV DNA positive group were more likely to experience duration of fever ≥ 3 days, had a higher incidence of severe M. pneumoniae-associated CAP at admission, and required longer hospital stays. However, these children had a lower incidence of wheezing, when compared to children in the BALF CMV DNA negative group. Furthermore, virus co-infection was common in the BALF CMV DNA negative group, when compared to the BALF CMV DNA positive group (60.5% vs. 35.7%, p = 0.046). The multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that severe M. pneumoniae-associated CAP at admission was significantly associated with positive BALF CMV DNA (odds ratio [OR]: 22.403, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 5.429-89.503, p < 0.001), and co-infection was significantly associated with wheezing (OR: 6.024, 95% CI: 2.037-17.857, p = 0.001). All children fully recovered after intravenous azithromycin administration. Both BALF CMV DNA positive and negative children with M. pneumoniae-associated CAP can reach full recovery after azithromycin treatment. However, the former group had stronger inflammations and required longer hospital stays, while the latter group were more likely to have virus co-infection. Not applicable.

title: Doxycycline versus azithromycin in combination with beta-lactams for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia: A propensity score-matched cohort study.
text: Azithromycin plus a beta-lactam is a commonly used empiric regimen for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Concerns about azithromycin resistance and patient-specific safety considerations have increased interest in doxycycline as an alternative; however, comparative effectiveness data for these two regimens remain scarce. Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (240 healthcare organizations; data accessed June 14, 2026), we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults hospitalized with CAP between January 2016 and December 2023. Doxycycline plus beta-lactam recipients were compared with azithromycin plus beta-lactam recipients following 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (11,906 patients per group). Thirty-day and 90-day all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between groups (HR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.95-1.12; and HR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.98-1.14, respectively), whereas 180-day mortality was modestly but significantly higher in the doxycycline cohort (HR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02-1.16; p = 0.014). Doxycycline-based therapy was associated with a consistently lower risk of antibiotic escalation at all time points assessed (RR: 0.59-0.65; p < 0.001). The 30-day risk of incident sepsis was significantly higher with doxycycline (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03-1.61; p = 0.024). ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, and Clostridioides difficile infection did not differ significantly between the two groups. No statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality was detected between doxycycline plus beta-lactams and azithromycin plus beta-lactams. This finding does not establish equivalence or noninferiority. Secondary findings, including 30-day sepsis and 180-day mortality, were exploratory and require confirmation in prospective randomized studies.

title: Pathogen spectrum and triple-criteria interpretation algorithm of BALF-targeted NGS in children with refractory severe community-acquired pneumonia in mountainous Northeastern Sichuan: a single-center retrospective study.
text: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (SCAP) causes substantial pediatric hospitalization and respiratory failure in mountainous western China. Conventional microbial assays show limited sensitivity for fastidious pathogens and mixed infections. Targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) using bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) enables broad-spectrum pathogen detection at lower cost than whole-metagenomic sequencing. However, many previous tNGS studies directly equate multiple microbial nucleic-acid signals with true coinfection, which may lead to unnecessary combined anti-infective therapy. This single-center retrospective study enrolled 86 children aged < 14 years with refractory SCAP who underwent BALF-tNGS testing at Guangyuan Central Hospital between March 2023 and September 2024. We developed a triple-criteria interpretive algorithm combining an exploratory empirical pathogen-load cut-off (>1.0 × 106 copies/mL), inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, PCT), and chest imaging to discriminate genuine active coinfection from airway colonization. This load threshold was empirical and not internally validated by ROC analysis in our dataset. Patients were stratified into four age subgroups; diagnostic concordance was assessed among 34 patients with parallel routine microbial tests. In total, 229 pathogen isolates were identified. Viruses predominated (58.9%, 135/229), followed by bacteria (32.8%, 75/229). The three most frequent pathogens were Haemophilus influenzae (32.56%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (30.23%), and respiratory syncytial virus A (RSV-A, 18.60%). While 82.6% (71/86) of patients harbored ≥2 pathogen nucleic-acid signals, only 17.4% (15/86) fulfilled criteria for clinical coinfection, dominated by virus-bacterial dual infection. Viral detection rates tended to decline with increasing age, whereas bacterial positivity was higher among preschool- and school-age children. A prominent spring epidemic peak was observed during May-June 2023. Only 22.86% of paired routine microbial tests showed full concordance with tNGS. These single-center data cannot be generalized to all pediatric severe-pneumonia populations. Most abundant multi-pathogen tNGS signals represented colonization or residual dead-microbe nucleic acid instead of true active infection. Our triple-criteria interpretive framework offers standardized rules for grassroots mountain hospitals to reduce over-prescription of combined antibiotics and antivirals when interpreting BALF-tNGS results for children with refractory SCAP.
source: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

title: Characterization of pulmonary bacterial composition in community-acquired pneumonia depending on sampling methods.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a major global health concern due to its high incidence, morbidity, mortality, and economic impact. Although Streptococcus pneumoniae is the primary bacterial cause, diverse bacterial and viral pathogens contribute to CAP etiology. Conventional microbiological methods provide limited characterization of the pulmonary microbiome, resulting in low diagnostic yield and frequent empirical antibiotic use. This pilot study aimed to characterize the pulmonary microbiome in adult CAP patients using high-throughput sequencing and to determine whether commonly used non-invasive samples accurately represent the lower respiratory tract. Pulmonary samples were obtained using invasive procedures (bronchoalveolar lavage, bronchial aspirate, bronchial brushing, and biopsy) and non-invasive methods (sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate). Classical microbiological testing identified pathogens in 24.1% of cases. DNA extracted was subjected to 16S rRNA gene amplification and sequencing, and microbial composition and diversity were compared across sampling types. Microbiome profiles differed significantly by sampling methodology. Non-invasive samples displayed high variability and limited correspondence with lower airway microbiota. In contrast, invasive samples demonstrated greater consistency and appeared more representative of the lower respiratory tract. The genus Ralstonia was significantly more abundant in invasive samples (p < 0.05), warranting further investigation of its potential biological and clinical relevance. 16S rRNA gene sequencing provides comprehensive detection of pulmonary microorganisms and offers added value in the microbiological diagnosis of CAP. The findings highlight the importance of using invasive specimens for accurate microbiome characterization and for detecting bacterial taxa not identified by routine microbiological methods.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency Among Hospitalized Children with Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Prevalence and Association with Disease Severity.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains an important cause of pediatric hospitalization and severe respiratory illness. Vitamin D has recognized roles in skeletal health and immune regulation, but its relationship with pneumonia severity in children remains uncertain. This study evaluated serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D status in hospitalized children with CAP and explored its association with disease severity and clinical outcomes. This single-center prospective observational cohort study included 100 hospitalized children aged 2 months to 15 years with radiographically confirmed CAP at a tertiary pediatric referral hospital in Tabriz, Iran. Pneumonia severity was classified as mild/moderate or severe according to British Thoracic Society criteria. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, inflammatory markers, clinical features, radiographic findings, hospitalization duration, pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission, and in-hospital mortality were assessed. Vitamin D deficiency was defined as serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D <30 nmol/L. Seventy-four children had mild/moderate pneumonia and 26 had severe pneumonia. Severe cases had lower oxygen saturation, more extensive radiographic involvement, longer hospitalization, and more frequent PICU admission. Mean serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was 21.8 ± 7.6 nmol/L in the severe group and 25.2 ± 10.1 nmol/L in the mild/moderate group (mean difference, -3.4 nmol/L; 95% CI, -7.2 to 0.4; p = 0.079). Vitamin D deficiency occurred in 92.3% and 78.4% of severe and mild/moderate cases, respectively (p = 0.144).
