Logit-transformed proportions were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp CIs; binomial-normal generalized linear mixed models were used in sensitivity analyses. Pathway stages were synthesized from outcome-specific study subsets rather than a single longitudinal cohort. Thirty-seven reports from 13 LMICs and 1 multinational cohort were included. Across 22 community- or population-based studies, confirmed AF averaged 1.24% (95% CI: 0.79%-1.94%; I2 = 98.8%; 95% prediction interval: 0.16%-8.83%). Newly detected AF averaged 0.95% (95% CI: 0.43%-2.11%; I2 = 99.2%; prediction interval: 0.08%-9.97%). In separate study subsets, prior AF awareness was 50.7%, study-defined high stroke risk or oral anticoagulation indication was 78.9%, and oral anticoagulation coverage among study-defined eligible/high-risk participants was 22.8%. Reach ranged from 9.7% to 98.8%, and confirmation completion was 57.5% to 61.8% in 2 programs. AF screening in LMICs identifies substantial but highly variable detection and treatment gaps. Pooled proportions should be interpreted as cross-study summaries rather than expected rates for a specific setting. Effective programs require representative reach, timely confirmation, appropriate stroke-risk and valvular assessment, access to anticoagulation, and longitudinal follow-up.

title: Surgical Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation.
text: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, mortality, and reduced quality of life. Although catheter ablation is the most widely used rhythm control strategy, its efficacy is limited in patients with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and large left atria. To address this therapeutic gap, surgical approaches, including minimally invasive ablation, hybrid epicardial-endocardial strategies, and left atrial appendage exclusion, have continued to evolve. In this review, we focus on recent evidence to guide clinical decision-making on patient selection, advances in minimally invasive surgical and hybrid techniques, left atrial appendage exclusion, and postoperative anticoagulation management. Minimally invasive standalone Cox-Maze IV procedure and hybrid epicardial-endocardial ablation have demonstrated superior long-term freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias compared with thoracoscopic epicardial surgical ablation or catheter ablation alone. Five-year arrhythmia-free survival has approached 85% to 95% in experienced centers after the Cox-Maze IV procedure and approximately 60% to 70% after hybrid ablation, compared with 35% to 45% after thoracoscopic epicardial ablation and 30% to 35% after single catheter ablation alone. Surgical left atrial appendage exclusion performed at the time of ablation may further reduce thromboembolic risk, although the optimal strategy for postprocedural anticoagulation remains uncertain. Careful patient selection remains essential, with atrial fibrillation type, duration, left atrial size, and previous treatment failure known to be key predictors of procedural success. As surgical techniques and supporting evidence continue to grow, standalone surgical ablation may assume a more important role in the contemporary management of atrial fibrillation, particularly for patients with advanced disease who are unlikely to achieve durable rhythm control with catheter ablation alone.

title: Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in adults with advanced kidney disease: UK kidney association clinical practice guideline.
text: Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have an increased risk of developing atrial fibrillation (AF). CKD is also associated with an increased risk of stroke and systemic embolism (SSE). Despite the increased thromboembolic risk associated with CKD and AF, patients with advanced CKD simultaneously have a higher risk of bleeding. Following results from large randomised controlled trials prophylaxis of thromboembolic events from atrial fibrillation (AF) has shifted from vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). However, trials of DOACs excluded patients with advanced kidney disease (CrCl < 30 ml/min), therefore good-quality data are limited in this population. This leads to decision-making around anticoagulation difficult. In those with advanced kidney disease, especially those on dialysis, there is limited data on the efficacy of anticoagulants for AF in terms of stroke reduction. There are ongoing studies to determine efficacy of anticoagulants in reducing the risk of thromboembolic stroke and systemic embolism in this population. These UK Kidney Association (UKKA) guidelines, which have been endorsed by the British Cardiovascular Society, provide best-practice guidance on the use of anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation in the context of advanced CKD. There are recommendations about the option of no anticoagulation, the use of DOACs, the monitoring of anticoagulants and the use of left atrial appendage occlusion. It also includes research recommendations. Not applicable.

title: Prognostic Value of Acute Glycemia Beyond Chronic Glycemic Status in Anticoagulated Patients with Atrial Fibrillation-Related Ischemic Stroke.
text: BackgroundDysglycemia is common in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF)-related acute ischemic stroke (AIS), yet the prognostic relevance of acute versus chronic glycemic status in anticoagulated patients remains unclear.MethodsConsecutive patients with AF-related AIS receiving anticoagulation therapy were enrolled. The endpoint was a composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic embolism, moderate-to-severe bleeding, and all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations of fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) with outcomes. Restricted cubic splines explored potential nonlinear relationships. Patients were categorized by American Diabetes Association HbA1c criteria, and an FPG × HbA1c interaction was tested. Kaplan-Meier analyses illustrated cumulative event rates.ResultsAmong 623 patients, higher baseline FPG was independently associated with the composite outcome at both 90 days (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 mmol/L increase = 1.084, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.014-1.160) and 1 year (HR = 1.075, 95% CI: 1.016-1.136). FPG remained significantly associated with adverse outcomes at 90 days (HR = 1.101, 95% CI: 1.018-1.191) and 1 year (HR = 1.087, 95% CI: 1.019-1.159), whereas HbA1c categories showed no significant associations. No significant interaction between FPG and HbA1c was observed. Kaplan-Meier analyses demonstrated no significant differences in cumulative event rates across HbA1c-defined glycemic groups.ConclusionsElevated baseline FPG was independently associated with short- and long-term adverse outcomes in anticoagulated patients with AF-related AIS. Acute-phase glycemia may provide prognostic information complementary to HbA1c, without significant effect modification by chronic glycemic status.
source: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis

title: The Europe-Asia-Pacific Divide in Atrial Fibrillation Management: Evidence, Practice, and Policy.
text: Atrial fibrillation affects approximately 60 million people worldwide, and Europe and the Asia-Pacific region together carry most of that burden. This state-of-the-art review compares the 2 regions across 6 domains: epidemiology and risk factors, lifestyle and comorbidity management, stroke prevention, rhythm control and catheter ablation, digital health and artificial intelligence-electrocardiogram, and health system infrastructure and policy. Practice diverges in all 6. European management follows European Society of Cardiology guidelines, whereas Asia-Pacific region care varies across socioeconomic settings and rests on population-scale evidence, with region-wide guidance so far limited to topic-specific Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society (APHRS) consensus statements until the first APHRS guideline was released in 2026. Anticoagulation gaps have narrowed in both regions, yet disparities in financing, electrophysiology capacity, and digital access persist, and differences within each region rival those between them. Closing these gaps requires region-specific, resource-adapted strategies and mutual adoption of evidence generated in each region.

title: Oral Anticoagulation Registry in Patients with Atrial Fibrillation Treated in Primary Care in Clinical Practice: The RACOVIR Study.
text: Objectives: This study aims to describe real-world oral anticoagulation management in patients with NVAF followed up in Spanish Primary Care, including anticoagulant use, VKA control, treatment switching, patient-reported satisfaction, and clinical outcomes during documented anticoagulant exposure. Methods: RACOVIR was a multicenter observational registry with cross-sectional enrolment and retrospective collection of electronic medical record data from AF diagnosis to inclusion. Adults with NVAF receiving oral anticoagulation for ≥6 months were included. The Barthel Index and Anti-Clot Treatment Scale assessed autonomy and treatment satisfaction at inclusion. Clinical events were evaluated using exposure-based incidence rates, supplemented by weighted marginal structural models and propensity-score-adjusted Cox sensitivity analyses restricted to patients receiving a single anticoagulant strategy. Results: Among 1901 patients, 428 received VKAs and 1473 DOACs at enrolment. Mean exposure duration was 7.6 years for VKAs and 3.8 years for DOACs. Adequate VKA control was achieved by 56.2% and 59.0% using the direct and Rosendaal methods, respectively. Reduced DOAC doses were recorded in 24.8% of apixaban, 54.7% of dabigatran, 26.9% of edoxaban, and 21.9% of rivaroxaban users; appropriateness could not be assessed for every patient. Overall, 395 patients (20.8%) received both strategies. DOAC users reported greater treatment satisfaction. Unadjusted exposure-based incidence rate ratios (DOAC/VKA) were 1.75 (95% CI 1.05-2.92) for stroke, 1.78 (95% CI 1.06-3.00) for ischemic stroke, 1.64 (95% CI 0.97-2.79) for myocardial infarction, and 3.68 (95% CI 1.81-7.46) for major bleeding. In weighted marginal structural models, adjusted incidence rate ratios (DOAC/VKA) were 1.627 (95% CI 0.785-3.375) for stroke and 6.725 (95% CI 2.106-21.473) for major bleeding. A propensity-score-adjusted Cox sensitivity analysis excluding treatment switchers (n = 1492) yielded corresponding hazard ratios of 2.577 (95% CI 0.930-7.144; p = 0.069) and 8.298 (95% CI 3.180-21.649; p < 0.001), respectively. Conclusions: RACOVIR shows substantial heterogeneity in anticoagulation management in Spanish Primary Care. DOACs predominated and were associated with greater patient-reported satisfaction, while suboptimal INR control remained common with VKAs. Although adjusted analyses suggested higher major bleeding rates during DOAC exposure, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the observational design, potential selection bias, treatment switching, and residual confounding. No causal conclusions regarding comparative anticoagulant safety or effectiveness can be established.

title: Net Clinical Benefit of Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion After Intracerebral Hemorrhage in Atrial Fibrillation: A Focused Review and Benchmark-Adjusted Secondary Analysis.
text: Background/Objectives: Atrial fibrillation (AF) after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) creates a therapeutic conflict: withholding oral anticoagulation may increase ischemic stroke risk, whereas resumption of anticoagulation may increase recurrent ICH. Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) offers a nonpharmacologic alternative, but isolated stroke or bleeding rates do not describe the overall benefit-harm balance. This focused review examines net clinical benefit (NCB) as a decision framework for LAAO after ICH and presents a secondary benchmark-adjusted analysis derived from our prior systemaatic review and meta-analysis. Methods: Thirteen endocardial LAAO cohorts with complete data for ischemic stroke, recurrent ICH, major bleeding, and all-cause death contributed to the analysis. The component event data and prespecified severity weights were carried forward from the prior meta-analysis; the external benchmark comparison, study-level benchmark-adjusted NCB synthesis, and benchmark-sensitivity analyses were not part of that report and constitute the distinct secondary analysis presented here. Results: Prespecified external benchmark rates were 8.0, 2.0, 3.0, and 6.0 events per 100 patient-years, respectively. Unweighted and severity-weighted NCB were evaluated using both pooled-rate and study-level Hartung-Knapp random-effects approaches. Study-level pooled NCB was 12.20 events per 100 patient-years (95% CI, 8.61-15.79; I2 = 96%), and weighted NCB was 14.39 (95% CI, 8.84-19.94; I2 = 94%). Additional two-component analyses using PRESTIGE-AF reference rates yielded unweighted NCB estimates of 5.65 and 2.06 events per 100 patient-years for no-OAC and DOAC comparator scenarios, respectively. Excluding all-cause mortality from the original model yielded an unweighted NCB of 8.41. These exploratory results highlight the sensitivity of NCB estimates to comparator selection and endpoint composition. Conclusions: Contemporary randomized evidence, including PRESTIGE-AF, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, reinforces that benefit-harm balance is population-, comparator-, endpoint-, and time-horizon-dependent. Accordingly, these NCB estimates should be interpreted as decision-analytic and hypothesis-generating rather than causal treatment effects. ICH-specific randomized comparisons remain essential.

title: Left Atrial Appendage Thrombus and Long-Term Clinical Outcomes in Anticoagulated Patients with Atrial Fibrillation and Atrial Flutter Referred for a Rhythm-Control Strategy: A Prospective Observational Cohort Study.
text: Background/Objectives: Whether long-term prognosis differs between patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and those with atrial flutter (AFL) after adjustment for baseline cardiovascular characteristics remains unclear. Methods: In this prospective observational cohort study, we enrolled 656 patients meeting predefined anticoagulation eligibility criteria with AF (n = 558) or AFL (n = 98) who underwent transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) before a planned rhythm-control intervention. The primary endpoint was left atrial appendage thrombus (LAAT) detected at the index TEE. Long-term outcomes included cardiovascular death, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, myocardial infarction, and systemic thromboembolism. Results: LAAT was detected in 14.2% of patients with AF and 10.2% of patients with AFL (p = 0.29). After multivariable adjustment, AFL versus AF was not independently associated with LAAT (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.25-1.11; p = 0.09). Median follow-up was 6.85 (3.64-8.53) years. Cardiovascular death occurred in 96 patients (14.6%; AF: n = 78, AFL: n = 18), and HF hospitalization occurred in 91 patients (13.9%; AF: n = 78, AFL: n = 13). Log-rank comparisons were not statistically significant for cardiovascular death (log-rank p = 0.42) or HF hospitalization (log-rank p = 0.73). In extended Cox models that accounted for nonproportional hazards, AFL versus AF was not independently associated with cardiovascular death (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.09; 95% CI, 0.64-1.85; p = 0.75) or HF hospitalization (aHR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.37-1.27; p = 0.23). Conclusions: Catheter ablation was recorded in 83.7% of AFL versus 24.6% of AF patients, including index-hospitalization ablation in 46.9% versus 0%, respectively. In this selected cohort meeting predefined anticoagulation eligibility criteria referred for TEE-guided rhythm control, no statistically significant independent association was detected between index arrhythmia type (AF versus AFL) and LAAT, cardiovascular death, or HF hospitalization. Importantly, these findings describe associations under markedly different subsequent rhythm-control treatment pathways and do not establish equivalent intrinsic risks for AF and AFL. The smaller AFL group (n = 98) and wide confidence intervals limit precision; clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded. These findings should not be extrapolated to unselected AF/AFL populations, including asymptomatic patients, those managed exclusively with rate control, or patients not receiving anticoagulation. The comparison is based on presenting arrhythmia, not a rhythm phenotype confirmed to persist throughout follow-up; incident AF among patients initially presenting with AFL was not systematically ascertained.

title: Chronological Magnetic Resonance Angiography Demonstration of Spontaneous Posterior Cerebral Artery Recanalization: Unmasking Cardioembolic Stroke and Postprandial Atrial Fibrillation Mislabeled as Dumping Syndrome.
text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and post-gastrectomy dumping syndrome share overlapping symptoms, such as palpitations, dizziness, and chest discomfort, making them clinically difficult to distinguish. We report a case where anchoring bias led both the patient and clinicians to misattribute postprandial symptoms to dumping syndrome, until a cardioembolic stroke unmasked latent AF. A 63-year-old man with a history of distal gastrectomy performed 5 years prior developed postprandial palpitations, chest discomfort, and dizziness triggered by rapid eating or cold drinks. A prior facility had empirically attributed these episodes to dumping syndrome without cardiac evaluation. Initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm. The next day, he developed acute diplopia and ptosis due to left oculomotor nerve palsy. Brain MRI demonstrated a left medial midbrain infarction, and MR angiography (MRA) showed 99% stenosis of the left P1 segment. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated left atrial enlargement and decreased left atrial appendage flow velocity with spontaneous echo contrast. Continuous electrocardiographic telemetry post-dinner captured paroxysmal AF, unmasking the arrhythmia. His CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores were calculated as 3 and 2, respectively. He was treated with anticoagulants and discharged with mild sequelae (modified Rankin Scale score 1). Follow-up MRA at 3 months showed complete recanalization of the P1 segment. This chronological MRA sequence provided visual proof differentiating cardioembolism from fixed intracranial atherosclerosis.

title: Apixaban Benefit in Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation Accounting for Competing Risks: A Reanalysis of the ARTESIA Trial.
text: In the ARTESIA trial, apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism compared with aspirin in patients with subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF), but the primary analysis treated death and AF progression as censoring rather than competing events. We estimated the absolute risk reduction (ARR) at 3.5 years treating death and AF progression as competing events. We used event-level data reconstructed from published Kaplan-Meier curves to probabilistically impute status and timing of competing events. The ARR was 1.94% when treating death and AF progression as censoring events vs. 1.62% treating them as competing events (difference 0.33 percentage points; 95% CI 0.04 to 0.62). Absolute benefit estimates depend on how competing events are handled. Competing risk analyses can provide more realistic estimates of expected therapeutic benefit at the point of treatment decisions when competing events are common.

title: Atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease - treatment standard.
text: The prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF) is high among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). While patients with CKD Stages G1 - G3b may be treated similarly to patients without CKD, little evidence guides therapeutic strategies for CKD G4 - G5 patients. Dosing of most drugs used for rate and rhythm control requires adjustment to kidney function. Recurrence rates after cardioversion and ablation for rhythm control are higher in patients with advanced CKD than those without it. Regarding the prevention of stroke and systemic embolism, the benefit-to-risk ratio of oral anticoagulation (OAC) is disputed among patients with CKD stages G4 - G5 with AF, in particular among those receiving hemodialysis given their high risk for severe bleeding events. Novel strategies for stroke and systemic embolism prevention, particularly factor XI inhibitors and left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), have not yet fulfilled their initial promise as safe and effective alternatives.
source: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association

title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure in Atrial Fibrillation Patients With High Risk of Stroke and Bleeding: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
text: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is increasingly used as an alternative to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Its comparative effectiveness and safety in patients at a high risk of both stroke and bleeding remain uncertain. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of LAAC vs contemporary medical therapy in a high-risk population using individual participant data from randomized trials. Bibliographic databases and trial registries through August 5, 2026, were searched for randomized trials comparing percutaneous LAAC with contemporary medical therapy in populations with a trial-level mean CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥4. A 1-stage common-effect analysis used Cox models stratified by trial and adjusted for age, sex, CHA2DS2-VASc score, and HAS-BLED score. Both primary outcomes were time to first stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/unknown death (efficacy) and time to first major bleeding (safety). A flexible time-varying Cox model was used for major bleeding. The protocol was submitted to PROSPERO (CRD420261335972). CLOSURE-AF (Left Atrial Appendage CLOSURE in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Compared to Medical Therapy) and PRAGUE-17 (Left Atrial Appendage Closure vs. Novel Anticoagulation Agents in Atrial Fibrillation) contributed 1,290 participants (647 assigned to LAAC and 643 to control). Median age was 77.3 years (Q1-Q3: 71.4-81.9 years), and 809 participants (62.7%) were men. The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 142 LAAC participants (21.9%) and 133 control subjects (20.7%) (adjusted HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.77-1.24; P = 0.842). Major bleeding occurred in 86 LAAC participants (13.3%) and 80 control subjects (12.4%) (adjusted HR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.75-1.39; P = 0.874). The treatment effect on major bleeding varied over time (P for treatment-by-time interaction < 0.001), with a cumulative major bleeding incidence of 9.4% with LAAC vs 6.0% with control (absolute risk difference, 3.4 percentage points; 95% CI: 0.4-6.3 percentage points) at 1 year and 13.2% vs 12.1% (absolute risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI: -2.8 to 5.0 percentage points) at 3 years. In high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation, no statistically significant difference was detected between LAAC and contemporary medical therapy for the primary efficacy outcome or major bleeding. The major bleeding hazard varied over time, with higher early and lower later conditional hazard estimates; however, a cumulative bleeding benefit was not demonstrated by 3 years. Long-term randomized data are needed to improve the precision of later treatment-effect estimates.
source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation: Navigating Heterogeneity in Clinical Evidence: JACC Evidence Review.
text: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation for preventing stroke or systemic embolism in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) based on several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that collectively enrolled >7,000 participants. In this JACC Evidence Review, we interpret the major RCTs as distinct experiments, clarify what each can and cannot establish, and offer a phenotype-based framework for interpreting the evidence. The most recent RCTs, OPTION, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, have prompted efforts to pool the evidence into a single summary estimate. However, these trials are not one coherent evidence base; they are distinct clinical experiments that asked different questions. They differ in patient phenotype, comparator, device generation, postprocedure antithrombotic regimen, endpoint construction, and follow-up duration. Study-level meta-analysis of published reports remains methodologically valid for estimating the broad direction of effect of a device class, but when the component trials differ materially in patient phenotype, comparator, and outcome construction, the pooled estimate does not map to a common patient group or treatment decision. Patient eligibility as well as thromboembolic and bleeding risk varied markedly across trials. In addition, device technology has progressed, and comparators have evolved from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. Heterogeneity and insufficient details also exist about the antithrombotic therapy regimen in LAAC arms and adjunct antiplatelet therapy in control arms. Methodological issues further complicate interpretation, including the use of bleeding events (ie, the putative ancillary benefit of LAAC compared with anticoagulation) within composite endpoints tested for noninferiority, varying noninferiority margins, analytical approaches that may undermine the interpretation of noninferiority, and exclusion of periprocedural bleeding from primary safety endpoints in some trials. Finally, the standard of care for anticoagulation in AF has evolved, obviating concomitant aspirin use in stable individuals on therapeutic anticoagulation, thereby reducing bleeding risk compared with that of the control arm of LAAC RCTs. For most anticoagulation-eligible patients, anticoagulation remains the preferred first-line strategy. LAAC is a reasonable option when long-term anticoagulation is unsafe or unsustainable provided that procedural risk, adjunct antithrombotic feasibility, surveillance needs, and competing mortality are carefully considered. RCT evidence in this latter population is limited, and RCTs in other populations have features that limit their support for LAAC as an alternative to anticoagulation. Because LAAC and anticoagulation offer different types of risk, aligning the most applicable evidence with patient values through shared decision-making is central to care.
source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

title: Comparison of Outcomes Between Men and Women Treated With Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Oral Anticoagulation After Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation: An OPTION Subanalysis.
text: Women sex is an established, nonmodifiable risk factor for adverse outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has been proposed as an alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in patients with AF; however, there are limited data on sex-based outcomes of LAAC following catheter ablation. This study sought to compare outcomes of LAAC vs OAC after AF ablation in men and women. Patients with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women were randomized 1:1 to either ablation + LAAC or ablation + OAC. The primary safety endpoint was nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding at 36 months. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months. The study included 1,053 men and 546 women. LAAC and OAC demonstrated comparable primary efficacy events in men (HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.56-1.65; P = 0.88) and women (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.41-1.62; P = 0.55), with no treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.71). Procedural complication rates were similar at 2.3% in men and 3.7% in women with only 1 pericardial effusion in each group, not related to the index LAAC procedure. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint was significantly lower in the device group among men (HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.23-0.50; P < 0.0001). In women, a similar but nonsignificant trend was observed (HR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0.42-1.09; P = 0.11), with a significant treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.02). No significant difference was seen in the secondary safety endpoint across both treatment arms for either sex. In this prespecified analysis of the OPTION (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]) trial, stroke, systemic embolism, and mortality outcomes were not significantly different between LAAC and OAC following AF ablation in either men or women. Compared with OAC, LAAC demonstrated a greater magnitude of major and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding reduction in men as compared with women. (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]; NCT03795298).
source: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

title: New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review of In-Hospital and Post-Discharge Outcomes.
text: This systematic review and meta-analysis determines the incidence of new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in critically ill patients, risks of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism, anticoagulation therapy, and the proportion diagnosed with AF post-discharge. A search of registered databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL) was performed from inception to April 20, 2026. Eligible studies included critically ill patients (≥ 18 yr old) who developed NOAF during admission to general ICUs or high-dependency units. NOAF was defined as AF in patients without prior history of AF. Data were independently extracted from full-text versions of included studies by nonblinded reviewers. A Bayesian meta-analysis was conducted on 54 studies (367,896 patients) with a random-effects model using R (Version 4.3.3). Pooled incidence of NOAF in critically ill patients was 10.6% (95% credible interval [CrI], 8.6-12.9%). Absolute risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism was 7.1% (95% CrI, 4.5-11.0%), changing to 6.9% (95% CrI, 4.2-11.6%) after age and sex adjustment. Evidence from six studies reports that critically ill patients with NOAF had 1.94 times (95% CrI, 1.23-3.29) higher relative risk of systemic thromboembolism post-discharge than patients without NOAF, rising to 2.01 (95% CrI, 1.54-2.80) with adjustment. Absolute and relative risk are evaluated with follow-up durations ranging from 1.5 months to 5 years, with variable anticoagulation exposure. Anticoagulation rates were low: 32.9% in-hospital (95% CrI, 14.6-57.9%) and 35.9% post-discharge (95% CrI, 19.7-55.9%). On follow-up, 23.9% (95% CrI, 13.9-38.5%) of critically ill patients with NOAF were subsequently diagnosed with AF. Our review suggests that NOAF during critical illness is associated with significantly increased risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism and subsequent AF diagnosis. However, rates of anticoagulation initiation remain low, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification and targeted strategies post-discharge.

title: Early Direct Oral Anticoagulant Initiation After Intracranial Hemorrhage Among Japanese Patients With Nonvalvular Atrial Fibrillation: SAFE-ICH Registry 12-Month Outcomes.
text: Understanding the effects of early direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) (re)initiation after intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) in atrial fibrillation is crucial. Previous 30-day outcomes in the SAFE-ICH Registry showed acceptable ischemic/hemorrhagic risks; therefore, we evaluated the 12-month outcomes. The SAFE-ICH Registry, a prospective, observational cohort study conducted at 32 hospitals in Japan, included 240 patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) who experienced ICH and in whom DOAC therapy was (re)initiated ≤14 days after ICH. Short-term (≤30 days) and long-term (≤12 months) ischemic/hemorrhagic outcomes were investigated. Data were collected through clinical assessments, imaging or telephone interviews over 12 months. The 12-month composite outcome incidence (symptomatic ICH, any stroke, all-cause death) was 22.5% (29.1/100 person-years). The secondary outcome incidence was 6.3% (7.9/100 person-years) for symptomatic ICH, 6.7% (8.4/100 person-years) for any stroke (ischemic: 2.9% [3.6/100 person-years]; hemorrhagic: 3.8% [4.6/100 person-years]), and 14.2% (17.3/100 person-years) for all-cause death. The major bleeding incidence was 6.7% (8.4/100 person-years). Hemorrhagic stroke first appeared approximately 3 months after DOAC (re)initiation, and by month 10, its rate was comparable to that of ischemic stroke. Most deaths were due to aspiration pneumonia. Early DOAC (re)initiation after ICH in NVAF was associated with a numerically higher long-term hemorrhagic than ischemic stroke risk. These risks warrant careful consideration when determining the optimal DOAC duration and timing after ICH.

title: Warfarin anticoagulation control and risks of cerebral small vessel disease and cognitive impairment among elderly patients with ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation: a retrospective cohort study.
text: This study applied individual exposure metrics derived from population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PopPK/PD) modelling to investigate the associations between warfarin anticoagulation quality, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) burden, and cognitive outcomes among older adults with ischemic stroke and non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF). We included 300 patients aged ≥65 years with ischemic stroke and AF who had received warfarin for ≥3 months between January and December 2025. A nonlinear mixed-effects model was used to estimate individualized pharmacokinetic parameters and steady-state exposure metrics. Multivariable regression was performed to assess the associations of these metrics with CSVD burden, cognitive impairment, and the composite endpoint; the ability to identify high CSVD burden was compared between model-derived exposure metrics and conventional anticoagulation quality metrics, including time in therapeutic range (TTR) and international normalized ratio (INR) variability. Steady-state average concentration (Cavgss) was significantly positively associated with CSVD burden (per 100 ng/mL increment: OR = 1.32, p < 0.001), whereas TTR was not associated with burden (p = 0.444). High CSVD burden was significantly associated with cognitive impairment (Cox HR = 2.04, p = 0.007). The incidence of cognitive impairment increased stepwise across exposure tertiles (42.2%, 54.0%, and 75.4%, p < 0.001). The composite endpoint occurred significantly more often in patients with INR standard deviation (INR_SD) > 0.5 (p = 0.009). For identifying high CSVD burden, PopPK/PD-derived exposure parameters demonstrated differing within-cohort discrimination for identifying high CSVD burden: steady-state peak concentration (Cmaxss), Cavgss, and degree of fluctuation (DF) (AUC = 0.695, 0.679, and 0.651, respectively), with better discrimination compared with INR_SD and TTR (AUC = 0.557 and 0.493, respectively; p < 0.05). Within this cohort, PopPK/PD-derived individualized exposure parameters showed better discrimination for identifying patients with high CSVD burden compared with traditional TTR and INR variability, although discriminative ability remained modest for all markers, including those whose anticoagulation quality appeared adequate by conventional metrics. These findings provide a pharmacological foundation for refined anticoagulation quality assessment in this high-risk elderly population.

title: Oral anticoagulation with or without antiplatelet therapy for secondary stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation and atherosclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: Patients with ischemic stroke (IS), atrial fibrillation (AF), and atherosclerosis have an increased risk of recurrent ischemic events. Addition of antiplatelet therapy (APT) to oral anticoagulant therapy (OAC) may offer additional protection against these events, at the cost of an increased risk of bleeding. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of combined antithrombotic therapy versus OAC alone in this population. PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from inception through September 2026 for randomized controlled trials and observational studies comparing OAC plus APT versus OAC alone in adults with IS, AF, and atherosclerosis. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251164174). Seven studies (4 retrospective, 2 prospective, 1 randomized trial; n= 9,924) were included. Combined therapy was not associated with a reduction in vascular composite outcome (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.61-1.96), recurrent IS (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91-1.16), major bleeding (HR 1.17, 95% CI 0.86-1.59), or all-cause mortality (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.60-1.36). In the subgroup with intracranial or extracranial atherosclerosis, combined therapy showed no significant difference in vascular composite risk (HR 1.67, 95% CI 0.83-3.33). Combined antithrombotic therapy with OAC plus APT was not associated with a reduction in recurrent IS, vascular composite outcome, major bleeding, or all-cause mortality in patients with IS, AF, and atherosclerosis. In patients with intracranial or extracranial atherosclerosis, combined therapy was not associated with a significant difference in the risk of the vascular composite outcome. These findings suggest that the addition of APT to OAC should be approached with caution in this population, and may be best reserved for select clinical contexts.

title: Oral anticoagulation therapy in nonagenarian patients with atrial fibrillation: usage patterns, predictors, and in-hospital outcomes from a single-center retrospective study.
text: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is highly prevalent in nonagenarians (≥ 90 years). However, this group is often excluded from clinical trials, leaving limited real-world evidence on oral anticoagulant (OAC) use, safety, and efficacy. This study sought to investigate the usage patterns, predictors, and in-hospital outcomes of OAC therapy in nonagenarian patients with AF to provide real-world evidence to inform clinical decision-making. A retrospective single-center analysis was conducted on 290 nonagenarian AF patients (Beijing Hospital, 2018-2024). Patients were grouped as OAC (n = 89) or non-OAC (n = 201). In-hospital stroke/SE (efficacy) and major bleeding (ISTH criteria; safety). Secondary endpoints included in-hospital composite efficacy, net clinical benefit (stroke/SE/major bleeding/all-cause death), and all-cause death. Multivariate logistic regression identified OAC predictors; OAC temporal trends were analyzed. The overall OAC utilization rate was 30.69% and showed a steady annual increase. Positive predictors of OAC use included a history of ischemic stroke (OR = 2.653) and heart failure (OR = 2.083), while negative predictors included bedridden status (OR = 0.134), and concomitant antiplatelet use (OR = 0.203). DOAC accounted for 82.02% of OAC prescription, and 63.01% of DOAC users were inappropriately underdosed. Compared with the non-OAC group, OAC use was significantly associated with a lower risk of in-hospital stroke/SE (6.74% vs. 15.42%, OR = 0.396, 95% CI = 0.159-0.987, p = 0.047) and improved secondary composite efficacy outcomes (OR = 0.491, p = 0.024). The OAC group also demonstrated a numerically lower incidence of net clinical benefit outcomes (20.22% vs. 30.85%), though it did not differ significantly between groups (2.25% vs. 0.50%, p = 0.215), though total bleeding events were higher in the OAC group (49.44% vs. 36.32%, p = 0.037). Although the overall OAC utilization rate in AF patients aged ≥ 90 years remains relatively low, it has shown a steady annual increase, with DOACs emerging as the predominant choice. OAC therapy is significantly associated with a lower risk of in-hospital stroke and demonstrates favorable net clinical benefit, highlighting the potential value of the judicious use of OAC in this population. title: The prognostic role of echocardiographic parameters in ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation.
text: Concomitant cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) in stroke patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) is associated with an unfavourable outcome, but the additional prognostic value of echocardiographic parameters remains unclear. We included consecutive patients with recent AF-associated ischemic stroke (IS) or transient ischemic attack (TIA) who underwent echocardiography and brain MRI from the prospective Novel Oral Anticoagulants in Ischemic Stroke Patients registry. We examined associations of left atrial and ventricular echocardiographic parameters with a primary composite outcome (recurrent IS; intracranial hemorrhage, all-cause death) and its components as secondary outcomes, using unadjusted and adjusted (age, sex, modified CHA2DS2VASc-Score, hyperlipidemia, oral anticoagulation before/after stroke, MRI markers of cSVD) Cox regression. Associations between echocardiographic parameters and MRI markers of cSVD were analyzed using logistic regression. We included 690 patients (median age 80, 45% female) with a total follow-up of 1084 patient-years. In unadjusted analyses, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) was associated with the composite outcome (HR 1.44 [1.05-1.97]) and all-cause death (HR 1.95 [1.33-2.84]), neither association persisted after adjustment (aHR 1.04 [0.74-1.46]; aHR 1.29 [0.85-1.96]) Reduced ejection fraction and concentric/eccentric hypertrophy were associated with all-cause death in unadjusted analysis only. No echocardiographic parameter was associated with recurrent IS. Left atrial dilatation (OR 1.96 [1.32-2.91]) and concentric hypertrophy were associated (OR 1.68 [1.08-2.62]) with white matter hyperintensities extent in unadjusted but not in adjusted analyses. In stroke patients with AF, structural changes of the left ventricle might be considered as indicator but not independent predictor of future cerebrovascular events or death. NCT03826927.

title: Sepsis-associated atrial fibrillation: Current insights and research priorities for standardized care.
text: Sepsis-associated atrial fibrillation (SAAF) is a common but serious complication in critically ill patients that is characterized by new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF) during sepsis. This secondary type of arrhythmia typically resolves with sepsis treatment but is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, including prolonged hospital stays, high recurrence rates of AF, and increased risks of heart failure, stroke, and short-term and long-term mortality. In contrast to primary AF, no standardized guidelines have been established for SAAF. To support the development of evidence-based protocols, we conducted a comprehensive review to synthesize the current knowledge of SAAF. Here, we highlight the definition, incidence, and risk factors of SAAF and distinguish it from primary AF and other types of secondary AF, including postoperative and post-myocardial infarction AF. We also describe the multifactorial pathophysiologic mechanisms of SAAF involving systemic inflammation, cytokine release, autonomic dysfunction, myocardial injury, and hemodynamic stress. Key outcomes of patients with SAAF and other types of secondary AF are compared, including in-hospital mortality, long-term AF recurrence, and stroke risk. Furthermore, we discuss various management strategies for SAAF, including methods of rhythm control and rate control in patients with SAAF. Anticoagulation recommendations and challenges for patients with SAAF are highlighted, particularly with respect to thrombotic risk, bleeding risk, and anticoagulation use. We propose a process for anticoagulation decisions in SAAF, which are challenging due to the dynamic interplay between sepsis-induced coagulopathy and thromboembolic risk. Finally, we provide a summary of future research priorities to support large-scale, multicenter trials to define evidence-based protocols that are critical for improving outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Revisiting the role of sex in stroke risk stratification in atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text: The 2024 European Society of Cardiology guidelines introduced the CHA2DS2-VA score, omitting female sex from stroke risk stratification in atrial fibrillation (AF). However, evidence on the relative predictive performance of CHA2DS2-VA versus CHA2DS2-VASc across diverse populations remains inconsistent. We therefore conducted a systematic evaluation of their discrimination and reclassification performance. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational cohort studies comparing CHA2DS2-VA and CHA2DS2-VASc for prediction of ischaemic stroke or thromboembolic events in patients with AF. Discrimination was evaluated using the difference in C-statistics (ΔAUC) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI), and reclassification using continuous net reclassification improvement (NRI). Pooled estimates were derived using random-effects models. Seven studies including 250,112 patients were analysed. In the overall population, discriminative performance was comparable between the CHA2DS2-VA and CHA2DS2-VASc scores (ΔAUC 0.00065, 95% CI -0.00288 to 0.00417; IDI 0.00010, 95% CI -0.00063 to 0.00083). Continuous NRI indicated a modest advantage for CHA2DS2-VASc (-0.05615; 95% CI: -0.10350 to -0.00880). Among patients not receiving oral anticoagulation, both discrimination and reclassification were similar between the two scores. Variability in reclassification performance was observed across regions and study periods. The CHA2DS2-VA and CHA2DS2-VASc scores showed comparable discrimination for stroke risk prediction in patients with AF when evaluated as continuous scores, although reclassification modestly favoured the CHA2DS2-VASc score. The clinical contribution of female sex to risk prediction appears context-dependent and warrants further evaluation.

title: Online information seeking behaviour and health outcomes among patients with hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia (the 'three highs'): a scoping review protocol.
text: Hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia are collectively referred to as ‘three highs’ in China. They act independently and synergistically, significantly contributing to cardiovascular disease and mortality. Many patients with the ‘three highs’ lack awareness of their conditions and risk factors, leading to poor self-management and underuse of healthcare. Online information seeking (OIS) behaviour may improve patients’ health literacy, promote early diagnosis, treatment and behavioural improvements, thus controlling the onset and progression of the ‘three highs’. To date, no review has synthesised the relationship between OIS behaviour and health outcomes in these patients. This scoping review will systematically examine the relationship between OIS behaviour and health outcomes in patients with the ‘three highs’ for the first time, encompassing three major dimensions: physiological health, behavioural health and mortality risk. According to the framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and enhanced by Levac et al, systematic searches will be conducted across five electronic databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, EBSCO and the Cochrane Library) as well as grey literature. The searches will cover database inception to 20 September 2026. Data will be charted and extracted based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews. The findings of the study will be presented through narrative analysis, tables and figures. This scoping review is based on published and publicly available data. Therefore, ethics approval is not required. The findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conference presentations, public engagement activities and a plain-language summary for patient and public audiences. The scoping review protocol has been registered in the Open Science Framework on 19 November 2025: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/KXR9W.

title: Beyond anticoagulation: defining the role of left atrial appendage closure in stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation.
text: Oral anticoagulation has a very strong evidence base for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) at elevated thromboembolic risk. Direct oral anticoagulants have improved the safety and convenience of treatment, yet important limitations remain, including residual ischaemic stroke, major bleeding, treatment discontinuation, and patient refusal. Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) offers an alternative strategy for selected patients by excluding the principal anatomical source of AF-related cardiac thrombi. However, the appropriate role of LAAC remains controversial, particularly in patients who can and do tolerate anticoagulation. This viewpoint argues for a more individualized approach that distinguishes absolute contraindications from modifiable bleeding risks, treatment refusal or non-persistence, and stroke occurring despite adequate anticoagulation.

title: The Construction and Validation of a Machine Learning Model for Major Depressive Disorder Based on Astrocytes and Mitochondrial Dynamics.
text: Astrocytes play an important role in depression. However, their specific mechanisms, especially their subcellular mechanisms, remain unclear. We aimed to identify key genes associated with mitochondrial dynamics and astrocytes in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), construct a diagnostic prediction model, and elucidate their regulatory mechanisms in neuroinflammation. Depression-related transcriptome datasets were retrieved from the GEO database. Overlapping differentially expressed genes between mitochondrial dynamics-related and astrocytes-associated genes were screened, followed by functional enrichment analysis. Machine learning algorithms were employed to establish a diagnostic model and identify hub genes. An LPS-induced mouse depression model was established, and depressive-like phenotypes were assessed through behavioral tests. Hub gene expression was validated by using quantitative real-time PCR and Western blotting. A machine learning model with favorable diagnostic performance was constructed. LPS markedly upregulated hexokinase 2 (HK2) and ribosomal protein S7 (RPS7) expression in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, suggesting that glycolytic metabolism and ribosomal function contribute to LPS-induced neuropathological changes. HK2 and RPS7 were identified and validated as crucial hub genes responsive to neuroinflammation. The combined action of mitochondrial dynamics and astrocyte metabolic abnormalities may play a key role in depression's pathogenesis, providing novel candidate biomarkers and theoretical support for the molecular diagnosis of MDD and anti-inflammatory targeted therapy.

title: Effectiveness of metformin as initial treatment on the metabolic profile of Saudi patients newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus: A prospective observational study.
text: The incidence of diabetes is increasing in several countries, including Saudi Arabia. Metformin is a common treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); however, its effect on the metabolic profile of patients newly diagnosed with T2DM remains unclear. To evaluate the effects of metformin on the metabolic profile, including hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) and lipid levels, in patients newly diagnosed with T2DM in Madinah, Saudi Arabia. This prospective observational study involved 82 participants newly diagnosed with T2DM. The participants were aged between 30 and 65 years, and their HbA1c level was ≥6.5% higher than the normal range. None of them had taken any oral hypoglycemic medication before metformin treatment. Fourteen patients did not undergo regular follow-ups. A total of 68 patients completed the study. The primary outcomes were changes in HbA1c, cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and hepatic enzyme marker levels. The HbA1c level significantly reduced after the 12-week treatment period (6.85% vs 7.29% at baseline, P = .001). Furthermore, 67.3% of the patients exhibited a noteworthy decrease in cholesterol (4.68 vs 5.18 mmol/L at baseline, P = .014) and LDL levels (3.03 vs 3.52 mmol/L at baseline, P = .006). However, no significant changes were observed in the levels of the other lipid profile markers. Various dosages of metformin showed comparable effects in reducing HbA1c, cholesterol, and LDL levels, but inconsistent effects on hepatic enzymes. The results suggest that metformin can be considered an initial treatment option for patients newly diagnosed with T2DM. These findings are significant given the increasing prevalence of diabetes in Saudi Arabia and the need for effective and safe treatment options. Further studies are required to explore the pharmacogenomics and metabolomics of metformin in this specific population.

title: Adjunct Corticosteroids in Children With Community-Acquired Pneumonia Presenting to the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
text: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a leading reason for acute pediatric presentation, and the exuberant host inflammatory response that characterizes severe disease has prompted interest in adjunct systemic corticosteroids. We systematically reviewed and, where feasible, meta-analyzed the randomized evidence in children. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, the Excerpta Medica database (Embase), the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov for randomized controlled trials comparing adjunct systemic corticosteroids plus standard care against standard care or placebo in children (<18 years) with CAP. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool for randomized trials. Outcomes reported by more than one trial were pooled with random-effects models, with sensitivity analyses across alternative variance estimators; medians were converted to means using an established conversion method. Trial-specific primary outcomes were synthesized narratively. Three trials (251 children) were included. Each reported a significant benefit on its own primary outcome: shorter fever duration and fewer complications with methylprednisolone in severe CAP; shorter time to recovery with dexamethasone in parapneumonic effusion; and lower early treatment failure with dexamethasone in severe CAP. Pooled length of hospital stay favored corticosteroids (mean difference -2.10 days, 95% CI -6.79 to 2.59), with substantial heterogeneity reflecting differing clinical settings (I² = 91%). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups (risk ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.85). Corticosteroids were well tolerated, with transient hyperglycemia the most common adverse effect. Across three small, clinically heterogeneous randomized trials, adjunct systemic corticosteroids improved each trial's own primary outcome and were well tolerated. Because the trials were few, diverse in population and regimen, and imprecise when pooled, the current evidence is preliminary and hypothesis-generating and is insufficient to support routine use. The consistent, favorable signal supports adequately powered, phenotype-enriched pediatric trials with harmonized outcomes.
